appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.43; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: The notice of an application to pass accounts, issued by the court after the estate trustee files the accounts and other material. It states the relief sought, the grounds, and the documentary evidence to be used.
appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.44; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: Served and filed by a person who was served with the accounts documents and wishes to object to the accounts.
appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.45; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: A request for further notice in a passing of accounts, served on the applicant and filed with proof of service.
appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.45.1; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: A notice of no objection to the accounts, one of the documents the Public Guardian and Trustee or the Children's Lawyer, when served in a passing of accounts for a person it represents, serves on the applicant and files.
appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.46; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: A notice of non-participation in a passing of accounts, one of the documents the Public Guardian and Trustee or the Children's Lawyer, when served for a person it represents, serves on the applicant and files.
appears_in: Forms guide, Form 74.46.1; the case forms page card for the same form

current_text: An affidavit of the applicant or their lawyer, filed to seek judgment on a passing of accounts without a hearing, stating that copies of the accounts went to those who asked, the objection period has expired, and no objection was received or any objection was withdrawn.

current_text: Time limits for starting a court case
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: This guide explains the time limits in Ontario's Limitations Act, 2002 for starting a court case, and the family law time limits the site has a source for. Other family law time limits (for example, under the Divorce Act or the Children's Law Reform Act) are not covered here because the site has not yet reviewed a source for them.
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: The basic limitation period
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: The Limitations Act, 2002 sets time limits for starting a court proceeding. It applies to “claims pursued in court proceedings”, with listed exceptions, such as proceedings to which the Provincial Offences Act applies and proceedings under the Judicial Review Procedure Act. The Act defines a “claim” as “a claim to remedy an injury, loss or damage that occurred as a result of an act or omission”. (Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 1, 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The basic limitation period"

current_text: The basic rule is in section 4: “Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.” So the starting point for counting is the day the claim was “discovered”, which the Act defines in section 5. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 4)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The basic limitation period"

current_text: The Act also says: “This Act binds the Crown.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 3)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The basic limitation period"

current_text: When a claim is “discovered”
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: A claim is discovered on “the earlier of” two days. First, the day the person with the claim “first knew”: “that the injury, loss or damage had occurred”; that it “was caused by or contributed to by an act or omission”; “that the act or omission was that of the person against whom the claim is made”; and that, “having regard to the nature of the injury, loss or damage, a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 5 (1) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: The second day is “the day on which a reasonable person with the abilities and in the circumstances of the person with the claim first ought to have known” of those same four things. Whichever of the two days comes first is the day the claim is discovered. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 5 (1) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: The Act starts from a presumption. A person with a claim “shall be presumed to have known of the matters referred to in clause (1) (a) on the day the act or omission on which the claim is based took place, unless the contrary is proved.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 5 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: Demand obligations have their own rule. For a demand obligation, the day the injury, loss or damage occurs “is the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.” This applies “in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 5 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: Where a person claims through a predecessor, the person is deemed to know the matters in clause 5 (1) (a) on the earlier of “The day the predecessor first knew or ought to have known of those matters” and “The day the person claiming first knew or ought to have known of them.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 12 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: A similar rule applies to a principal, where the agent had a duty to communicate knowledge of those matters to the principal. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 12 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: A person against whom another person may have a claim “may serve a notice of possible claim on the other person.” A court may consider that notice “in determining when the limitation period in respect of the person's claim began to run.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 14 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: A court may not consider the notice in that way for a person who, when served, is a minor or is incapable, and is not represented by a litigation guardian. The notice is not an acknowledgment under section 13, and “is not an admission of the validity of the claim.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 14 (4), (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "When a claim is “discovered”"

current_text: Attempted resolution and acknowledgments
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: If the person with a claim and the person against whom it is made “have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or assist them in resolving it”, the limitation periods in sections 4 and 15 do not run from the date of the agreement until the claim is resolved, the process is terminated, or a party terminates or withdraws from the agreement. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 11 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Attempted resolution and acknowledgments"

current_text: A person or entity that resolves or assists in resolving claims “on an impartial basis, is an independent third party no matter how it is funded.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 11 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Attempted resolution and acknowledgments"

current_text: If a person acknowledges liability for a claim for “payment of a liquidated sum”, the recovery of personal property, or certain claims about a charge on personal property, the act or omission “shall be deemed to have taken place on the day on which the acknowledgment was made.” For a liquidated sum, this applies even if the person making the acknowledgment “refuses or does not promise to pay”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (1), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Attempted resolution and acknowledgments"

current_text: Limits apply. An acknowledgment counts only if made to the person with the claim, the person's agent, or a bankruptcy official or trustee “before the expiry of the limitation period applicable to the claim.” For the claims in subsection 13 (1), it must be “in writing and signed”. For a liquidated sum, “part payment” has the same effect as a written acknowledgment. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (9), (10), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Attempted resolution and acknowledgments"

current_text: Minors and people who are incapable
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: The basic limitation period “does not run during any time in which the person with the claim” is a minor and “is not represented by a litigation guardian in relation to the claim.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 6)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Minors and people who are incapable"

current_text: It also does not run while the person with the claim “is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim because of his or her physical, mental or psychological condition” and is not represented by a litigation guardian. A person “shall be presumed to have been capable of commencing a proceeding in respect of a claim at all times unless the contrary is proved.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 7 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Minors and people who are incapable"

current_text: If the running of a limitation period is postponed or suspended under section 7 and “has less than six months to run when the postponement or suspension ends, the period is extended to include the day that is six months after the day on which the postponement or suspension ends.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 7 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Minors and people who are incapable"

current_text: If a person is represented by a litigation guardian, section 5 (discovery) “applies as if the litigation guardian were the person with the claim.” If the running of the limitation period is postponed or suspended under section 6 or 7, a potential defendant may also “make an application or a motion to have a litigation guardian appointed for a potential plaintiff”, and the Act sets conditions for when such an appointment ends the suspension. (Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 8, 9 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Minors and people who are incapable"

current_text: The ultimate limitation period
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: Separate from the basic limitation period, section 15 sets an ultimate limitation period. “No proceeding shall be commenced in respect of any claim after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place.” This applies “Even if the limitation period established by any other section of this Act in respect of a claim has not expired”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 15 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The ultimate limitation period"

current_text: The ultimate limitation period does not run while the person with the claim is incapable and not represented by a litigation guardian, is a minor not represented by a litigation guardian, or while the person against whom the claim is made “wilfully conceals” the injury, loss or damage or its cause, or “wilfully misleads the person with the claim” about whether a proceeding is appropriate. “The burden of proving that subsection (4) applies is on the person with the claim.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 15 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The ultimate limitation period"

current_text: For the ultimate limitation period, the day an act or omission takes place is, for “a continuous act or omission, the day on which the act or omission ceases”; for “a series of acts or omissions in respect of the same obligation, the day on which the last act or omission in the series occurs”; and for a demand obligation, “the first day on which there is a failure to perform the obligation, once a demand for the performance is made.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 15 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The ultimate limitation period"

current_text: The demand obligation rule in clause 15 (6) (c) “applies in respect of every demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 15 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The ultimate limitation period"

current_text: A shorter rule applies to one situation: “no proceeding against a purchaser of personal property for value acting in good faith shall be commenced in respect of conversion of the property after the second anniversary of the day on which the property was converted.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 15 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "The ultimate limitation period"

current_text: Claims with no limitation period
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: Section 16 lists proceedings for which “There is no limitation period”. They include “a proceeding for a declaration if no consequential relief is sought”; “a proceeding to enforce an order of a court, or any other order that may be enforced in the same way as an order of a court”; and “a proceeding to obtain support under the Family Law Act”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (a), (b), (c))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Claims with no limitation period"

current_text: The list also includes “a proceeding based on a sexual assault”, and proceedings based on other misconduct of a sexual nature or on an assault where, at the time, the person with the claim was a minor or was in one of the relationships the section describes. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (h), (h.1), (h.2))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Claims with no limitation period"

current_text: Other listed proceedings include certain proceedings to recover money owing to the Crown for “fines, taxes and penalties”, and “a proceeding to recover money owing in respect of student loans, medical resident loans, awards or grants” made under the listed Acts. Section 16 and section 17 “prevail over anything in section 15.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (i), (k), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Claims with no limitation period"

current_text: Separately, “There is no limitation period in respect of an environmental claim that has not been discovered.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 17)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Claims with no limitation period"

current_text: Agreements to extend or change a limitation period
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: The general rule is that “A limitation period under this Act applies despite any agreement to vary or exclude it, subject only to the exceptions in subsections (2) to (6).” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 22 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Agreements to extend or change a limitation period"

current_text: A limitation period other than the ultimate limitation period in section 15 “may be suspended or extended by an agreement made on or after October 19, 2006.” The section 15 period may be suspended or extended by such an agreement “but only if the relevant claim has been discovered.” An agreement made before January 1, 2004 may vary or exclude a limitation period. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 22 (2), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Agreements to extend or change a limitation period"

current_text: Wider exceptions apply “only in respect of business agreements”, meaning an agreement “made by parties none of whom is a consumer as defined in the Consumer Protection Act, 2002”. In those agreements, made on or after October 19, 2006, a limitation period other than the section 15 period “may be varied or excluded”, and the section 15 period may be varied but suspended or extended only as subsection (4) allows. The Act says “vary” includes “extend, shorten and suspend.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 22 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Agreements to extend or change a limitation period"

current_text: Time limits in other laws, adding parties and older claims
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: A limitation period in another Act that applies to a claim under the Limitations Act, 2002 “is of no effect unless” the provision is listed in the Schedule to the Act, or the provision “is in existence on January 1, 2004” and “incorporates by reference a provision listed in the Schedule to this Act.” If a listed provision conflicts with the Act, the listed provision “prevails”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 19 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Time limits in other laws, adding parties and older claims"

current_text: The Act “does not affect the extension, suspension or other variation of a limitation period or other time limit by or under another Act.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 20)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Time limits in other laws, adding parties and older claims"

current_text: “If a limitation period in respect of a claim against a person has expired, the claim shall not be pursued by adding the person as a party to any existing proceeding.” This “does not prevent the correction of a misnaming or misdescription of a party.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 21)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Time limits in other laws, adding parties and older claims"

current_text: Section 24 sets transition rules for claims “based on acts or omissions that took place before January 1, 2004 and in respect of which no proceeding has been commenced before that date.” For example, if the former limitation period expired before January 1, 2004, “no proceeding shall be commenced in respect of the claim.” Section 24 “does not apply to a claim in respect of which clause 16 (1) (h), (h.1) or (h.2) applies.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 24 (2), (2.1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Time limits in other laws, adding parties and older claims"

current_text: Family law time limits
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case

current_text: The Family Law Act sets its own time limit for applications to equalize net family property. An application based on subsection 5 (1) or (2) “shall not be brought after the earliest of” these: “two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity”; “six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; and “six months after the first spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Family law time limits"

current_text: Subsection 7 (3) of the Family Law Act is one of the provisions listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002. Under section 19 of that Act, a listed provision keeps its effect, and it prevails over the Limitations Act, 2002 if the two conflict. Sections 6, 7 and 11 (minors, incapable persons and attempted resolution) “apply, with necessary modifications,” to a limitation period set by a listed provision. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 19 (1), (4), (5), Schedule)
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Family law time limits"

current_text: The Family Law Act lets a court, on motion, “extend a time prescribed by this Act” if it is satisfied that “there are apparent grounds for relief”, that “relief is unavailable because of delay that has been incurred in good faith”, and that “no person will suffer substantial prejudice by reason of the delay.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Family law time limits"

current_text: There is no limitation period for “a proceeding to obtain support under the Family Law Act or to enforce a provision for support or maintenance contained in a contract or agreement that could be filed under section 35 of that Act”. The Limitations Act, 2002 applies to a support application by a dependant's parent or an agency “as if it were made by the dependant himself or herself.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (c); Family Law Act, s. 33 (2.1))
appears_in: Guides, Time limits for starting a court case, "Family law time limits"

current_text: Starting a civil action
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: This guide explains what the Rules of Civil Procedure and the Courts of Justice Act say about starting a case in the Superior Court of Justice, serving it, the time to defend, and what pleadings contain. It also describes the ontario.ca information on filing civil documents online.
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: How a civil proceeding starts
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: Under the rules, “A proceeding shall be commenced by the issuing of an originating process.” The rules also say “Every proceeding in the court shall be by action, except where a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.01 (1), 14.02)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"

current_text: For an action, the originating process is usually “a statement of claim (Form 14A (general) or 14B (mortgage actions))”. An originating process is issued “by the registrar's act of dating, signing and sealing it with the seal of the court and assigning to it a court file number.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (1), 14.07 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"

current_text: The title of the proceeding in an action “shall name the party commencing the action as the plaintiff and the opposite party as the defendant.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.06 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"

current_text: Notice of action and the time to serve a claim
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: “Where there is insufficient time to prepare a statement of claim, an action may be commenced by the issuing of a notice of action (Form 14C) that contains a short statement of the nature of the claim.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"

current_text: Where a notice of action is used, the plaintiff “shall file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within thirty days after the notice of action is issued”. After that, a statement of claim may be filed only with the defendant's written consent or with leave of the court “obtained on notice to the defendant.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"

current_text: “The notice of action shall not be served separately from the statement of claim.” A statement of claim “shall be served within six months after it is issued.” Where the action started with a notice of action, the notice and the statement of claim “shall be served together within six months after the notice of action is issued.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (4), 14.08 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"

current_text: When an application may be used
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: Some proceedings start with a notice of application instead of a statement of claim. “A proceeding may be commenced by an application to the Superior Court of Justice or to a judge of that court, if a statute so authorizes.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"

current_text: The rules also allow an application where the rules authorize it or where the relief claimed is one of a listed set. The list includes “the determination of rights that depend on the interpretation of a deed, will, contract or other instrument”, a remedy under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and any matter “where it is unlikely that there will be any material facts in dispute requiring a trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.05 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"

current_text: In an application, the title names the party starting it “as the applicant and the opposite party, if any, as the respondent and the notice of application shall state the statutory provision or rule, if any, under which the application is made.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.06 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"

current_text: Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says: “An action that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not, despite subsection 11 (2), be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice as provided in the rules of court.” This does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim where the main action was started in the Superior Court of Justice. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1.1), (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit"

current_text: Under the rules, where leave to commence a proceeding is required, “it shall be obtained by motion except where a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” A motion for leave under subsection 23 (1.1) “may be made without notice, unless the court orders otherwise.” The court “may grant leave under subsection 23 (1.1) of the Courts of Justice Act only if it is in the interest of justice.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.01.1 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit"

current_text: Serving the claim
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: “An originating process shall be served personally as provided in rule 16.02 or by an alternative to personal service as provided in rule 16.03.” Personal service on an individual, other than a person under disability, is made “by leaving a copy of the document with the individual”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.01 (1), 16.02 (1) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"

current_text: Personal service on a corporation other than a municipal corporation is made by leaving a copy with “an officer, director or agent of the corporation”, or with a person at any place of business of the corporation who appears to be in control or management of it. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.02 (1) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"

current_text: Alternatives to personal service include mail with an acknowledgment of receipt card, which is “only effective as of the date the sender receives the card.” If personal service at a residence fails, a copy may be left in a sealed envelope with “anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household”, with another copy mailed the same or next day. That service “is effective on the fifth day after the document is mailed.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.03 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"

current_text: Where prompt service is impractical, “the court may make an order for substituted service or, where necessary in the interest of justice, may dispense with service.” The court may also validate service made in an unauthorized way if the document came to the person's notice, or would have except for the person's “own attempts to evade service.” Service may be proved “by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.04 (1), 16.08, 16.09 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"

current_text: Time to defend
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: Except as provided in rule 18.02 and certain other rules (late delivery of a defence, and a counterclaim against the plaintiff and a non-party), a statement of defence (Form 18A) is delivered “within twenty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served in Ontario”; within forty days if served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States of America; and within sixty days if served anywhere else. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.01)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Time to defend"

current_text: A defendant who intends to defend “may deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) within the time prescribed for delivery of a statement of defence.” A defendant who does so “is entitled to ten days, in addition to the time prescribed by rule 18.01, within which to deliver a statement of defence.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Time to defend"

current_text: What a pleading contains
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: In an action, pleadings “shall consist of the statement of claim (Form 14A, 14B or 14D), statement of defence (Form 18A) and reply (Form 25A), if any.” Pleadings “shall be divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.01 (1), 25.02)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"

current_text: “Every pleading shall contain a concise statement of the material facts on which the party relies for the claim or defence, but not the evidence by which those facts are to be proved.” A party may raise a point of law, “but conclusions of law may be pleaded only if the material facts supporting them are pleaded.” Where damages are claimed, “the amount claimed for each claimant in respect of each claim shall be stated”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.06 (1), (2), (9))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"

current_text: In a defence, a party “shall admit every allegation of fact in the opposite party's pleading that the party does not dispute.” Allegations of fact not denied “shall be deemed to be admitted unless the party pleads having no knowledge in respect of the fact.” But “In an action for damages, the amount of damages shall be deemed to be in issue unless specifically admitted.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.07 (1), (2), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"

current_text: Where a party intends to prove a version of the facts different from that pleaded by the opposite party, “a denial of the version so pleaded is not sufficient, but the party shall plead the party's own version of the facts in the defence.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.07 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"

current_text: Reply and close of pleadings
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: A party who intends to prove a different version of the facts from the defence “shall deliver a reply setting out the different version, unless it has already been pleaded in the claim.” But “A party shall not deliver a reply except where required to do so by subrule (1) or (2).” A party who does not deliver a reply within the prescribed time is “deemed to deny the allegations of fact made in the defence of the opposite party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.08 (1), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Reply and close of pleadings"

current_text: A reply “shall be delivered within ten days after service of the statement of defence”, or within twenty days where the defendant counterclaims. Pleadings are closed when the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence or the time for a reply has expired, and every defendant in default has been noted in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.04 (3), 25.05)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Reply and close of pleadings"

current_text: Filing civil documents online
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action

current_text: Ontario.ca says that starting October 14, 2025, “all online filings for the Toronto region must be submitted using the Ontario Courts Public Portal.” Outside Toronto, the Civil Claims Online and Civil Submissions Online portals remain available. Documents cannot be submitted online “to request an urgent court hearing” or for a court date or deadline 3 business days or fewer away. (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"

current_text: The page says a person filing online needs “an online Ontario.ca Login” and a payment card if filing fees apply. For filings outside Toronto, a person with a fee waiver, or applying for one, “must use the Civil Submissions Online portal”, because the Civil Claims Online portal “will not apply the relevant fee exemptions.” It also says “Once you file a document, online or at a courthouse, you cannot change it.” (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"

current_text: Through Civil Claims Online, a document filed on a weekday between 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. (excluding holidays) “will be considered filed at that time”; outside those hours “it will be considered filed on the next business day.” Through Civil Submissions Online, “Court staff will review your documents within 3 business days to determine if they are accepted for filing or issuance.” (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"

current_text: When a defendant or respondent does not respond
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: This guide explains what the court rules say happens when a person who is sued, or who is named as a respondent, does not file a defence or answer in time, and how the rules deal with setting that aside. It covers Small Claims Court briefly and the Rules of Civil Procedure (Superior Court civil actions) and the Family Law Rules in more detail.
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: Small Claims Court: a short summary
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: “A defendant generally has 20 calendar days to serve and file a defence to a claim.” “If a defendant does not file a defence in time, then the plaintiff may ask the Court to note the defendant in default.” The request to note a defendant in default “may be made in Form 9B”. (ontariocourts.ca, Small Claims Court — Default Proceedings; Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: A defendant who has been noted in default “shall not file a defence or take any other step in the proceeding, except making a motion under rule 11.06, without leave of the court or the plaintiff's consent.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.05 (1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: If a defendant has been noted in default, the clerk may sign default judgment (Form 11B) for the claim, or any part of the claim to which the default applies, that is “for a debt or liquidated demand in money, including interest if claimed”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: If all defendants are noted in default, the plaintiff may seek judgment on the rest of the claim by a motion in writing for an assessment of damages or at an assessment hearing, where the plaintiff “is not required to prove liability against a defendant noted in default, but is required to prove the amount of the claim.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.03 (1), (2), (5))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: If one or more defendants have filed a defence, a plaintiff requiring an assessment of damages against a defendant noted in default “shall proceed to a settlement conference under rule 13 and, if necessary, a trial”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.03 (7))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: The court may set aside the noting in default or default judgment “on such terms as are just” if it is satisfied that “the party has a meritorious defence and a reasonable explanation for the default” and that “the motion is made as soon as is reasonably possible in all the circumstances.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.06)
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: The court's Small Claims page adds that a defendant noted in default may also seek the plaintiff's consent to set these things aside, “except for any enforcement steps that have been completed.” The court's page links to more information on asking to have a defendant noted in default and asking to set aside default proceedings. (ontariocourts.ca, Small Claims Court — Default Proceedings)
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

current_text: Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: In a Superior Court civil action, a statement of defence is delivered “within twenty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served in Ontario”. The time is forty days if the defendant is served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, and sixty days if served anywhere else. These times are subject to listed exceptions, including rule 18.02 (notice of intent to defend). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.01)
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default"

current_text: If a defendant does not deliver a statement of defence in time, the plaintiff may, on filing proof of service of the statement of claim, “require the registrar to note the defendant in default.” The plaintiff may also, on filing a copy of the order, have the defendant noted in default where the defence was struck out without leave to deliver another, or with leave and no other was delivered within the time allowed. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.01 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default"

current_text: “A defendant may deliver a statement of defence at any time before being noted in default under this rule.” A party under disability “may be noted in default only with leave of a judge”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.01 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default"

current_text: Civil actions: what being noted in default means
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: A defendant who has been noted in default “is deemed to admit the truth of all allegations of fact made in the statement of claim”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (1) (a))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: what being noted in default means"

current_text: That defendant also “shall not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action, other than a motion to set aside the noting of default or any judgment obtained by reason of the default, except with leave of the court or the consent of the plaintiff.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (1) (b))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: what being noted in default means"

current_text: A defendant noted in default “is not entitled to notice of any step in the action and need not be served with any document in the action”, except where the court orders otherwise, where a party requires the defendant's personal attendance, and for certain listed documents, such as an amended pleading or a counterclaim. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (3))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: what being noted in default means"

current_text: Civil actions: default judgment
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: Once a defendant is noted in default, the plaintiff may require the registrar to sign judgment for certain claims, including “a debt or liquidated demand in money, including interest if claimed in the statement of claim (Form 19A)”, recovery of possession of land, and recovery of possession of personal property. The plaintiff first files a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.04 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"

current_text: The registrar may decline to sign default judgment if uncertain whether the claim fits the class of cases allowed, or about the interest properly recoverable. The plaintiff may then move before a judge for judgment under rule 19.05 or, for a claim listed in subrule 19.04 (1), make a motion to the court for default judgment. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.04 (3), (3.1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"

current_text: Where a defendant has been noted in default, the plaintiff may move before a judge for judgment on the statement of claim for any claim for which default judgment has not been signed. The motion “shall be supported by evidence given by affidavit if the claim is for unliquidated damages.” The judge “may grant judgment, dismiss the action or order that the action proceed to trial”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.05 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"

current_text: “A plaintiff is not entitled to judgment on a motion for judgment or at trial merely because the facts alleged in the statement of claim are deemed to be admitted, unless the facts entitle the plaintiff to judgment.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.06)
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"

current_text: Civil actions: setting aside the noting of default or a default judgment
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: “The noting of default may be set aside by the court on such terms as are just.” If the defendant delivers a statement of defence with the plaintiff's consent, the noting of default “shall be deemed to have been set aside.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: setting aside the noting of default or a default judgment"

current_text: A default judgment signed by the registrar or granted on motion under rule 19.04 “may be set aside or varied by the court on such terms as are just.” A judgment obtained on a motion for judgment or after trial may be set aside or varied by a judge. When setting aside a judgment, the court or judge may also set aside the noting of default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.08 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: setting aside the noting of default or a default judgment"

current_text: Rule 19 itself does not list the factors a court weighs when deciding whether to set aside a noting of default or a default judgment in a civil action. The site does not yet have a source for those factors. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.03, r. 19.08)
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: setting aside the noting of default or a default judgment"

current_text: Family cases: time to answer
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: In a family case, “A person against whom an application is made shall serve an answer (Form 10, 33B, 33B.1, 33B.2 or 33D.3) on every other party and file it within 30 days after being served with the application.” (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: time to answer"

current_text: “If an application is served outside Canada or the United States of America, the time for serving and filing an answer is 60 days.” A respondent added through a claim in an answer has 14 days, or 30 days if served outside Canada or the United States. Different times apply to an application to dispense with a parent's consent before adoption placement. (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (2), (2.1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: time to answer"

current_text: “The court may make an order to lengthen or shorten any time set out in these rules or in an order, subject to any limitations provided for by these rules.” Parties may also, by consent in writing, change any time set out in the rules, except the times listed in subrule 3 (6). (Family Law Rules, r. 3 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: time to answer"

current_text: Family cases: when no answer is served and filed
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: The Family Law Rules do not use the phrase noted in default for this step. Instead, the consequences in paragraphs 1 to 4 of subrule 1 (8.4) “apply, with necessary changes, if a respondent does not serve and file an answer.” (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (5))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: when no answer is served and filed"

current_text: Those consequences are: “The party is not entitled to any further notice of steps in the case, except as provided by subrule 25 (13) (service of order).” “The party is not entitled to participate in the case in any way.” “The court may deal with the case in the party’s absence.” “A date may be set for an uncontested trial of the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 1 (8.4))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: when no answer is served and filed"

current_text: An “uncontested trial” means “a trial at which only the party making the claim provides evidence and submissions.” If no answer is filed, the clerk “shall, on request, schedule a case conference or set a date for an uncontested trial or, in an uncontested divorce case, prepare the documents for a judge”. (Family Law Rules, r. 2 (1), r. 17 (2))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: when no answer is served and filed"

current_text: At an uncontested trial, evidence by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C and, if applicable, Forms 35.1 and 35.1A may be used “unless the court directs that oral evidence must be given.” Unless the court orders otherwise, the person who prepared an order serves it on every other party, including a party to whom the no-notice consequence applies. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (22), r. 25 (13))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: when no answer is served and filed"

current_text: Family cases: failing to follow the rules
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: “If a person fails to follow these rules, the court may deal with the failure by making any order described in subrule (8), other than a contempt order”. (Family Law Rules, r. 1 (8.1))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: failing to follow the rules"

current_text: The orders in subrule 1 (8) include “an order for costs”, “an order dismissing a claim”, an order striking out a document filed by a party, and, if the failure was by a party, “an order that the party is not entitled to any further order from the court unless the court orders otherwise”. (Family Law Rules, r. 1 (8))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: failing to follow the rules"

current_text: Family cases: changing an order made without a party
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

current_text: The court may, on motion, change an order that “was made without notice”, or one that “was made with notice, if an affected party was not present when the order was made because the notice was inadequate or the party was unable, for a reason satisfactory to the court, to be present.” (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (19) (d), (e))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: changing an order made without a party"

current_text: The court may also change an order that “was obtained by fraud” or “contains a mistake”. Rule 14 (motions for temporary orders) applies with necessary changes to a motion to change a final order under this subrule. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (19) (a), (b), (20))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: changing an order made without a party"

current_text: The Family Law Rules read for this guide do not state a separate test for this kind of motion beyond the grounds listed in subrule 25 (19). The site does not yet have a source for how courts apply those grounds. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (19))
appears_in: Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Family cases: changing an order made without a party"

current_text: Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: A motion is how a party asks a judge to make an order while a case is under way. This guide sets out what the rules say about motions in Small Claims Court, in civil cases in the Superior Court of Justice, and in family cases, with each rule cited.
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: What a motion is in Small Claims Court
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: The ontario.ca guide describes a motion as “a process for requesting that a judge make an order.” It says a party generally makes a motion “to have a matter addressed before judgment, or in some circumstances after judgment or to support an enforcement process.” The guide adds that, usually, a motion is a hearing in court before a judge. There is a fee to file a motion. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"

current_text: The guide says anyone who is a party in the case can make a motion. The person who makes it is called the “moving party.” The person who responds is called the “responding party.” In special circumstances, a judge may allow a person who is not a party to make a motion, because the outcome would affect that person. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"

current_text: Under the Small Claims Court rules, “A motion shall be made by a notice of motion and supporting affidavit (Form 15A).” The supporting affidavit is where the moving party states the order asked for and the facts behind the request. The guide explains that the statements must be sworn or affirmed as true and signed in front of a commissioner for taking affidavits. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"

current_text: Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: The moving party “shall obtain a hearing date from the clerk before serving the notice of motion and supporting affidavit”. The notice of motion and supporting affidavit “shall be served on every party who has filed a claim and any defendant who has not been noted in default, at least seven days before the hearing date”. They must be filed, with proof of service, “at least three days before the hearing date”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"

current_text: A party who prepares an affidavit (Form 15B) in response must serve it on every party who has filed a claim or defence and file it, with proof of service, “at least two days before the hearing date.” The moving party may serve and file a supplementary affidavit, also at least two days before the hearing date. A motion made after judgment has been signed must be served on all parties, including those noted in default. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (4), (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"

current_text: A motion may be conducted with the parties attending by a method determined under rule 1.07. It may instead be in writing if the rules provide for that, or “if the judge determines that it is fair and reasonable for the motion to be in writing.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.02)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"

current_text: A motion “shall not be adjourned at a party's request before the hearing date unless the written consent of all parties is filed when the request is made, unless the court orders otherwise.” A motion cannot be withdrawn without the written consent of all the parties or leave of the court. The costs of a motion, other than disbursements, “shall not exceed $100 unless the court orders otherwise because there are special circumstances.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.05, 15.06, 15.07)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"

current_text: Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: A motion may be made without notice “if the nature or circumstances of the motion make notice unnecessary or not reasonably possible.” A party who gets an order this way must serve it on every affected party, with the notice of motion and supporting affidavit, “within five days after the order is signed.” An affected party may move to set aside or vary the order “within 30 days after being served with the order.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.03)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"

current_text: The guide describes a “motion in writing for assessment of damages”. A plaintiff can make it when the claim is an “unliquidated” claim and all defendants have been served with the claim, none has filed a defence, and all have been noted in default. For this motion, “the plaintiff does not have to attend court for a hearing.” The judge reviews the papers and may grant judgment, ask for another affidavit, or order an assessment hearing. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"

current_text: The guide also explains clerk’s orders. The clerk can make certain orders listed in Rule 11.2. The guide says “These orders can only be made if the written consent of all parties has been provided to the clerk.” The request uses Form 11.2A, and “No hearing is required.” If a party does not consent, a motion to a judge is the route the guide describes. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"

current_text: If the court is satisfied that a party has tried to delay the action, add to its costs or otherwise abuse the court’s process “by making numerous motions without merit”, the court may, on motion, order that the party make no further motions in the action without leave of the court. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.04)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"

current_text: Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: In the Superior Court of Justice, a motion is made by a notice of motion in Form 37A “unless the nature of the motion or the circumstances make a notice of motion unnecessary or these rules provide otherwise.” Every notice of motion must “state the precise relief sought”, state the grounds to be argued, and “list the documentary evidence to be used at the hearing of the motion.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.01, 37.06)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: “A judge has jurisdiction to hear any motion in a proceeding.” An associate judge can hear most motions, except those listed in the rule. On a motion for an order on consent, the registrar makes the order if all parties consent, the consent states no affected party is under disability, and the order is one of the kinds listed, such as setting aside the noting of a party in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.02)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: The notice of motion is served on any party or other person who will be affected by the order sought, unless the rules provide otherwise. Where a motion is made on notice, it “shall be served at least seven days before the date on which the motion is to be heard.” It must also be filed with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing date, in the court office where the motion is to be heard. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.07 (1), (6), 37.08 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: Where a motion is made on notice, the moving party serves and files a motion record at least seven days before the hearing, unless the court orders otherwise. It contains a table of contents, the notice of motion, the affidavits and other material served, and other listed items. A responding party who considers it incomplete may serve and file a responding party’s motion record at least four days before the hearing. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.10 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: A party “may serve on every other party a factum”. A factum required by the rules is “a concise argument stating the facts and law relied on”. If served, the moving party’s factum is served and filed at least seven days before the hearing and the responding party’s at least four days before. On an opposed motion proposed for a hearing in writing, the moving party must serve and file a factum (see below). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 4.06.1 (1), 37.10 (6)-(8), 37.12.1 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: A party who makes a motion on notice must confer or attempt to confer with the other party and, “not later than 2 p.m. five days before the hearing date”, give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) and send a copy of it to the other party by email. If no confirmation is given, “the motion shall not be heard and is deemed to have been abandoned, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.10.1 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: On the hearing, the judge or officer “may grant the relief sought or dismiss or adjourn the motion, in whole or in part and with or without terms”. On a motion by any party, a judge or associate judge may also prohibit another party from making further motions without leave where that party is attempting to delay or add to costs “by a multiplicity of frivolous or vexatious motions.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.13 (1), 37.16)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"

current_text: Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: Where serving the notice is impracticable or unnecessary, the court may make an order without notice. “Where the delay necessary to effect service might entail serious consequences, the court may make an interim order without notice.” On a motion without notice, the moving party must “make full and fair disclosure of all material facts”, and failing to do so is itself enough to set the order aside. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.07 (2), (3), 39.01 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"

current_text: A person affected by an order made without notice, or who missed a motion “through accident, mistake or insufficient notice”, may move to set aside or vary it. That notice of motion is served right after the order comes to the person’s attention. It names the first available hearing date at least three days after service. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.14 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"

current_text: Rule 37.05 sets hearing dates where no practice direction on scheduling motions is in effect. There, an urgent motion may be set down on any day a judge or associate judge is scheduled to hear motions, even if it is expected to take more than two hours. “In an urgent case, a motion may be made before the commencement of a proceeding on the moving party's undertaking to commence the proceeding forthwith.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.05 (1), (3), 37.17)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"

current_text: A motion on consent, unopposed, or made without notice under rule 37.07 (2) “may be heard in writing without the attendance of the parties, unless the court orders otherwise.” An opposed motion can also be proposed for a hearing in writing. In that case, it “shall be made on at least fourteen days notice” and the moving party files a motion record, a draft order and a factum. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.12.1)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"

current_text: Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: “Evidence on a motion or application may be given by affidavit unless a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” Where a motion is made on notice, the moving party’s affidavits are served with the notice of motion and filed at least seven days before the hearing. Affidavits in opposition or in reply are served and filed “at least four days before the hearing.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.01 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"

current_text: An affidavit for a motion may include what the person signing it was told and believes, “if the source of the information and the fact of the belief are specified in the affidavit.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.01 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"

current_text: A party who has served every affidavit it relies on and completed all examinations under rule 39.03 may cross-examine anyone who swore an affidavit for an adverse party (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"

current_text: On a motion other than for summary judgment or a contempt order, the cross-examining party is liable for the adverse party’s partial indemnity costs of the cross-examination, “regardless of the outcome of the proceeding, unless the court orders otherwise.” With leave, a person may be examined at the hearing “in the same manner as at a trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.02 (4), 39.03 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"

current_text: Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, a person may make a motion for “A temporary order for a claim made in an application”, for “Directions on how to carry on the case”, or for “A change in a temporary order.” A motion may be made “by a party to the case or by a person with an interest in the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"

current_text: A motion “requires a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A)” and may be supported by more evidence. If a motion is limited to “procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters”, the party may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (9), (10))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"

current_text: As a general rule, “No notice of motion or supporting evidence may be served and no motion may be heard before a conference dealing with the substantive issues in the case has been completed.” This does not apply “if the court is of the opinion that there is a situation of urgency or hardship or that a case conference is not required for some other reason in the interest of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (4), (4.2))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"

current_text: The rule also lists motions that may go ahead before that conference. They include a motion for summary judgment under rule 16, a motion in a child protection case, and a motion “made without notice, made on consent, that is unopposed or that is limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters (Form 14B)”. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"

current_text: Family cases: service, confirmation and responding
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: A party making a motion with notice serves the documents on all other parties “not later than six days before the motion date”. The party files them as soon as possible after service, “but not later than four days before the motion date”. The party must also “confer or make best efforts to confer orally or in writing with every other party” about the issues in dispute, subject to the exceptions the rule lists. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11) (a)-(c))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"

current_text: The party gives the clerk a confirmation of motion (Form 14C) “not later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date”, after giving a copy to every other party (the rule excepts child protection cases, other than applications under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of O. Reg. 155/18, from giving that copy). Unless the court orders otherwise, “a motion shall not be heard if confirmation of the motion is not given to the clerk” as required. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11) (d), (e), (11.0.1), (11.1))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"

current_text: A response to a notice of motion (Form 14) is served and filed “not later than four days before the motion date.” A response to a motion form (Form 14B) is served and filed not later than seven days after the motion form is served. The party who used Form 14 may reply “not later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date.” No reply is allowed to a response to Form 14B. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11.3)-(11.6))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"

current_text: Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

current_text: A motion may be made without notice if notice is unnecessary or not reasonably possible, if service “would probably have serious consequences”, or where there is an immediate danger of a child being removed from Ontario, or to the health or safety of a child or of the party making the motion, and the delay of serving notice would probably have serious consequences. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (12))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"

current_text: An order made without notice (Form 14D) “shall require the matter to come back to the court and, if possible, to the same judge, within 14 days or on a date chosen by the court.” It must be served immediately on all parties affected, together with all documents used on the motion, unless the court orders otherwise. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (14), (15))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"

current_text: Evidence on a motion may be given by affidavit or other admissible evidence in writing, by a transcript of questioning under rule 20, or, with the court’s permission, orally (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (17))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"

current_text: An affidavit “shall, as much as possible, contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the affidavit.” Information from someone else is allowed only if the source is named and the affidavit states the person believes it is true; on a contempt motion under rule 31, it must also be unlikely to be disputed. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (18), (19))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"

current_text: Unless the court orders otherwise, the moving party serves all supporting evidence with the notice of motion, the responding party then serves its evidence, and the moving party may reply only to new matters. “No other evidence may be used.” A party who makes “numerous motions without merit” to delay the case or add to its costs may be ordered not to make other motions without the court’s permission. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (20), (21))
appears_in: Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"

current_text: Discovery in a civil action
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: This guide explains what the Rules of Civil Procedure say about discovery in a Superior Court of Justice action: the discovery plan, proportionality, sharing documents, and examinations for discovery, whether oral or by written questions.
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: The discovery plan
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: Where a party intends to obtain evidence under the discovery rules, including Rule 30 (Discovery of Documents), Rule 31 (Examination for Discovery) and Rule 35 (Examination for Discovery by Written Questions), “the parties to the action shall agree to a discovery plan”. The plan is agreed before the earlier of “60 days after the close of pleadings or such longer period as the parties may agree to” and attempting to obtain the evidence. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"

current_text: “The discovery plan shall be in writing”. It includes the intended scope of documentary discovery, dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents, information on the timing, costs and manner of producing documents, and “the names of persons intended to be produced for oral examination for discovery under Rule 31 and information respecting the timing and length of the examinations”. The parties “shall ensure that the discovery plan is updated”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (3), 29.1.04)
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"

current_text: On a discovery motion, “the court may refuse to grant any relief or to award any costs if the parties have failed to agree to or update a discovery plan”. If the parties fail to agree, the court may order examinations “in accordance with a discovery plan established by the court”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"

current_text: Proportionality
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: When deciding whether a party or other person must answer a question or produce a document, the court shall consider whether the time required “would be unreasonable”, whether the expense “would be unjustified”, whether it “would cause him or her undue prejudice”, whether it “would unduly interfere with the orderly progress of the action”, and whether the information or document “is readily available to the party requesting it from another source.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Proportionality"

current_text: For documents, the court also considers “whether such an order would result in an excessive volume of documents required to be produced by the party or other person.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Proportionality"

current_text: Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: For these rules, “document” includes “a sound recording, videotape, film, photograph, chart, graph, map, plan, survey, book of account, and data and information in electronic form”. “Every document relevant to any matter in issue in an action that is or has been in the possession, control or power of a party to the action shall be disclosed”, “whether or not privilege is claimed in respect of the document.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.01 (1) (a), 30.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents"

current_text: A party “shall serve on every other party an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B)”. It lists, in separate schedules, relevant documents the party does not object to producing, documents for which the party claims privilege “and the grounds for the claim”, and documents no longer in the party's possession, control or power, with a statement of when and how that happened and their present location. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents"

current_text: A party who serves a request to inspect documents (Form 30C) “is entitled to inspect any document that is not privileged and that is referred to in the other party's affidavit of documents”. The party served names a date “within five days after the service of the request”. “An affidavit of documents shall not be filed unless it is relevant to an issue on a pending motion or at trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.03 (5), 30.04 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents"

current_text: If a party later obtains a relevant non-privileged document, or finds the affidavit inaccurate or incomplete, “the party shall forthwith serve a supplementary affidavit”. Disclosing or producing a document “shall not be taken as an admission of its relevance or admissibility.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.05, 30.07)
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Documentary discovery and the affidavit of documents"

current_text: Privilege and failing to disclose
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: Relevant documents must be produced for inspection if requested, “unless privilege is claimed in respect of the document.” “Where privilege is claimed for a document, the court may inspect the document to determine the validity of the claim.” Rule 30 does not explain what privilege is, and this site does not yet have a source that does. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.02 (2), 30.04 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Privilege and failing to disclose"

current_text: A party that claims privilege for a document and does not abandon the claim, by giving notice in writing and providing a copy of the document or producing it for inspection, “at least 90 days before the commencement of the trial”, “may not use the document at the trial, except to impeach the testimony of a witness or with leave of the trial judge.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.09)
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Privilege and failing to disclose"
