current_text: If a party fails to disclose a document in an affidavit of documents or supplementary affidavit, or fails to produce it as required by the rules, a court order or an undertaking, then if the document is favourable to the party's case, “the party may not use the document at the trial, except with leave of the trial judge”. If it is not favourable, “the court may make such order as is just.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.08 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Privilege and failing to disclose"

current_text: If a party fails to serve an affidavit of documents, fails to produce a document for inspection as the rules require, or fails to comply with an order under rules 30.02 to 30.11, the court may, among other things, “dismiss the action, if the party is a plaintiff, or strike out the statement of defence, if the party is a defendant”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.08 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Privilege and failing to disclose"

current_text: On a motion by a party, the court may order a non-party to produce a non-privileged document for inspection where it is satisfied that “the document is relevant to a material issue in the action” and “it would be unfair to require the moving party to proceed to trial without having discovery of the document.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 30.10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Privilege and failing to disclose"

current_text: Examination for discovery: who, when and how long
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: An examination for discovery “may take the form of an oral examination or, at the option of the examining party, an examination by written questions and answers”, but not both without leave. Where more than one party is entitled to examine a person, the examination is oral “unless all the parties entitled to examine the person agree otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: A party “may examine for discovery any other party adverse in interest, once”, and more than once only with leave of the court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: A party may examine more than one person only as subrules 31.03 (2) to (8) permit. For example, where a corporation may be examined, the examining party may examine any officer, director or employee on its behalf, but more than one “only with the consent of the parties or the leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: A party who seeks to examine a plaintiff may serve a notice of examination or written questions “only after delivering a statement of defence and, unless the parties agree otherwise, serving an affidavit of documents.” A defendant may be examined after delivering a defence (with the examining party's affidavit of documents served, unless agreed otherwise) or after being noted in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.04 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: “No party shall, in conducting oral examinations for discovery, exceed a total of seven hours of examination, regardless of the number of parties or other persons to be examined, except with the consent of the parties or with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.05.1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: In an action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76), “no party shall, in conducting oral examinations for discovery in relation to an action proceeding under this Rule, exceed a total of three hours of examination, regardless of the number of parties or other persons to be examined.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.04 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: who, when and how long"

current_text: Examination for discovery: scope and answers
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: A person examined “shall answer, to the best of his or her knowledge, information and belief, any proper question relevant to any matter in issue in the action”. A question may not be objected to on the ground that “the information sought is evidence”. A party may also obtain “the names and addresses of persons who might reasonably be expected to have knowledge of transactions or occurrences in issue in the action, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.06 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: scope and answers"

current_text: A party, or a person examined on behalf of or in place of a party, fails to answer if they refuse, or if a question taken under advisement or an undertaking is not answered “within 60 days after the response.” The party then “may not introduce at the trial the information that was not provided, except with leave of the trial judge.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.07 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: scope and answers"

current_text: If a party later finds an answer “was incorrect or incomplete when made” or “is no longer correct and complete”, “the party shall forthwith provide the information in writing to every other party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.09 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: scope and answers"

current_text: The court may grant leave to examine for discovery a person “who there is reason to believe has information relevant to a material issue in the action”, other than an expert engaged by or for a party in preparation for contemplated or pending litigation. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: scope and answers"

current_text: Leave is granted only if the court is satisfied that the moving party could not obtain the information from persons it is entitled to examine or from that person, that it would be unfair to proceed to trial without examining the person, and that the examination will not unduly delay the trial, entail unreasonable expense for other parties or be unfair to the person. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 31.10 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination for discovery: scope and answers"

current_text: How oral examinations are conducted
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: Where a party acts in person, a notice of examination (Form 34A) is served on the party “personally or by an alternative to personal service.” A person to be examined who resides in Ontario “shall be given not less than two days notice of the time and place of the examination, unless the court orders otherwise.” Every other party is also given not less than two days notice. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.04 (1), 34.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "How oral examinations are conducted"

current_text: The person examined “shall take an oath or make an affirmation”. They produce the non-privileged documents rule 30.04 (4) requires, and those the notice of examination requires. Where a question is objected to, “the objector shall state briefly the reason for the objection, and the question and the brief statement shall be recorded.” A ruling may be obtained on motion. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.08 (1), 34.10 (2), 34.12 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "How oral examinations are conducted"

current_text: An examination may be adjourned to seek directions where, for example, it “is being conducted in bad faith, or in an unreasonable manner so as to annoy, embarrass or oppress the person being examined”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.14 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "How oral examinations are conducted"

current_text: If a person fails to attend, or refuses to answer a proper question or produce a required document, the court may, among other things, order the person to reattend and answer where an objection is held to be improper, and, where the person is a party or is examined on a party's behalf, “dismiss the party's proceeding or strike out the party's defence”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.15 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "How oral examinations are conducted"

current_text: “Every examination shall be recorded in its entirety in question and answer form in a manner that permits the preparation of a typed transcript”, unless ordered or agreed otherwise. On request, a typed transcript is to be completed “within four weeks after receipt of the request.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 34.16, 34.17 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "How oral examinations are conducted"

current_text: Examination by written questions
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action

current_text: A written examination is conducted “by serving a list of the questions to be answered (Form 35A) on the person to be examined and every other party.” The questions are answered by affidavit (Form 35B), served on the examining party “within fifteen days after service of the list of questions.” An objection is made in the affidavit “with a brief statement of the reason for the objection.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 35.01, 35.02 (1), 35.03)
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination by written questions"

current_text: If the examining party is not satisfied with an answer, it may, “within ten days after receiving the answer, serve a further list of written questions which shall be answered within fifteen days after service.” If answers are “evasive, unresponsive or otherwise unsatisfactory”, the court may order an oral examination. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 35.04 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination by written questions"

current_text: “Examination for discovery by written questions and answers under Rule 35” is “not permitted in an action under this Rule”, meaning an action under the simplified procedure. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.04 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Examination by written questions"

current_text: Mandatory mediation in civil actions
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: This guide explains what Rule 24.1 of the Rules of Civil Procedure says about mandatory mediation in some Superior Court of Justice actions: where it applies, when the session happens, choosing a mediator, attendance, documents, and what happens afterwards.
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: What mandatory mediation is
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: Rule 24.1 “provides for mandatory mediation in specified actions, in order to reduce cost and delay in litigation and facilitate the early and fair resolution of disputes.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.01)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "What mandatory mediation is"

current_text: “In mediation, a neutral third party facilitates communication among the parties to a dispute, to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable resolution.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.02)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "What mandatory mediation is"

current_text: In this Rule, a “defence” means “a notice of intent to defend”, “a statement of defence”, or a notice of motion in response to an action, other than a motion challenging the court's jurisdiction. Several time limits in this Rule run from the first defence filed. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.03, 24.1.09 (1), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "What mandatory mediation is"

current_text: Where it applies
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: The Rule applies to actions governed by it immediately before January 1, 2010, and to actions commenced on or after January 1, 2010 in “The City of Ottawa.”, “The City of Toronto.” or “The County of Essex.” It also applies to actions transferred to one of those counties on or after January 1, 2014, unless the court orders otherwise. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.04 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Where it applies"

current_text: The Rule does not apply to some actions, including “actions under Rule 64 (Mortgage Actions)”, actions on the Toronto Region Commercial List, actions under the Construction Act (except trust claims), and actions under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). It does not apply to actions certified as class proceedings, and applies to an action started under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992 “only if certification as a class proceeding has been denied”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.04 (2), (2.1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Where it applies"

current_text: “The court may make an order on a party's motion exempting the action from this Rule.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.05)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Where it applies"

current_text: When the session happens
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: “A mediation session shall take place within 180 days after the first defence has been filed, unless the court orders otherwise.” In deciding whether to extend or shorten that time, the court considers all the circumstances, including the number of parties, the state of the pleadings, the complexity of the issues, and whether a party intends to bring a summary judgment motion. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.09 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "When the session happens"

current_text: For an action transferred to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex on or after January 1, 2014, the 180-day time limit and the automatic assignment of a mediator after 180 days do not apply, and “the court may make an order, on motion or otherwise, specifying the date by which a mediation session must take place.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.09 (2.1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "When the session happens"

current_text: The session “may be postponed to a later date if, (a) the parties consent to the date in writing; and (b) the consent is filed with the mediation co-ordinator.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.09 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "When the session happens"

current_text: The mediator
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: The mediation is conducted by “a person chosen by the agreement of the parties from the list for a county”, a person assigned from the list by the mediation co-ordinator, or “a person who is not named on a list, if the parties consent.” “The parties shall choose a mediator under subrule 24.1.08 (2).” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.08 (2), 24.1.09 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "The mediator"

current_text: Before the action is set down for trial, one of the parties files with the mediation co-ordinator a notice (Form 24.1A) “stating the mediator's name and the date of the mediation session”, or a mediator's report showing the mediation has concluded. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.09 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "The mediator"

current_text: If the co-ordinator receives none of the listed documents or orders within 180 days after the first defence is filed, the co-ordinator “shall immediately assign a mediator from the list, unless the court orders otherwise.” The assigned mediator serves a notice (Form 24.1B) at least 20 days before the session, “advising that attendance is obligatory.” The date is to be “within 90 days after the appointment of the mediator, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.09 (6), (7), (7.1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "The mediator"

current_text: Documents before the session
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: “At least seven days before the mediation session, every party shall prepare a statement in Form 24.1C and provide a copy to every other party and to the mediator.” The statement “shall identify the factual and legal issues in dispute and briefly set out the position and interests of the party making the statement.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.10 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Documents before the session"

current_text: The party making the statement “shall attach to it any documents that the party considers of central importance in the action.” “The plaintiff shall include a copy of the pleadings with the copy of the statement that is provided to the mediator.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.10 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Documents before the session"

current_text: Attendance and confidentiality
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: “The parties, and their lawyers if the parties are represented, are required to attend the mediation session unless the court orders otherwise.” A party who needs another person's approval to settle arranges, before the mediation session, “to have ready telephone access to the other person throughout the session”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.11 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Attendance and confidentiality"

current_text: Unless the court orders otherwise, where an insurer may be liable to satisfy all or part of a judgment in the action, or to indemnify or reimburse an insured party for money paid under it, a representative of the insurer attends, and the insured party is not required to. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.11 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Attendance and confidentiality"

current_text: “All communications at a mediation session and the mediator's notes and records shall be deemed to be without prejudice settlement discussions.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.14)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "Attendance and confidentiality"

current_text: When a party does not comply
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: If a session cannot practically go ahead because a party did not provide the statement of issues, or “fails to attend within the first 30 minutes of the time appointed”, the mediator cancels the session and files “a certificate of non-compliance (Form 24.1D).” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.10 (5), 24.1.12)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "When a party does not comply"

current_text: The co-ordinator then refers the matter to a judge or associate judge, who may convene a case conference and may, among other things, “establish a timetable for the action”, “dismiss the action, if the non-complying party is a plaintiff, or strike out the statement of defence, if that party is a defendant”, or “order a party to pay costs”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.13 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "When a party does not comply"

current_text: After the mediation
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions

current_text: “Within 10 days after the mediation is concluded, the mediator shall give the mediation co-ordinator and the parties a report on the mediation.” An agreement resolving some or all of the issues “shall be signed by the parties or their lawyers.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.15 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "After the mediation"

current_text: If the agreement settles the action, “the defendant shall file a notice to that effect”, within 10 days after an unconditional agreement is signed, or within 10 days after the condition of a conditional agreement is satisfied. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.15 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "After the mediation"

current_text: If a party to a signed agreement does not comply with it, any other party may “make a motion to a judge for judgment in the terms of the agreement” or “continue the action as if there had been no agreement.” With the parties' consent, the court may at any stage order an additional mediation session. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1.15 (5), 24.1.16 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "After the mediation"

current_text: Rule 24.1 does not set out mediators' fees, and this site does not yet have a source for them. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 24.1)
appears_in: Guides, Mandatory mediation in civil actions, "After the mediation"

current_text: Summary judgment and simplified procedure
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: This guide explains what the court rules say about deciding a case, or part of one, without a full trial (summary judgment) in civil and family cases, and about the simplified procedure for some civil actions in the Superior Court of Justice.
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: Civil summary judgment: who can ask, and when
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: A plaintiff may, “after the defendant has delivered a statement of defence or served a notice of motion, move with supporting affidavit material or other evidence for summary judgment on all or part of the claim in the statement of claim.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.01 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: who can ask, and when"

current_text: A defendant may, “after delivering a statement of defence, move with supporting affidavit material or other evidence for summary judgment dismissing all or part of the claim in the statement of claim.” A plaintiff may also ask, without notice, for leave to serve the motion with the statement of claim, which “may be given where special urgency is shown”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.01 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: who can ask, and when"

current_text: Civil summary judgment: evidence and factums
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: A responding party “may not rest solely on the allegations or denials in the party's pleadings, but must set out, in affidavit material or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue requiring a trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.02 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: evidence and factums"

current_text: An affidavit may be made on information and belief, but on the hearing of the motion the court may, if appropriate, “draw an adverse inference from the failure of a party to provide the evidence of any person having personal knowledge of contested facts.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: evidence and factums"

current_text: Each party serves a factum. The moving party's factum is served and filed “at least seven days before the hearing”, and the responding party's “at least four days before the hearing.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.03 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: evidence and factums"

current_text: Civil summary judgment: how the court decides
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: The court “shall grant summary judgment if” it “is satisfied that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial with respect to a claim or defence”, or the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way and the court is satisfied that it is appropriate. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.04 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: how the court decides"

current_text: In deciding whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial, a judge may weigh the evidence, evaluate the credibility of a deponent, and draw any reasonable inference from the evidence, “unless it is in the interest of justice for such powers to be exercised only at a trial”. A judge may also order that oral evidence be presented. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.04 (2.1), (2.2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: how the court decides"

current_text: If the only genuine issue is the amount, the court “may order a trial of that issue or grant judgment with a reference to determine the amount.” If the only genuine issue is a question of law, the court may decide it and grant judgment, but a motion made to an associate judge is adjourned to be heard by a judge. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.04 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: how the court decides"

current_text: Civil summary judgment: if a trial is still needed, and costs
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: Where summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may specify “what material facts are not in dispute” and define the issues to be tried, and order that the action proceed to trial expeditiously. It may also give directions, such as time limits for motions or a discovery plan. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: if a trial is still needed, and costs"

current_text: The court may order a party to pay the costs of a summary judgment motion on a substantial indemnity basis if “the party acted unreasonably by making or responding to the motion” or “the party acted in bad faith for the purpose of delay.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.06)
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Civil summary judgment: if a trial is still needed, and costs"

current_text: Simplified procedure: when it applies
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: The simplified procedure in Rule 76 “shall be used” in an action when the plaintiff's claim is exclusively for money, real property or personal property, and the total of the money claimed and the fair market value of the property “is $200,000 or less exclusive of interest and costs”. Property value is taken as at the date the action is commenced. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: when it applies"

current_text: With two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is considered separately. With two or more defendants, the claim against each defendant is considered separately. In any other action, the procedure “may be used” at the option of the plaintiff, subject to subrules (4) to (9). The statement of claim or notice of action “shall indicate” that the action is brought under Rule 76. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.02 (2), (2.1), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: when it applies"

current_text: Rule 76 does not apply to class proceedings, to actions under the Construction Act “except trust claims”, to actions assigned for case management under rule 77.05, or to actions where a jury notice is delivered under subrule 76.02.1 (2). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.01 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: when it applies"

current_text: An action started under Rule 76 stops proceeding under it if, among other things, a defendant objects in the statement of defence that the claim does not meet the conditions and the plaintiff does not abandon, in the reply, the parts that do not comply. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.02 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: when it applies"

current_text: Simplified procedure: how it differs from an ordinary action
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: Within 10 days after the close of pleadings, each party serves an affidavit of documents and copies of the documents in its Schedule A. The affidavit includes a list of people who might reasonably be expected to know about matters in issue. A party may not call an undisclosed person as a witness at trial “unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.03 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: how it differs from an ordinary action"

current_text: Written discovery, cross-examination on an affidavit, and examination of a witness on a motion are not permitted. No party may “exceed a total of three hours of examination” in oral discovery. An action under Rule 76 “shall not be tried with a jury”. A jury notice may be delivered only for listed claims such as slander and libel, and the action then “may no longer proceed under this Rule”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.04 (1), (2), r. 76.02.1 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: how it differs from an ordinary action"

current_text: The plaintiff sets the action down for trial within 180 days after the first defence or notice of intent to defend is filed. The trial management plan's total time “shall not exceed five days”. In an action started on or after January 1, 2020, no party may recover costs exceeding $50,000 or disbursements exceeding $25,000, exclusive of HST, except as Rule 76.13 or an Act provides. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.09 (1), r. 76.10 (2), r. 76.12.1 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: how it differs from an ordinary action"

current_text: Under Rule 76, the registrar “shall make an order granting the relief sought” on certain motions that are on consent, or have no responding material, where the filed material states that no affected party is under disability, including motions for “setting aside the noting of a party in default” and “setting aside a default judgment”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 76.05 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Simplified procedure: how it differs from an ordinary action"

current_text: Family summary judgment: when it is available
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: “After the respondent has served an answer or after the time for serving an answer has expired, a party may make a motion for summary judgment for a final order without a trial on all or part of any claim made or any defence presented in the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family summary judgment: when it is available"

current_text: The motion “may be made in any case (including a child protection case) that does not include a divorce claim.” In a case with a divorce claim, the uncontested divorce procedure in rule 36 may be used, or the divorce claim may be split from the rest of the case. (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family summary judgment: when it is available"

current_text: Family summary judgment: evidence and how the court decides
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: The party making the motion serves “an affidavit or other evidence that sets out specific facts showing that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial.” The responding party “may not rest on mere allegations or denials” but sets out specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial. (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (4), (4.1))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family summary judgment: evidence and how the court decides"

current_text: “If there is no genuine issue requiring a trial of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order accordingly.” The court may weigh the evidence, evaluate credibility and draw reasonable inferences, and may order oral evidence. If a party's evidence is not from a person with personal knowledge, “the court may draw conclusions unfavourable to the party.” (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (5), (6), (6.1), (6.2))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family summary judgment: evidence and how the court decides"

current_text: “If the only genuine issue is the amount to which a party is entitled, the court shall order a trial to decide the amount.” If the only genuine issue is a question of law, the court decides it. If no final order is made, the court may specify facts not in dispute, state the issues and give directions. (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (7), (8), (9))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family summary judgment: evidence and how the court decides"

current_text: Family: summary decision on a legal issue
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure

current_text: Separately, the court may, on motion, “decide a question of law before trial, if the decision may dispose of all or part of the case, substantially shorten the trial or save substantial costs”. It may also strike out an application, answer or reply “because it sets out no reasonable claim or defence in law”, or dismiss or suspend a case for reasons listed in the rule. (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (12))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family: summary decision on a legal issue"

current_text: On that kind of motion, “evidence is admissible only if the parties consent or the court gives permission.” (Family Law Rules, r. 16 (13))
appears_in: Guides, Summary judgment and simplified procedure, "Family: summary decision on a legal issue"

current_text: Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: This guide sets out what Ontario's Evidence Act and the court rules say about witnesses, documents, records and affidavits in Small Claims Court, in civil cases in the Superior Court of Justice, and in family cases. Each statement is taken from the Act or rule cited after it.
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: The Evidence Act is an Ontario statute about evidence. It says “This Act applies to all actions and other matters whatsoever respecting which the Legislature has jurisdiction.” In the Act, “court” “includes a judge, arbitrator, umpire, commissioner, justice of the peace or other officer or person having by law or by consent of parties authority to hear, receive and examine evidence”. (Evidence Act, ss. 1, 2)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: The Act says “A person of any age is presumed to be competent to give evidence.” It also says every person offered as a witness “shall be admitted to give evidence although he or she has an interest in the matter in question or in the event of the action and although he or she has been previously convicted of a crime or offence.” (Evidence Act, ss. 7, 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: The parties to an action are, except as the Act otherwise provides, “competent and compellable to give evidence on behalf of themselves or of any of the parties”. The Act says the same of the parties' spouses, who are “competent and compellable to give evidence on behalf of any of the parties.” For this Act, “spouse” means a spouse as defined in section 1 of the Family Law Act. (Evidence Act, ss. 1, 8 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: One limit concerns what a spouse said: “A person is not compellable to disclose any communication made to the person by his or her spouse during the marriage.” (Evidence Act, s. 11)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: “Every court has power to administer or cause to be administered an oath or affirmation to every witness who is called to give evidence before the court.” The Act also says “A person may, instead of taking an oath, make an affirmation or declaration that is of the same force and effect as if the person had taken an oath in the usual form.” (Evidence Act, ss. 3 (2), 17 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: “A witness shall not be excused from answering any question upon the ground that the answer may tend to criminate the witness”, or may tend to establish liability to a civil proceeding or to a prosecution under an Act of the Legislature. (Evidence Act, s. 9 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: If the witness objects on those grounds, would have been excused but for this section or a federal Act, and is made to answer, “the answer so given shall not be used or receivable in evidence against him or her in any civil proceeding or in any proceeding under any Act of the Legislature.” (Evidence Act, s. 9 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Who can be a witness, and oaths and affirmations"

current_text: Business records, electronic records and copies of documents
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: Section 35 of the Evidence Act deals with business records. There, “business” includes “every kind of business, profession, occupation, calling, operation or activity, whether carried on for profit or otherwise”. A “record” “includes any information that is recorded or stored by means of any device.” (Evidence Act, s. 35 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: Under section 35, “Any writing or record made of any act, transaction, occurrence or event is admissible as evidence of such act, transaction, occurrence or event if made in the usual and ordinary course of any business”, and if it was in the usual and ordinary course of that business to make it at the time, “or within a reasonable time thereafter.” (Evidence Act, s. 35 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: This rule applies only if “the party tendering the writing or record has given at least seven days notice of the party’s intention to all other parties in the action”. Any party can get the record produced for inspection “within five days after giving notice to produce the same.” The circumstances of making the record, “including lack of personal knowledge by the maker, may be shown to affect its weight, but such circumstances do not affect its admissibility.” (Evidence Act, s. 35 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: An “electronic record” is data recorded or stored in or by a computer system or similar device, and it “includes a display, printout or other output of that data”. “The person seeking to introduce an electronic record has the burden of proving its authenticity by evidence capable of supporting a finding that the electronic record is what the person claims it to be.” (Evidence Act, s. 34.1 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: Where the best evidence rule applies to an electronic record, “it is satisfied on proof of the integrity of the electronic record.” That integrity may be proved by evidence of the integrity of the electronic records system that recorded or stored the data, “or by evidence that reliable encryption techniques were used to support the integrity of the electronic record.” (Evidence Act, s. 34.1 (5), (5.1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: The Act sets out when the integrity of an electronic records system is proved “In the absence of evidence to the contrary”, and says those matters “may be established by an affidavit given to the best of the deponent’s knowledge and belief.” An adverse party may cross-examine the person who made that affidavit “as of right”. (Evidence Act, s. 34.1 (7), (9), (10))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: Section 34 is about photographic copies of items such as a cheque, receipt, agreement, document or record kept or held by a person. It covers an item photographed “in the course of an established practice” of that person of photographing similar items “in order to keep a permanent record thereof”, and then destroyed by or in the presence of that person or their employees, delivered to another person in the ordinary course of business, or lost. (Evidence Act, s. 34 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: For such an item, “a print from the photographic film is admissible in evidence in all cases and for all purposes for which the object photographed would have been admissible.” (Evidence Act, s. 34 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: Section 55 covers “a telegram, letter, shipping bill, bill of lading, delivery order, receipt, account or other written instrument used in business or other transactions”. A party may give the opposite party notice, “ten days at least before the trial”, that it intends to use a copy as proof of the contents, naming a time and place to inspect it. (Evidence Act, s. 55 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: The copy is then enough evidence of the original's contents unless the party who got the notice, “within four days after the time mentioned for such inspection gives notice that the party intends to dispute the correctness or genuineness of the copy at the trial or proceeding, and to require proof of the original”. (Evidence Act, s. 55 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Business records, electronic records and copies of documents"

current_text: Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: A “practitioner” includes “a member of a College as defined in subsection 1 (1) of the Regulated Health Professions Act, 1991”. A report signed by a practitioner and obtained by or prepared for a party is admissible “with leave of the court and after at least ten days notice has been given to all other parties”. “Leave” means the court's permission. Unless the court orders otherwise, a party is entitled to a copy of the report when notice is given. (Evidence Act, s. 52 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: “Except by leave of the judge presiding at the trial, a practitioner who signs a report with respect to a party shall not give evidence at the trial unless the report is given to all other parties” as the Act requires. If the court finds the practitioner's evidence “could have been produced as effectively by way of a report”, it may order the party who required the practitioner to attend to pay costs. (Evidence Act, s. 52 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: For witnesses who give opinion evidence, the Act says “not more than three of such witnesses may be called upon either side without the leave of the judge or other person presiding.” (Evidence Act, s. 12)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: “A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him or her in writing, or reduced into writing, relative to the matter in question, without the writing being shown to the witness”. If the writing is to be used to contradict the witness, the witness's attention must first be called to the parts to be used. (Evidence Act, s. 20)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: If a witness, on cross-examination about an earlier statement that differs from their testimony, does not clearly admit making it, proof may be given that they made it. First, “the circumstances of the supposed statement sufficient to designate the particular occasion shall be mentioned to the witness, and the witness shall be asked whether or not he or she did make such statement.” (Evidence Act, s. 21)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: No informality in the heading or other formal parts of an affidavit made before a person authorized to take affidavits “is any objection to its reception in evidence if the court or judge before whom it is tendered thinks proper to receive it.” When evidence is in an affidavit and the person affirms, the person taking it “shall certify that the deponent satisfied him or her that the deponent was a person entitled to affirm.” (Evidence Act, ss. 17 (2), 46)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Health reports, expert witnesses, earlier statements and affidavits"

current_text: Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says the Small Claims Court “may admit as evidence at a hearing and act upon any oral testimony and any document or other thing so long as the evidence is relevant to the” subject-matter of the proceeding, “but the court may exclude anything unduly repetitious.” This “applies whether or not the evidence is given or proven under oath or affirmation or admissible as evidence in any other court.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 27 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: There are limits. Nothing is admissible “that would be inadmissible by reason of any privilege under the law of evidence” or “that is inadmissible by any Act.” The court's power also does not override any Act “expressly limiting the extent to or purposes for which any oral testimony, documents or things may be admitted or used in evidence in any proceeding.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 27 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: On copies, “A copy of a document or any other thing may be admitted as evidence at a hearing if the presiding judge is satisfied as to its authenticity.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 27 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: Under the Small Claims Court rules, “At the trial of an undefended action, the plaintiff's case may be proved by affidavit, unless the trial judge orders otherwise.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.01)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: “A document or written statement or an audio or visual record that has been served, at least 30 days before the trial date, on all parties who were served with the notice of trial, shall be received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: This covers “The signed written statement of any witness, including the written report of an expert”, to the extent it relates to things the witness could testify to in person. It also covers any other document, “including but not limited to a hospital record or medical report made in the course of care and treatment, a financial record, a receipt, a bill, documentary evidence of loss of income or property damage, and a repair estimate.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: A party serving such a statement or document must include “the name, telephone number and address for service of the witness or author”, and, for an expert, “a summary of his or her qualifications.” A party who was served and wishes to cross-examine the witness or author “may summon him or her as a witness under subrule 18.03 (1).” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: what evidence the court may receive"

current_text: Small Claims Court: summoning a witness
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: “A party who requires the attendance of a person in Ontario as a witness at a trial may serve the person with a summons to witness (Form 18A)”. The summons may also require the witness to bring to the trial documents or other things in their possession, control or power “relating to the matters in question in the action that are specified in the summons.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: summoning a witness"

current_text: A summons to witness “shall be served personally by the party who requires the presence of the witness, or by the party's representative, at least 10 days before the trial date”. At the time of service, attendance money calculated under the regulations under the Administration of Justice Act “shall be paid or tendered to the witness.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 8.01 (7), 18.03 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: summoning a witness"

current_text: A party who serves a summons on a witness or author of a served statement or document must, at the same time, “serve a copy of the summons on every other party.” A party not served with that copy “may request an adjournment of the trial, with costs.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (5), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: summoning a witness"

current_text: If a party summons a witness who needs an interpreter, “the party shall arrange for a qualified interpreter to attend at the trial”, unless the interpretation is between English and French and the Ministry of the Attorney General provides the interpreter. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (5.1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: summoning a witness"

current_text: If a witness “whose evidence is material to the conduct of an action” does not attend or remain as the summons requires, the trial judge may issue a warrant (Form 18B) to have the witness brought before the court. If a party has “abused the power to summon a witness”, the court may order that party to pay the witness compensation. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (6), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Small Claims Court: summoning a witness"

current_text: Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: “Unless these rules provide otherwise, witnesses at the trial of an action shall be examined orally in court and the examination may consist of direct examination, cross-examination and re-examination.” The trial judge “may disallow a question put to a witness that is vexatious or irrelevant”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: Where a witness does not understand the language of the examination, or is deaf or mute, a competent and independent interpreter must take an oath or affirmation before the witness is called. The party calling the witness “shall provide the interpreter”, unless the interpretation is between English and French and the Ministry of the Attorney General provides one. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: The court may allow “the evidence of a witness or proof of a particular fact or document to be given by affidavit, unless an adverse party reasonably requires the attendance of the deponent at trial for cross-examination.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: A party who intends to call an expert witness at trial must, “not less than 90 days before the pre-trial conference”, serve on every other party a report signed by the expert with the listed information. A responding expert's report is due “not less than 60 days before the pre-trial conference”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.03 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: Without leave of the trial judge, an expert may not testify on an issue unless the substance of that testimony is set out in a served report, a supplementary report served “not less than 45 days before the commencement of the trial”, or a responding supplementary report served “not less than 15 days before” it. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.03 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: These times for serving reports may be extended or abridged by a judge or associate judge at a pre-trial or Rule 77 conference, by the court on motion, or on the parties' written consent, except that the parties may not consent to an extension that would affect the scheduled trial date. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.03 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: A party may serve a person in Ontario with a summons to witness (Form 53A). It “shall be served on the witness personally”, and at the same time “attendance money calculated in accordance with Tariff A shall be paid or tendered to the witness.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.04 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: If a witness whose evidence is material was served and paid or tendered proper attendance money, but does not attend or remain as the summons requires, the presiding judge may issue a warrant for arrest (Form 53B) to have the witness apprehended and brought before the court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.04 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: A party may call an adverse party as a witness unless that person has already testified or the adverse party or its lawyer undertakes to call them. Attendance is secured by serving a summons, or by serving on the adverse party or their lawyer, “at least 10 days before the commencement of the trial, a notice of intention to call the person as a witness”, and paying or tendering attendance money. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.07 (1), (2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: witnesses and evidence at trial"

current_text: Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: An affidavit used in a civil proceeding must “be in Form 4D”, “be expressed in the first person”, state the full name of the deponent (the person making it), be divided into numbered paragraphs, and “be signed by the deponent and sworn or affirmed in accordance with the Commissioners for Taking Affidavits Act.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 4.06 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit"

current_text: “An affidavit shall be confined to the statement of facts within the personal knowledge of the deponent or to other evidence that the deponent could give if testifying as a witness in court, except where these rules provide otherwise.” An exhibit referred to in an affidavit is marked by the person taking the affidavit. If it is a document, “a copy shall be served with the affidavit, unless it is impractical to do so.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 4.06 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit"

current_text: “A party may at any time, by serving a request to admit (Form 51A), request any other party to admit, for the purposes of the proceeding only, the truth of a fact or the authenticity of a document.” For a copy of a letter or email, “authenticity” includes that “the original was sent as it purports to have been sent and received by the person to whom it is addressed.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 51.01, 51.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit"

current_text: The party served must respond “within twenty days after it is served” with a response to request to admit (Form 51B). A party who does not respond is deemed, “for the purposes of the proceeding only”, to admit the facts or documents. A party is also deemed to admit them unless the response specifically denies them, or refuses to admit and “sets out the reason for the refusal.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 51.03)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit"

current_text: If a party denies or refuses to admit a fact or document that is later proved at the hearing, “the court may take the denial or refusal into account in exercising its discretion respecting costs.” An admission “may be withdrawn on consent or with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 51.04, 51.05)
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Civil cases: affidavits and requests to admit"

current_text: Family cases: evidence on motions
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, evidence on a motion may be given by “An affidavit or other admissible evidence in writing”, by “A transcript of the questions and answers on a questioning under rule 20”, or, “With the court’s permission, oral evidence.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (17))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence on motions"

current_text: “An affidavit for use on a motion shall, as much as possible, contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the affidavit.” It may also contain information the person learned from someone else, but only if “the source of the information is identified by name and the affidavit states that the person signing it believes the information is true”, and, on a contempt motion under rule 31, only if “the information is not likely to be disputed.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (18), (19))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence on motions"

current_text: Unless the court orders otherwise, the party making the motion “shall serve all the evidence in support of the motion with the notice of motion.” The responding party then serves all its evidence in response. The moving party may then serve evidence replying to new matters. “No other evidence may be used.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (20))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence on motions"

current_text: Family cases: evidence at trial
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits

current_text: At least 20 days before the earlier of the start of the trial and the trial sitting, “the applicant shall serve and file a trial record”, containing a table of contents and the listed documents. “Not later than seven days before the start of the trial”, a respondent may add listed documents not already in it. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: “A party who wants a witness to give evidence in court or to be questioned and to bring documents or other things shall serve on the witness a summons to witness (Form 23)” by special service, with the witness fee. The summons and fee must be served “at least seven days before the person is required to be present in court or at a questioning”, or, if clause 20 (14) (b) applies, “within the time specified by the court under that clause.” (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (3), (3.2))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: The witness fee, for each day the person is needed, includes “$50 for coming to court or to be questioned” and travel money. For a person living in the city or town where they give evidence, the travel amount is “$5”. Other amounts apply to people who live elsewhere or need to stay overnight. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: A party “may call the opposing party as a witness” and may cross-examine the opposing party. The opposing party may be made to attend by a summons, or by serving on the opposing party's lawyer, “at least 10 days before the start of the trial, a notice of intention to call the opposing party as a witness.” (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (11), (11.1))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: Questioning under rule 20 “shall take place orally under oath or affirmation.” “An answer or information given under rule 20 (questioning) by an opposing party may be read into evidence at trial if it is otherwise proper evidence, even if the opposing party has already testified at trial.” (Family Law Rules, r. 20 (1), 23 (13))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: This is subject to conditions. For example, if the answer is read in to show that a witness’s trial testimony is not to be believed, earlier answers “must be put to the witness as sections 20 and 21 of the Evidence Act require”, and a special party’s or child party’s answers may be read in “only with the trial judge’s permission.” (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (15))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: Evidence at trial by affidavit, or by another method not requiring a party or witness to attend in person, may be used only if a court order allows it, “the evidence is served at least 30 days before the start of the trial”, and “the evidence would have been admissible if given by the party or witness in court.” At an uncontested trial, affidavit evidence in the listed forms may be used without such an order, unless the court directs oral evidence. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (20), (21), (22))
appears_in: Guides, Evidence: witnesses, documents and affidavits, "Family cases: evidence at trial"

current_text: Getting ready for trial
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: This guide sets out the steps the court rules describe between the end of the written pleadings and the trial itself: conferences, exchanging evidence, bringing witnesses, and what happens on the trial day. It covers Small Claims Court, civil cases in the Superior Court of Justice, and family cases, with each rule cited.
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: Small Claims Court: the settlement conference
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: “A settlement conference shall be held in every defended action.” The clerk sets the time and place and serves a notice of settlement conference with a list of proposed witnesses (Form 13A) (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.01 (1)-(4), 13.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: These requirements do not apply if the defence admits liability for all of the plaintiff's claim and proposes terms of payment. The conference “shall be held within 90 days after the first defence is filed.” A party and the party’s representative, if any, must participate unless the court orders otherwise. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.01 (1)-(4), 13.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: The rule lists the purposes of a settlement conference: “to resolve or narrow the issues in the action”, to expedite the action, to encourage settlement, “to assist the parties in effective preparation for trial”, and “to provide full disclosure between the parties of the relevant facts and evidence.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: “At least 14 days before the date of the settlement conference”, each party serves on every other party and files with the court a copy of any document to be relied on at trial that was not attached to the claim or defence, including an expert report, and a list of proposed witnesses (Form 13A) and other people with knowledge of the matters in dispute. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.03 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: The court may award costs against a person who is “so inadequately prepared as to frustrate the purposes of the conference”, or who does not file the required material. If a defendant misses a first settlement conference and then an additional one, the court may strike out the defence, dismiss the defendant's claim, if any, and allow the plaintiff to prove the claim, or make another just order. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.02 (6), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: Except as the rules otherwise provide or with the parties’ consent (Form 13B), what is discussed at the conference is not disclosed to others until the action is disposed of. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.03 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: At the end, the court prepares a memorandum of the issues still in dispute and matters agreed on; it is filed with the clerk, who gives a copy to the trial judge. “A judge who conducts a settlement conference in an action shall not preside at the trial of the action.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.06, 13.08)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: At or after the conference, the clerk gives the parties a notice that one of them “must request a trial date if the action is not disposed of within 30 days after the settlement conference”, and pay the fee for setting the action down. The clerk fixes a trial date once a settlement conference has been held and a party has filed a request (Form 9B) and paid the fee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 13.07, 16.01 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the settlement conference"

current_text: Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: A document, written statement, or audio or visual record “that has been served, at least 30 days before the trial date, on all parties who were served with the notice of trial, shall be received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise.” This includes a signed witness statement or expert report, to the extent it relates to facts and opinions the witness would be permitted to testify to in person, and receipts, bills, financial records and repair estimates. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses"

current_text: A party serving such a statement or document must include the name, telephone number and address for service of the witness or author and, for expert evidence, a summary of qualifications. A party served with it who wants to cross-examine the witness or author may summon that person as a witness. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.02 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses"

current_text: A party who requires a person in Ontario to attend as a witness may serve a summons to witness (Form 18A). The summons may also require the witness to bring documents or things listed in it. The ontario.ca guide says the summons “must be served personally on the witness at least 10 days before the trial date together with attendance money.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (1), (2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses"

current_text: If a summoned witness needs an interpreter, the party who served the summons arranges a qualified interpreter, unless the interpretation is between English and French and the Ministry of the Attorney General provides one. If a summoned witness whose evidence is material fails to attend, the trial judge may issue a warrant (Form 18B) to have the witness brought before the court. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (5.1), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses"

current_text: The guide says to bring “the original documents and at least three copies of each document to the trial.” It explains that the original may be entered as an exhibit, and the copies are for the judge, the other party and the party presenting them. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: evidence, documents and witnesses"

current_text: Small Claims Court: the trial
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: Steps to Justice explains that, to prove a claim at trial, a party must present evidence. “Evidence includes documents and witnesses.” It adds that the evidence must relate to the facts that need to be proved. The judge decides using the evidence both sides give and what the law says, and that decision is called a judgment. (CLEO Steps to Justice, What happens at my Small Claims Court trial?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: Small Claims Court usually holds trials in person, according to Steps to Justice. A party may ask the court in writing to hold the trial a different way, for example by video. The ontario.ca guide describes a trial as “a public process where each party tells their own side of the case to a judge who makes a decision about the issues in the case.” (CLEO Steps to Justice, What happens at my Small Claims Court trial?; ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: If a party fails to attend, the trial judge may proceed without that party, strike out the defence or dismiss the action as the rule describes, or make another just order. If the defence is struck or the action dismissed, the party with the claim need not prove liability but must prove the amount (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 17.01 (2), (2.1), (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: A judgment against a party who did not attend may be set aside or varied only if that party moves within 30 days after learning of it, or gets an extension for special circumstances. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 17.01 (2), (2.1), (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: “A trial may be adjourned only by order of the court.” The court may adjourn on just terms, including payment by one party to another for inconvenience and expense. A party may move for a new trial within 30 days after a final order (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 17.02, 17.04)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: A party may make a motion for a new trial “within 30 days after a final order is made.” The court may grant a new trial, or give the judgment that ought to have been given, only if the party shows a purely arithmetical error in damages, or relevant evidence that was not available at trial and could not reasonably have been expected to be. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 17.04)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Small Claims Court: the trial"

current_text: Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: After the close of pleadings, a party who is not in default “and who is ready for trial may set the action down for trial”. In a defended action, this is done by serving a trial record on every party and promptly filing it with proof of service. The trial record contains the pleadings, any jury notice, any order respecting the trial, and the other items the rule lists. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 48.01, 48.02 (1), 48.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)"

current_text: Once a party has set an action down, that party “shall not initiate or continue any motion or form of discovery without leave of the court”, subject to exceptions in the rule. When the action is placed on a trial list, “all parties shall be deemed to be ready for trial”. Every party must promptly tell the registrar of any settlement and confirm it in writing. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 48.04 (1), 48.07, 48.12)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)"

current_text: Unless the court orders otherwise, the registrar dismisses an action for delay if it “has not been set down for trial or terminated by any means by the fifth anniversary of the commencement of the action.” A similar rule applies to an action struck off a trial list. It does not apply if a timetable signed by all parties is filed in time, and a party may instead move for a status hearing. Some actions are excluded. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 48.14 (1), (1.1), (4), (5), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)"

current_text: Dismissal also does not happen if, at least 30 days before the period expires, a party files a timetable signed by all parties, with a draft order. The timetable identifies the remaining steps and their dates, and a date, “no more than two years after” the period expires, by which the action is to be set down or restored. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 48.14 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)"

current_text: If the parties do not consent to a timetable, any party may, before the period expires, move for a status hearing, where the plaintiff must show cause why the action should not be dismissed for delay. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 48.14 (5), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: setting the action down for trial (Rule 48)"

current_text: Civil cases: the pre-trial conference (Rule 50)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: The purpose of Rule 50 is to give a chance for issues “to be settled without a hearing” and, for issues not settled, to get orders or directions for the just, most expeditious and least expensive disposition. Unless the court orders otherwise, within 180 days after an action is set down, the parties schedule a pre-trial conference with the registrar. If they do not, the registrar schedules it, subject to any previous order. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 50.01, 50.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: the pre-trial conference (Rule 50)"

current_text: Unless an order or practice direction says otherwise, the pre-trial conference is scheduled for a date “not more than 120 days and not less than 30 days before” the first trial day or the first day of the trial sitting, whichever is later. At least 30 days before it, each party delivers a certificate of readiness (Form 50A) about any expert evidence. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 50.02 (2.1), 50.03.1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: the pre-trial conference (Rule 50)"

current_text: “At least five days before a pre-trial conference”, each party files, with proof of service, a pre-trial conference brief. It gives concise statements, without argument, of the nature of the proceeding, the issues and the party’s position, likely witnesses and how long each will take, the steps still needed before trial and how long they will take, and, if separate hearings will be sought, the party’s position on that. The parties participate unless the judge or associate judge orders otherwise. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 50.04, 50.05 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: the pre-trial conference (Rule 50)"
