current_text: Matters considered include settlement, simplifying the issues, admissions, liability, damages, and the estimated length of trial. If the case does not settle, the judge or associate judge may set a timetable and make orders about the conduct of the proceeding. After the conference, the judge or associate judge completes a pre-trial conference report. Statements made at the conference are not communicated to the trial judge, except as disclosed in an order or the report. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 50.06, 50.07 (1), 50.08, 50.09)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: the pre-trial conference (Rule 50)"

current_text: Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: “Unless these rules provide otherwise, witnesses at the trial of an action shall be examined orally in court and the examination may consist of direct examination, cross-examination and re-examination.” Before or at trial, the court may allow evidence by affidavit, “unless an adverse party reasonably requires the attendance of the deponent at trial for cross-examination.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (1), 53.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)"

current_text: A party who intends to call an expert witness serves a signed report on every other party “not less than 90 days before the pre-trial conference”. A responding expert report is due not less than 60 days before it. The report must include the information listed in the rule, such as the expert’s qualifications, instructions, opinion and reasons. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.03 (1), (2), (2.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)"

current_text: A party may serve a summons to witness (Form 53A) on a person in Ontario. The summons “shall be served on the witness personally” and attendance money under Tariff A is paid or tendered at the same time. An adverse party may instead be called by serving a notice of intention to call the person “at least 10 days before the commencement of the trial”, with attendance money. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.04 (1), (4), 53.07 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)"

current_text: If a party fails to attend when the action is called for trial, the judge may proceed in that party’s absence or make another order the rule lists (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 52.01 (2), 52.02, 52.06 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)"

current_text: “A judge may postpone or adjourn a trial to such time and place, and on such terms, as are just.” At a party’s request, the judge may order a witness excluded from the courtroom until called, but not a party to the action or a witness whose presence is essential to instruct the lawyer for the party calling the witness. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 52.02, 52.06 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Civil cases: evidence and procedure at trial (Rules 52 and 53)"

current_text: Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: In each case in which an answer is filed, “a judge shall conduct at least one conference”, subject to exceptions for child protection and international child abduction cases. The rule describes three kinds: a case conference, a settlement conference and a trial management conference. A judge may combine them. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (1), (1.1), (1.2), (4)-(7))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: Before a conference, each party must “confer or make best efforts to confer orally or in writing with every other party” about financial disclosure requests and a temporary resolution of the issues, and, for a settlement or trial management conference, a final resolution. This does not apply where a court order prohibits it or there is a risk of domestic violence as the rule describes. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (3.1), (3.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: The purposes of a settlement conference include “exploring the chances of settling the case”, “settling or narrowing the issues in dispute”, and, if the case is not settled, “identifying the witnesses and other evidence to be presented at trial, estimating the time needed for trial and scheduling the case for trial”. A case is not scheduled for trial unless a settlement conference has been held or a judge has ordered it. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (5), (10))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: A trial management conference is for matters such as “deciding how the trial will proceed”, “estimating the time needed for trial”, and making sure the parties know what witnesses and other evidence will be presented. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: In the Superior Court of Justice and its Family Court, a case is not scheduled for trial until the parties complete the trial scheduling endorsement form and the court endorses it, unless the court orders otherwise in advance, which “may only be made in exceptional circumstances”. Some cases are excepted, such as child protection cases and uncontested trials. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (11), (11.1), (11.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: Each party serves and files the conference documents the rule lists, such as a case conference or settlement conference brief (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (13), (13.1), (14), (14.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: The party who asked for the conference (or otherwise the applicant or moving party) does so “not later than six days before the date scheduled for the conference” and the other party “not later than four days before that date.” Each party gives the clerk a confirmation of conference (Form 17F) by 2 p.m. three days before; without it, the conference is not held unless the court orders otherwise. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (13), (13.1), (14), (14.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: No brief, evidence or statement from a settlement conference is disclosed to any other judge, except in an agreement reached there or an order. A judge who conducts a settlement conference about an issue “shall not hear the issue”, except in the child protection situation the rule describes. An agreement at a conference is not effective until signed by the parties, witnessed and, in a case involving a special party or a child party, approved by the court. (Family Law Rules, r. 17 (19), (23), (24), (25))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: conferences before trial (rule 17)"

current_text: Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial

current_text: At least 20 days before the start of the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier, the applicant serves and files a trial record. It has a table of contents and documents such as the application, answer and reply, any agreed statement of facts, any temporary order on a matter still in dispute, and any order relating to the trial. The respondent may add documents “Not later than seven days before the start of the trial”. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)"

current_text: A party who wants a witness to give evidence in court or to be questioned serves a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service, with the witness fee. It must be served “at least seven days before the person is required to be present in court”, subject to an exception in the rule (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (3), (3.2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)"

current_text: The fee includes $50 for each day the person is needed, plus travel money and, where the person needs to stay overnight, money for meals and lodging, as set out in the rule. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (3), (3.2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)"

current_text: If a witness served as required does not obey the summons and needs to be present, the court may issue a warrant for arrest (Form 32B). “A party may call the opposing party as a witness” and may cross-examine the opposing party. The opposing party can be brought by summons, or by serving a notice on the opposing party’s lawyer at least 10 days before trial. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (7), (11), (11.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)"

current_text: A party may ask the court for an order allowing evidence by affidavit or another method that does not require attending in person. That evidence may be used only if it follows the order, is “served at least 30 days before the start of the trial”, and would have been admissible if given in court. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (20), (21))
appears_in: Guides, Getting ready for trial, "Family cases: trial record, witnesses and evidence (rule 23)"

current_text: Legal costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: This guide describes what Ontario's laws and court rules say about legal costs in Small Claims Court, in civil cases in the Superior Court of Justice, and in family cases. It explains the rules in general terms; it does not predict any costs award.
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: What costs are and who decides
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says “the costs of and incidental to a proceeding or a step in a proceeding are in the discretion of the court, and the court may determine by whom and to what extent the costs shall be paid.” This is “Subject to the provisions of an Act or rules of court”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 131 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "What costs are and who decides"

current_text: The Act also limits appeals about costs. “No appeal lies without leave of the court to which the appeal is to be taken,” where “the appeal is only as to costs that are in the discretion of the court that made the order for costs.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 133)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "What costs are and who decides"

current_text: Small Claims Court: the limit on costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: In Small Claims Court, “An award of costs in the Small Claims Court, other than disbursements, shall not exceed 15 per cent of the amount claimed or the value of the property sought to be recovered”. The exception is where “the court considers it necessary in the interests of justice to penalize a party or a party's representative for unreasonable behaviour in the proceeding.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 29)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: the limit on costs"

current_text: The Small Claims Court rules repeat this: “Any power under this rule to award costs is subject to section 29 of the Courts of Justice Act, which limits the amount of costs that may be awarded.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.07)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: the limit on costs"

current_text: Small Claims Court: what can be awarded
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: Under the rules, a successful party “is entitled to have the party's reasonable disbursements” paid by the unsuccessful party, “unless the court orders otherwise”. These include “any amounts paid for effecting service or preparing a plaintiff's or defendant's claim or a defence and expenses for travel, accommodation, photocopying and experts' reports”, and fees associated with the electronic filing or issuance of documents. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.01 (1), (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: what can be awarded"

current_text: The clerk assesses disbursements, and the court can review that assessment. Disbursements for service “shall not exceed $60 for each person served” unless the court finds special circumstances. Disbursements for preparing a claim or a defence “shall not exceed $200.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.01 (2), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: what can be awarded"

current_text: If a successful party is represented by a lawyer, student-at-law or paralegal, the court “may award the party a reasonable representation fee at trial or at an assessment hearing.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.04)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: what can be awarded"

current_text: For a successful party who is self-represented, the court may order the unsuccessful party to pay “an amount not exceeding $500 as compensation for inconvenience and expense.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.05)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: what can be awarded"

current_text: If a party or a party's representative “has unduly complicated or prolonged an action or has otherwise acted unreasonably”, the court may order the party or the representative to pay an amount to another party “as a penalty, as provided by section 29 of the Courts of Justice Act.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 19.06)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: what can be awarded"

current_text: Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: If a plaintiff's offer to settle is not accepted, the court may award the plaintiff “an amount not exceeding twice the costs of the action, other than disbursements”. The conditions are that the plaintiff “obtains a judgment as favourable as or more favourable than the terms of the offer”, the offer was made at least seven days before the trial, and it was not withdrawn and did not expire before the trial. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 14.07 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If a defendant's offer is not accepted, the court may award the defendant “an amount not exceeding twice the costs awardable to a successful party, other than disbursements, from the date the offer was served”. This applies if the plaintiff “obtains a judgment as favourable as or less favourable than the terms of the offer”, and the same timing conditions are met. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 14.07 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If an amount is awarded under either of those subrules to a self-represented party, the court may, “despite rule 19.05”, also award the party “an amount not exceeding $1,500 as compensation for inconvenience and expense.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 14.07 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: These costs consequences “apply only if the offer to settle is served on the party to whom it is made at least seven days before the trial commences.” An offer that is not accepted is not mentioned to the trial judge “until all questions of liability and the relief to be granted, other than costs, have been determined.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 14.02 (2), r. 14.04)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, the plaintiff is entitled to the plaintiff's disbursements assessed to the date the plaintiff was served with the offer (for a defendant's offer), or to the date the notice of acceptance was served (for a plaintiff's offer). (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 14.05 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Small Claims Court: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: Civil cases: how the court decides costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: In the Superior Court of Justice, the court may consider, “in addition to the result in the proceeding and any offer to settle or to contribute made in writing”, factors including “the amount claimed and the amount recovered in the proceeding”, “the complexity of the proceeding”, “the importance of the issues”, and conduct “that tended to shorten or to lengthen unnecessarily the duration of the proceeding”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 57.01 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: “The fact that a party is successful in a proceeding or a step in a proceeding does not prevent the court from awarding costs against the party in a proper case.” When the court awards costs, “it shall fix them in accordance with subrule (1) and the Tariffs.” However, “in an exceptional case the court may refer costs for assessment under Rule 58.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 57.01 (2), (3), (3.1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: The rules define “partial indemnity costs” as “costs awarded in accordance with Part I of Tariff A”, and “substantial indemnity costs” as “costs awarded in an amount that is 1.5 times what would otherwise be awarded in accordance with Part I of Tariff A”. Rule 57 does not affect the court's authority “to award costs in an amount that represents full indemnity” or “to award costs to a party acting in person.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 1.03 (1), r. 57.01 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: A party who intends to seek costs for a step gives the other parties, and brings to the hearing, a costs outline (Form 57B) “not exceeding three pages in length”, unless the parties agreed on costs. On a contested motion, unless the court is satisfied that a different order would be more just, the court fixes the costs and orders them “to be paid within 30 days”, or in an exceptional case refers them for assessment. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 57.01 (6), r. 57.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: If a plaintiff recovers an amount within the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court, “the court may order that the plaintiff shall not recover any costs.” This does not apply to an action transferred to the Superior Court of Justice under section 107 of the Courts of Justice Act. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 57.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: Civil cases: offers to settle and costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: A party may serve an offer to settle (Form 49A) on any other party. An offer can be made at any time, but if it is made “less than seven days before the hearing of the proceeding commences, the costs consequences referred to in rule 49.10 do not apply.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.02 (1), r. 49.03)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If a plaintiff's offer is made “at least seven days before the commencement of the hearing of the proceeding”, is not withdrawn and does not expire before the hearing begins, and is not accepted, and the plaintiff “obtains a judgment as favourable as or more favourable than the terms of the offer to settle, the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs to the date the offer to settle was served and substantial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If a defendant's offer meets the same timing conditions and is not accepted, and the plaintiff “obtains a judgment as favourable as or less favourable than the terms of the offer to settle, the plaintiff is entitled to partial indemnity costs to the date the offer was served and the defendant is entitled to partial indemnity costs from that date, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.10 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: Where two or more defendants are alleged to be “jointly or jointly and severally liable” and rights of contribution or indemnity may exist between them, “the costs consequences prescribed by rule 49.10 do not apply to an offer to settle” unless the offer meets further conditions in the rule, for example a plaintiff's offer that “is made to all the defendants, and is an offer to settle the claim against all the defendants”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.11)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: The burden of proving the result compared with the offer “is on the party who claims the benefit of subrule (1) or (2).” The court may also “take into account any offer to settle made in writing, the date the offer was made and the terms of the offer.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.10 (3), r. 49.13)
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, the plaintiff is entitled to the plaintiff's costs assessed to the date the plaintiff was served with the offer (for a defendant's offer), or to the date the notice of acceptance was served (for a plaintiff's offer). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 49.07 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Civil cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: Family cases: how the court decides costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: Promptly after dealing with a step in a case, the court decides “who, if anyone, is entitled to costs in relation to that step” and sets the amount, or expressly reserves the decision for later. “Except as otherwise provided in this rule, there is a presumption that a successful party is entitled to the costs of a step in a case.” If success is divided, the court may apportion costs. The presumption does not apply in a child protection case. (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (1), (3), (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: A successful party who behaved unreasonably during a step may lose all or part of their own costs, or be ordered to pay all or part of the unsuccessful party's costs. If a party “has acted in bad faith, the court shall decide costs on a full recovery basis and shall order the party to pay them immediately.” (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (7), (10))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: If a party “is required to appear at a step in the case but does not do so”, is not properly prepared, or “otherwise contributes to the step being unproductive”, the court “shall award costs against the party unless the court orders otherwise in the interests of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (9))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: In setting the amount, the court may consider the reasonableness and proportionality of factors such as each party's behaviour, the time spent, written offers to settle, legal fees and expert fees, as they relate to “the importance and complexity of the issues in the step”. A claim for fees or expenses “shall be supported by documentation satisfactory to the court.” (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (14), (15))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: Before each step, each party is to “confer or make best efforts to confer orally or in writing with every other party with a view to settling costs”, subject to listed exceptions. Each party is to be ready to “make an oral submission as to costs in relation to that step”. (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (17), (18))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: If the court requires written costs submissions, then “unless the court orders otherwise” each is “no longer than three pages or, if it relates to costs of a trial, five pages”, not counting documentation. (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (19))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: how the court decides costs"

current_text: Family cases: offers to settle and costs
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs

current_text: A party may serve an offer on any other party, even before the case is started. An offer “must be signed personally by the party making it and by their licensed representative.” An offer cannot be accepted “after the court begins to give a decision that disposes of a claim dealt with in the offer.” (Family Law Rules, r. 18 (2), (3), (4), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: Offers “are subject to the costs consequences provided for under rule 24.” Under rule 24, a party who makes an offer is, unless the court orders otherwise, “entitled to costs to the date the offer was served and full recovery of costs from that date to the conclusion of the step”, if the listed conditions are met. (Family Law Rules, r. 18 (12.1), r. 24 (12))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: The conditions include: an offer about a motion is made “at least one day before the motion date”; an offer about a trial or other hearing is made “at least seven days before the trial or hearing date”; the offer does not expire and is not withdrawn before the hearing starts; it is not accepted; and the party who made it “obtains an order that is as good as or better than the offer.” (Family Law Rules, r. 24 (12))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: “If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, either party is entitled to ask the court for costs.” The terms of an offer are not mentioned to the judge hearing the claim “until the judge has dealt with all the issues in dispute except costs.” (Family Law Rules, r. 18 (8), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Legal costs, "Family cases: offers to settle and costs"

current_text: Collecting on a court order
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: Winning a court order does not always mean the money is paid. This guide describes the enforcement steps the court rules and statutes set out in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice (civil), and for family support orders.
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: A judgment is not automatic payment
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: The ontario.ca guide explains: “A judgment is an order of the court; it is not a guarantee of payment.” CLEO adds that “the court does not collect the money for you.” Taking steps to collect is called enforcing the judgment. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment; CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I collect the money I'm owed?)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "A judgment is not automatic payment"

current_text: The court rules use two terms. A “creditor” is “a person who is entitled to enforce an order for the payment or recovery of money”. A “debtor” is “a person against whom an order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.01; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.01)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "A judgment is not automatic payment"

current_text: Under the Limitations Act, 2002, “There is no limitation period in respect of” “a proceeding to enforce an order of a court, or any other order that may be enforced in the same way as an order of a court” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 16 (1) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "A judgment is not automatic payment"

current_text: The court rules still require the court's permission (leave) for some enforcement steps once six years have passed since the order, as described below. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, rr. 20.06 (1.1), 20.07 (1.1), 20.08 (2.1); Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.07 (2), 60.08 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "A judgment is not automatic payment"

current_text: Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: “In addition to any other method of enforcement provided by law”, a Small Claims order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced by a writ of seizure and sale of personal property (Form 20C), a writ of seizure and sale of land (Form 20D), and garnishment. A further order as to payment may also be made “After the examination or if the debtor's consent is filed”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, rr. 20.03, 20.10 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps"

current_text: The guide says: “You can start taking enforcement steps immediately after judgment is given.” It says “the best place to start is often with a simple written request for payment”, and notes that a creditor who does not know where the debtor banks, works or what the debtor owns “could begin the enforcement process by requesting an examination hearing.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps"

current_text: If the debtor lives or carries on business in the area of a different court, the guide says a Certificate of Judgment (Form 20A) is needed before that court can issue a notice of garnishment or notice of examination. If there is default under the order, the clerk issues it on the creditor's request, supported by an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P) “stating the amount still owing”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.04 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps"

current_text: After judgment, the guide explains that “post-judgment interest accrues automatically” on the amount owing under the judgment. It describes this as “simple (not compound) interest”, recalculated as payments reduce the balance. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps"

current_text: The guide also notes that “The orders of some boards, tribunals and agencies, as well as other levels of court in Ontario can be filed and enforced in the Small Claims Court”, for example orders under the Residential Tenancies Act and the Employment Standards Act. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the tools and first steps"

current_text: Small Claims Court: the examination hearing
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: If there is default under a payment order, the clerk of a court in the territorial division where the debtor or other person to be examined “resides or carries on business” shall, at the creditor's request, issue a notice of examination (Form 20H). The request is supported by an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P), and a certificate of judgment if the order was made elsewhere. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: The debtor and other persons may be examined about “the reason for nonpayment”, “the debtor's income and property”, “the debts owed to and by the debtor”, any disposal of property before or after the order, “the debtor's present, past and future means to satisfy the order”, whether the debtor intends to obey the order, and “any other matter pertinent to the enforcement of the order.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: A debtor who is an individual must complete a financial information form (Form 20I), serve it on the creditor but “not file it with the court”, and provide a copy to the judge. The debtor brings documents that support it. An officer or director of a corporate debtor may be examined on its behalf. The examination is held in the absence of the public unless the court orders otherwise, “conducted under oath” and “recorded.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (4.1), (4.2), (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: According to the guide, the creditor serves the notice of examination “at least 30 days before the hearing”, together with a blank Financial Information Form if the debtor is an individual, and files an affidavit of service “at least 3 days prior to the date set for the examination.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: “After the examination or if the debtor's consent is filed, the court may make an order as to payment.” While that order is in force, a creditor named in it may take no other enforcement step “except issuing a writ of seizure and sale of land and filing it with the sheriff.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.10 (7), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: If a person served with a notice of examination does not attend, or attends but refuses to answer questions or produce documents, the court may order a contempt hearing. At that hearing the court may order the person to attend an examination, or “be jailed for a period of not more than five days”, among other orders. The guide notes: “Paying the debt does not expunge (remove) the contempt.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.11 (1), (2), (7); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: the examination hearing"

current_text: Small Claims Court: garnishment
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: “A creditor may enforce an order for the payment or recovery of money by garnishment of debts payable to the debtor by other persons.” The guide says: “Most often, people garnish wages or bank accounts.” The person who owes money to the debtor, such as a bank or employer, is the garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: The creditor files an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P) “naming one debtor and one garnishee” with the clerk of a court in the territorial division where the debtor resides or carries on business. The clerk then issues a notice of garnishment (Form 20E). A separate notice is needed for each garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (3), (4), (5); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: The creditor serves the notice on the garnishee, and on the debtor “within five days of serving it on the garnishee.” If the garnishee is a financial institution, notices are served “at the branch at which the debt is payable.” The guide says a blank Garnishee's Statement (Form 20F) is served on the garnishee. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (6.1), (6.2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: A garnishee who admits owing a debt to the debtor pays the clerk, up to the amount in the notice, within 10 days after service or 10 days after the debt becomes payable, “whichever is later.” This includes debts payable within six years after the notice is issued. Payments cannot exceed the portion of wages subject to garnishment under section 7 of the Wages Act. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (7), (8), (9))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: A garnishee that disputes the garnishment, or pays less than the amount in the notice, files a garnishee's statement (Form 20F) within 10 days after service of the notice. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (11), (12))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: CLEO states: “You cannot garnish more than 20 percent of a person's wages.” That CLEO page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. The guide says “employment insurance, social assistance and pension payments cannot be garnished, even if the funds have been deposited into an account at a financial institution.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can the court take money from someone's bank account if I have a court order against them?; ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: If a debt is payable to the debtor and co-owners, such as a joint account, “one-half of the indebtedness” or another amount set by the court may be garnished. A co-owner served with a notice to co-owner of debt may dispute only by requesting a garnishment hearing “within 30 days after the notice is sent.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (2), (16))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: A creditor, debtor, garnishee, co-owner or other interested person may ask the clerk to schedule a garnishment hearing. The court may decide rights and liabilities, and “vary or suspend periodic payments under a notice of garnishment”. The guide says a debtor facing “real financial hardship” may ask a judge to increase the exempt portion of wages. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (15), (15.2); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: Once proof of service on the debtor is filed, and unless a hearing or certain motions or requests are pending, the clerk pays out the first payment 30 days after receiving it and later payments as received, shared equally among creditors who filed garnishments and are not yet paid in full. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (10), (20), (20.1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: A notice of garnishment lasts “six years from the date of its issue” and may be renewed. Leave is needed to issue one if more than six years have passed since the order or enforcement is conditional. Once the amount owing is paid, the creditor must “immediately serve a notice of termination of garnishment (Form 20R) on the garnishee and on the clerk.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.08 (2.1), (5.1), (20.2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: garnishment"

current_text: Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: On default, the clerk issues to a bailiff, at the creditor's request with an affidavit for enforcement request, a writ of seizure and sale of personal property (Form 20C). The bailiff enforces it “for the amount owing, postjudgment interest and the bailiff's fees and expenses.” The creditor may file a direction to enforce (Form 20O). Seized goods are not sold unless notice is mailed “at least 10 days before the sale” and advertised. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.06 (1), (4), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: The guide notes that under the Execution Act a debtor has certain exemptions from seizure, such as clothing and household furniture “up to a certain amount”, and that “The debtor has a right to choose the goods that make up the exemptions.” The creditor pays an enforcement fee and a deposit, and the enforcement office “can refuse to act if the estimated costs of executing the writ of seizure and sale are greater than the debtor's equity”. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: For land, if an order for the payment or recovery of money is unsatisfied, the clerk issues a writ of seizure and sale of land (Form 20D) to the sheriff the creditor names, at the creditor’s request supported by an affidavit for enforcement request (Form 20P). If more than six years have passed since the order was made, the writ “may be issued only with leave of the court.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.07 (1), (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: Once issued, subject to the Small Claims rules on its duration and renewal, the Rules of Civil Procedure apply to the writ of seizure and sale of land as if it were issued under rule 60.07. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.07 (2), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: The guide says a writ filed in a county or district encumbers land the debtor owns there now or buys later, and a separate writ is needed for each location. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: The guide explains that four months after the writ is filed the creditor can direct the sheriff to seize and sell the land, “but the actual sale cannot proceed until the writ has been on file for six months.” The Rules of Civil Procedure contain the same four-month and six-month limits. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.07 (17), (18))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: Both writs expire “on the sixth anniversary of the date of its issue” unless renewed; a request to renew (Form 20N) is filed with the bailiff or sheriff before the writ expires (a land writ may instead be renewed under the Rules of Civil Procedure). If more than six years have passed since the order, either writ “may be issued only with leave of the court.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.06 (1.1), (2), (3), 20.07 (1.1), (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: “An order for the delivery of personal property may be enforced by a writ of delivery (Form 20B)” issued by the clerk to a bailiff, supported by an affidavit that the property has not been delivered. If the property cannot be found or taken, the person may bring a motion for an order directing the bailiff to seize other personal property of the person against whom the order was made. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.05 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: seizing property and writs of delivery"

current_text: Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: The court may stay enforcement “for such time and on such terms as are just”, and may vary the times and proportions in which money is payable “if it is satisfied that the debtor's circumstances have changed.” While an order for periodic payment is in force, a named creditor may take no other step except issuing and filing a writ of seizure and sale of land. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment"

current_text: If the debtor misses payments under a periodic payment order, the creditor may serve a notice of default of payment (Form 20L) and file it with an affidavit of default of payment (Form 20M). The order “terminates on the day that is 15 days after” service, unless a consent (Form 13B) waiving the default is filed within that period. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.02 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment"

current_text: “A debtor against whom there are two or more unsatisfied orders for the payment of money may make a motion to the court for a consolidation order.” The motion is served on each creditor “at least seven days before the hearing date.” The order ends immediately after 21 days of default, and then no new consolidation order may be made for one year. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.09 (1), (3), (10), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment"

current_text: When the order is paid in full, a party may file a request for clerk's order on consent (Form 11.2A) if all parties consent, or the debtor may bring a motion for an order confirming full payment. The guide says that a creditor who has used any of the enforcement processes is responsible for telling the court and the enforcement office(s) when the debt has been paid in full. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 20.12; ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Small Claims Court: limits on enforcement and full payment"

current_text: Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: “In addition to any other method of enforcement provided by law”, a civil order for the payment or recovery of money may be enforced by a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and “the appointment of a receiver.” An order to do or not do an act, other than pay money, may be enforced by a contempt order. (Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.02 (1), 60.05)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: A creditor obtains a writ of seizure and sale by filing a requisition with the registrar, with the order “as entered”. Leave is needed if “six years or more have elapsed since the date of the order”, or if its enforcement “is subject to a condition”. A writ “expires on the sixth anniversary of the date of its issue” unless renewed; a writ filed with a sheriff is renewed by filing a request to renew (Form 60E). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.07 (1), (2), (6), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: For garnishment, the creditor files a requisition for garnishment (Form 60G) and an affidavit, and the registrar issues a notice of garnishment (Form 60H) naming “one debtor and one garnishee.” A garnishee who admits owing a debt pays the sheriff, “less $10 for the cost of making each payment”, within the ten-day periods in the rule, subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.08 (4), (6), (6.1), (11), (14))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: For a bank, a garnished debt does not include “money in an account opened after the notice of garnishment is served”. A garnishee who disputes must serve and file a garnishee's statement (Form 60I) within 10 days. Any interested person may move for a garnishment hearing, and on receiving a copy of the notice of motion the sheriff suspends payments to the creditor until the motion is determined or abandoned. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.08 (13), (15), (16), (16.1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: Under rule 60.18, a creditor may examine the debtor about the same matters listed in the Small Claims rule, including “the debtor's income and property”. “Only one examination under subrule (2) or (3) may be held in a twelve month period in respect of a debtor in the same proceeding, unless the court orders otherwise.” “Where any difficulty arises concerning the enforcement of an order”, the court may also order others with knowledge to be examined. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.18 (2), (4), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: If an examination shows that a debtor “has concealed or made away with property to defeat or defraud creditors, a judge may make a contempt order against the debtor.” The notice of examination is served on the debtor personally or by an alternative to personal service. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 60.18 (5), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: A writ of sequestration “may be issued only with leave of the court”, and only where the court “is satisfied that other enforcement measures are or are likely to be ineffective.” A party entitled to enforce an order is entitled to the costs of enforcement steps “on a partial indemnity scale, unless the court on motion orders otherwise”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, rr. 60.09 (1), (2), 60.19 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Superior Court of Justice (civil): Rule 60"

current_text: Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: The Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996 creates the “Director of the Family Responsibility Office”. “It is the duty of the Director to enforce support orders where the support order and the related support deduction order, if any, are filed in the Director’s office and to pay the amounts collected to the person to whom they are owed.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 2, 5 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: The Director may refuse to enforce a filed order, or part of one, if, in the Director's opinion, one of the circumstances the Act lists applies, for example “the meaning of the order is unclear or ambiguous”. This power applies “Despite section 5”. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: “An Ontario court that makes a support order, as defined in subsection 1 (1), shall also make a support deduction order.” It must be made “even though the court cannot identify an income source”, but not for a provisional order. The clerk or registrar files both orders with the Director’s office “promptly after it is signed.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 10 (1), (4), (5), 12 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: The Director may serve notice of a support deduction order on each income source, such as an employer. The income source deducts the support owed and pays it to the Director, starting no later than the first payment to the payor that falls “at least 14 days after” service (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 20 (2), 22 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: Deductions “shall not exceed 50 per cent of the net amount owed by the income source to the payor”, but up to 100 per cent of an income tax refund or other lump sum attachable under federal law may be deducted. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 23 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: Until deductions begin, or if they stop, the payor must pay the Director if the order is filed there, or the recipient if it is not. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 22 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: A support order and support deduction order “may be withdrawn at any time” by written notice, unless the order says they cannot be. Withdrawal needs the recipient's signature, and the payor's too if the payor is in compliance. Orders assigned to an agency under subsection 14 (1) may be withdrawn only by or with the consent of that agency while assigned. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 16 (1), (1.1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: When a filed support order is in default, the Director may serve a first notice that the payor’s driver’s licence may be suspended unless, within 30 days, the payor makes a satisfactory arrangement, obtains and files an order to refrain, or pays all arrears. The Director may also require the payor to appear at a default hearing, where the payor is presumed able to pay “unless the contrary is shown”. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 34, 41 (1), (9))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: Part VI of the Act lists other enforcement mechanisms, including registration of a support order against land, writs of seizure and sale, garnishment of joint accounts and lottery prizes, and reporting default to a consumer reporting agency. (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, ss. 42 to 47)
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family support orders: the Family Responsibility Office"

current_text: Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order

current_text: Under rule 26, a payment order may be enforced by a request for a financial statement, a request for disclosure from an income source, a financial examination, seizure and sale, garnishment, “a default hearing (rule 30), if the order is a support order”, the appointment of a receiver, and registration under section 42 of the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order"

current_text: An order other than a payment order may be enforced by “a writ of temporary seizure of property”, “a contempt order (rule 31)”, and the appointment of a receiver. A statement of money owed is in Form 26, with a copy of the order in default attached. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order"

current_text: If the Director enforces an order, the rules about enforcement by the person the order favours apply to the Director. A recipient who files a support order with the Director must, on the Director's request, assign any enforcement already started to the Director. If the parties withdraw the order, the Director assigns its enforcement to the recipient if the recipient asks at the same time as giving the notice of withdrawal. (Family Law Rules, r. 26 (10), (12), (13))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order"

current_text: If a payment order is in default, the recipient may serve an appointment for a financial examination (Form 27C). The payor must attend, bring the named documents, and serve a financial statement (Form 13) “not later than seven days before the date of the examination.” (Family Law Rules, r. 27 (11))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order"

current_text: When a support order not filed with the Director is in default, the recipient may file a request with the court with a statement of arrears. The clerk then requires the payor “to file a financial statement and appear before the court to explain the default.” (Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, s. 41 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Collecting on a court order, "Family Law Rules: enforcing a family order"

current_text: Appealing a decision
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, which Ontario court hears an appeal and how the court rules say an appeal is started. It explains what the law and rules say; it does not say whether any particular decision can or should be appealed.
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: Which court hears an appeal
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says “An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from,” among other things, “a final order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, as described in subsections (1.1) and (1.2)” and “an interlocutory order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, with leave as provided in the rules of court”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Which court hears an appeal"

current_text: If the notice of appeal is filed on or after October 1, 2007, the final orders that go to the Divisional Court include an order “for a single payment of not more than $50,000, exclusive of costs” and an order “dismissing a claim for an amount that is not more than the amount set out in clause (a) or (b)”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Which court hears an appeal"

current_text: An appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from “a final order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice”, with exceptions, including the orders that go to the Divisional Court under section 19. An order of the Divisional Court can be appealed to the Court of Appeal “on a question that is not a question of fact alone, with leave of the Court of Appeal as provided in the rules of court”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Which court hears an appeal"

current_text: Leave of the Court of Appeal is not required for a Divisional Court order on an appeal under Part V or VIII of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1.0.1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Which court hears an appeal"

current_text: “Unless otherwise provided”, a court hearing an appeal may “make any order or decision that ought to or could have been made by the court or tribunal appealed from”, may “order a new trial”, or may “make any other order or decision that is considered just”. The Act also says “A judge shall not sit as a member of a court hearing an appeal from his or her own decision.” (Courts of Justice Act, ss. 132, 134 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Which court hears an appeal"

current_text: Appeals from Small Claims Court
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says “An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from a final order of the Small Claims Court in an action,” either “for the payment of money in excess of the prescribed amount, excluding costs” or “for the recovery of possession of personal property exceeding the prescribed amount in value”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 31)
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: A regulation sets the “prescribed amount”. For both clauses of section 31, “the prescribed amount is $5,000.” (O. Reg. 626/00, s. 2)
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: The ontario.ca guide puts it this way: a judgment can be appealed to a higher court “if the amount of the judgment, not including court costs, is more than $5,000, or there is an order directing recovery of personal property valued at more than $5,000.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: The same guide says an appeal “is not an opportunity to retell your story.” It also says “The judge who hears the appeal will not hear any new evidence; they will rely entirely on the transcript of the trial and the court record.” The Courts of Justice Act does allow an appeal court, “in a proper case”, to receive further evidence. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court; Courts of Justice Act, s. 134 (4) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act, however, says that unless otherwise provided, a court to which an appeal is taken may, “in a proper case”, “receive further evidence by affidavit, transcript of oral examination, oral examination before the court or in such other manner as the court directs”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 134 (4) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: A proceeding in the Divisional Court “shall be heard and determined by three judges sitting together”. But it “may be heard and determined by one judge” where it is “an appeal under section 31 from a person referred to in subsection 24 (2) presiding over the Small Claims Court”. The persons referred to in subsection 24 (2) are a deputy judge and the Small Claims Court Administrative Judge. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 21 (1), (2), s. 24 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: In the Rules of Civil Procedure, “appellate court” means “the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court, as the circumstances require”. Rules 61.02 to 61.16 apply “to all appeals to an appellate court”, with some listed exceptions. The steps for starting an appeal under Rule 61 are described in the civil section of this guide. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 1.03 (1), r. 61.01)
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Appeals from Small Claims Court"

current_text: Leave to appeal
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: Some appeals can only go ahead with “leave” of the appeal court. The Courts of Justice Act says “No appeal lies without leave of the court to which the appeal is to be taken,” from “an order made with the consent of the parties” or “where the appeal is only as to costs that are in the discretion of the court that made the order for costs.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 133)
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: Leave to appeal to the Divisional Court from “An interlocutory order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice” is obtained from a panel of that court. The motion for leave “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: Leave to appeal from an interlocutory order “shall not be granted unless” there is “a conflicting decision by another judge or court in Ontario or elsewhere on the matter involved in the proposed appeal” and the panel considers leave desirable, or there appears to the panel “good reason to doubt the correctness of the order in question” and the proposed appeal “involves matters of such importance that, in the panel's opinion, leave to appeal should be granted”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: A notice of motion for leave to appeal to the Divisional Court is to be served “within 15 days after the making of the order or decision from which leave to appeal is sought, unless a statute provides otherwise”, and filed with proof of service “within five days after service”. The same 15-day and five-day times apply to a motion for leave from an interlocutory order under rule 62.02. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (1), r. 61.03.1 (3), r. 62.02 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: Where the Court of Appeal's leave is required, the motion “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers”, and the notice of motion has the same 15-day service and five-day filing times. If the court decides an oral hearing is warranted, it orders one. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03.1 (1), (3), (15))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: In both courts, “Where leave is granted, the notice of appeal shall be delivered within seven days after the granting of leave.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (6), r. 61.03.1 (16), r. 62.02 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"

current_text: Starting an appeal in a civil case
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: An appeal to the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court starts by serving a notice of appeal in Form 61A.2 (Court of Appeal) or 61A.3 (Divisional Court), with a certificate respecting evidence, “within 30 days after the making of the order appealed from, unless a statute or these rules provide otherwise”. It is served on “every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal” and on “any person entitled by statute to be heard on the appeal”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: It need not be served on a defendant who was noted in default, or on a respondent who has not delivered a notice of appearance unless that respondent was heard at the hearing with leave. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: The notice of appeal states “the relief sought”, “the grounds of appeal”, and the basis for the appeal court's jurisdiction, including whether the order is final or interlocutory and whether leave is needed. It is filed with proof of service “within ten days after service”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: With the notice of appeal, the appellant serves and files a certificate (Form 61C) “setting out only the portions of the evidence that, in the appellant's opinion, are required for the appeal.” Instead, the parties may, within thirty days after service of the notice of appeal, make an agreement about the documents and transcript required for the appeal. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: Within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal, the appellant files proof of having ordered a transcript of all oral evidence that the parties have not agreed to omit. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: The appellant “perfects” the appeal by serving and filing the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and a factum. This is due “within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal” if no transcript is needed, or “within 60 days after receiving notice that the evidence has been transcribed” if one is. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.09 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: “No grounds other than those stated in the notice of appeal or cross-appeal or supplementary notice may be relied on at the hearing, except with leave of the court hearing the appeal.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.08 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: A different procedure, in rule 62.01, applies to an appeal made to a judge, such as an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice from “an interlocutory order of a master, case management master or associate judge”. That appeal starts by serving a notice of appeal (Form 62A) “within seven days after the making of the order or certificate appealed from.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 17; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.01 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"

current_text: What happens to the order during an appeal
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: Delivering a notice of appeal “stays, until the disposition of the appeal, any provision of the order for the payment of money, except a provision that awards support or enforces a support order.” When an order is stayed, “no steps may be taken under the order or for its enforcement,” except by order of a judge of the appeal court or as the rules otherwise provide. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (1), r. 63.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "What happens to the order during an appeal"

current_text: An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment “does not stay the default judgment”, but it may be stayed by order. A judge of the appeal court may also order that the automatic stay does not apply. An order may be stayed “on such terms as are just” by the court that made it or by a judge of the appeal court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (2), (5), r. 63.02 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "What happens to the order during an appeal"

current_text: Family cases: which court and which rules
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from “a final order of a judge of the Family Court made only under a provision of an Act or regulation of Ontario”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1) (a.1))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"

current_text: For family appeals to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, including where leave is required, “Rules 61, 62 and 63 of the Rules of Civil Procedure apply with necessary changes”, including changes the rule sets out, such as different time periods in an appeal in a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"

current_text: Rule 38 of the Family Law Rules sets out its own steps for appeals from an order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under provisions such as section 48 of the Family Law Act and section 73 of the Children's Law Reform Act. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"

current_text: A final order of a Superior Court judge made on a first appeal from certain Ontario Court of Justice orders (under the Change of Name Act, the Children's Law Reform Act except sections 59 and 60, or section 6 of the Marriage Act) “may be appealed to the Court of Appeal only with leave from the Court of Appeal, as provided in the rules of court.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1.1), (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"

current_text: Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision

current_text: To appeal a final order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under a provision listed in rule 38 (4), a party serves a notice of appeal (Form 38) “within 30 days after the date of the order or decision being appealed from”. It goes to every other party affected by or entitled to appeal, the clerk of the court that made the order and, in some child protection appeals, certain other persons. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"

current_text: The notice of appeal is filed “within 10 days after serving the notice of appeal”. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"

current_text: For a temporary order, the notice of appeal is served “within seven days after the date of the temporary order.” In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, the time for appealing a temporary order is 30 days. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (6), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"

current_text: The notice of appeal states “the order that the appellant wants the appeal court to make and the legal grounds for the appeal.” At the hearing, “no grounds other than the ones stated in the notice of appeal may be argued unless the court gives permission.” (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (10), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"

current_text: If a transcript is needed, the appellant files proof it was ordered “within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal”. Outside child protection cases, the appellant's appeal record and factum are due within 60 days after notice that the evidence was transcribed, or within 30 days of filing the notice of appeal if no transcript is needed. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (12), (21))
appears_in: Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"

current_text: What court steps cost
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: This guide lists the fees the Ontario government charges for the main steps in Small Claims Court, civil proceedings in the Superior Court of Justice, and family proceedings. Fees as published on ontario.ca and in the regulations on e-Laws, read 2026-09-30 (the fee waiver page was read 2026-09-27).
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: How court fees are set and paid
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: The ontario.ca pages say “You must pay a fee for most steps in a Small Claims Court proceeding” and “You must pay a fee for most steps in a civil court proceeding”. The Small Claims page says “Court fees are set out in regulations made under the Administration of Justice Act”; the civil page says they are “primarily set out” in those regulations. The Small Claims tables are described as “an unofficial presentation of the fees prescribed by an Ontario regulation.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court; ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: In Small Claims Court, fees are payable in Canadian funds by cash at the court or enforcement office counter, by “cheque or money order, payable to the Minister of Finance”, or by debit or credit card “in certain locations, and when filing Small Claims Court documents online”. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: For civil and family proceedings, the pages list cash, cheque or money order payable to the Minister of Finance, debit card in person and when filing online, and credit card “in person, over the phone and when filing civil court documents online” (the family page says the same for family court documents). (ontario.ca, Civil court fees; ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: “Starting October 14, 2025, there are different online portals to file court documents online depending on the region you are filing in.” “Use the Ontario Courts Public Portal for matters in the Toronto region.” “Use the Justice Services Online portal for matters outside of Toronto.” For the Court of Appeal, the civil page says “Use the Ontario Court of Appeal Public Portal for matters at the Court of Appeal.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court; ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: The Small Claims Court page says “If there is a fee associated with your submission, you can pay online through these portals or request a fee waiver”. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: Both regulations say: “If the applicable filing fee is paid on the filing of a document electronically in accordance with the rules of court, the fee is not payable again on the subsequent filing of a paper copy of the document.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (4); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 7)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: The amounts can change. Both regulations say that “Beginning on January 1, 2027, and on every third January 1 that follows, the fees payable under this Regulation shall be adjusted” using the Ontario Consumer Price Index. If the change “results in a negative amount, the fees shall not be increased.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 4 (1); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 6 (1))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: A fee is not adjusted if, before the adjustment would take effect, the Minister determines that the adjusted fee “would exceed full cost recovery” and publishes notice confirming the amount of the fee on a Government of Ontario website. (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 4 (3); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 6 (3))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: A person who cannot afford court fees “may request a fee waiver”; the court decides “whether you meet the requirements to qualify.” “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” “There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.” Some fees “cannot be waived”, including fees paid “to someone who is not part of the court”. The site’s fee waiver guide covers this in full. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees; ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"

current_text: Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: Some Small Claims Court fees depend on whether the person filing is a frequent or infrequent claimant. A “frequent claimant” “means a claimant who files a claim in a Small Claims Court office on or after January 1 in any calendar year and who has already filed 10 or more claims in the same office in that calendar year”. An “infrequent claimant” “means a claimant who is not a frequent claimant.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"
