current_text: A “claimant” “includes an individual, a sole proprietorship, a partnership, an unincorporated organization and a corporation”. For these fees, a claim does not include a defendant’s claim. (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"

current_text: The fees to start a claim are: “On the filing of a claim by an infrequent claimant, $108.” “On the filing of a claim by a frequent claimant, $228.” “On the filing of a defendant’s claim, $108.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 1-3)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"

current_text: The fee to answer a claim is: “On the filing of a defence, $77.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 5)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"

current_text: Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: For a motion: “On the filing of a notice of motion served on another party, a notice of motion without notice or a notice of motion for a consent order (except a notice of motion under the Wages Act), $127.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 4)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: For default judgment: “For the filing of a request for default judgment by an infrequent claimant, $94.” “For the filing of a request for default judgment by a frequent claimant, $128.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 8-9)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: For a trial date: “For the fixing of a date for a trial or an assessment hearing by an infrequent claimant, $308.” “For the fixing of a date for a trial or an assessment hearing by a frequent claimant, $403.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 6-7)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: For a witness: “On the issue of a summons to a witness, $33.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 10)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: The page says “If you summons a witness to attend your trial, you must pay attendance money to the witness at the time you personally serve them.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: Witnesses are paid “For attendance in court, $11 per day, subject to paragraph 2.” A professional who is not a party and gives evidence of a professional service or a professional opinion is paid “$27 per day.” Travel is paid as “those reasonable travelling expenses actually incurred, but not exceeding the kilometre allowance set out in Regulation 11”. (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 3)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"

current_text: Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: Clerk fees after judgment include: “On the issue of a certificate of judgment, $30.” “On the issue of a writ of delivery, a writ of seizure and sale or a notice of examination, $68.” “On the issue or renewal of a notice of garnishment, $144.” “For preparing and filing a consolidation order, $127.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 12-15)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals"

current_text: Bailiff fees include: “For each attempt to enforce a writ of delivery, $38.” For each attempt to enforce a writ of seizure and sale of personal property, “where no sale is necessary, $38, or” “where a sale is necessary, $64.” “A fee under subsection (1) for attempted enforcement by a bailiff is payable whether or not the attempt was successful.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 2)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals"

current_text: The page says that to enforce a judgment, a party “may need to pay some of the fees listed in the Sheriffs – Fees regulation.” Some of those sheriff fees are listed in the civil section of this guide. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals"

current_text: For an appeal, the Small Claims Court clerk charges “For forwarding a court file to Divisional Court for appeal, $105.” The fee for filing the notice of appeal is set by the Superior Court fee regulation: “A notice of appeal or cross-appeal to an appellate court of a final order of the Small Claims Court, $138.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 16; O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 3 xi)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals"

current_text: The page also says a person who wishes to appeal the judge’s decision at trial “will need to pay fees listed in the Fees for Court Transcripts regulation for the preparation of a transcript of your case, as well as a fee for filing your appeal.” These transcript fees are paid to an Authorized Court Transcriptionist. For a certified transcript in electronic format, with no faster delivery time, the page lists “$6.30 per page or $25.00, whichever is greater”. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: after judgment and appeals"

current_text: Superior Court (civil): starting and defending
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: The civil page says civil proceedings are mostly conducted in the Superior Court of Justice, the Divisional Court branch of the Superior Court of Justice, and the Court of Appeal for Ontario. Its general fee table is “an unofficial overview of the fees set by Ontario regulation, Superior Court of Justice and Court of Appeal – Fees”, which is O. Reg. 293/92. Sheriff fees are set by a different regulation, O. Reg. 294/92. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): starting and defending"

current_text: To start a proceeding: “A statement of claim, notice of action or notice of application, $243.” “A third or subsequent party claim, $243.” “A statement of defence and counterclaim adding a party, $243.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 1 i-iii)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): starting and defending"

current_text: To defend: “A notice of intent to defend, $194.” “If no notice of intent to defend has been filed by the same party, a statement of defence, a defence to counterclaim, a defence to crossclaim or a third party defence, $194.” “A notice of appearance, $172.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 3 i-iii)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): starting and defending"

current_text: Additional fees are set for estate matters, payable on top of the general section 1 fees, and for actions under the Construction Act and applications under the Repair and Storage Liens Act, where the general section 1 fees still apply other than those in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 of subsection 1 (1). The civil page notes that “Estate Administration Tax is not a court fee.” (O. Reg. 293/92, ss. 2-4; ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): starting and defending"

current_text: Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: For motions: “A notice of motion served on another party, a notice of motion without notice, a notice of motion for a consent order or a notice of motion for leave to appeal, other than a notice of motion in a family law appeal, $339.” “A notice of return of motion, other than a notice of return of motion in a family law appeal, $339.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 3 iv-v)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals"

current_text: Other steps: “A requisition for signing of default judgment by registrar, $177.” “A trial record, $859, for the first time only.” “A jury notice in a civil proceeding, $138.” “A summons to a witness, $33.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), paras. 1 iv, 3 viii, ix, xiv)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals"

current_text: For appeals: “A notice of appeal or cross-appeal from an interlocutory order, $243.” “A notice of appeal or cross-appeal to an appellate court of a final order of any court or tribunal, other than the Small Claims Court or the Consent and Capacity Board, $243.” “For perfecting an appeal or judicial review application, $645.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), paras. 3 x, xii, 5)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals"

current_text: Other listed fees include “For the taking of an affidavit or declaration by a commissioner for taking affidavits, $22.” Copies cost “$1 per page” not requiring certification and “$4 per page” requiring certification. (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), paras. 7, 10)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals"

current_text: For witnesses, “In civil court proceedings, the attendance money payable is set out in Tariff A of the Rules of Civil Procedure”. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): motions, trial and appeals"

current_text: Superior Court (civil): enforcing an order
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: Court fees to enforce include: “A writ of execution, $77.” “A notice of garnishment or notice of renewal of garnishment (including the filing of the notice with the sheriff), $155.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 1 vii-viii)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): enforcing an order"

current_text: The sheriff’s duties “are carried out by the Enforcement Office.” “Fees are paid to the Enforcement Office at the time an enforcement request is filed, either in person or by mail.” The page describes its table as “an unofficial presentation of the fees prescribed by an Ontario regulation called Sheriff - Fees”. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): enforcing an order"

current_text: Sheriff fees listed on the page include “$100 for each person to be served” for up to three attempts to serve a document; $100 to file or renew a writ of execution or order and deliver a copy to a land registrar, and $75 where the writ or order “is not required to be delivered to a land registrar”; and $240 “For each attempt, whether or not successful, to enforce a writ of seizure and sale or an order directing a sale”. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): enforcing an order"

current_text: The page also lists $400 “For each attempt, whether or not successful, to enforce a writ of delivery, a writ of sequestration, an order for interim recovery of personal property, an order for interim preservation of personal property, or a writ of seizure or direction to seize under the Repair and Storage Liens Act” and “$12.65 per name” for a search for writs. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Superior Court (civil): enforcing an order"

current_text: Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: Family proceedings are conducted in “the Superior Court of Justice”, “the Family Court branch of the Superior Court of Justice (sometimes called the Unified Family Court)” and “the Ontario Court of Justice”. The family page says the fees below “are for family proceedings in the Superior Court of Justice. In some cases, they also apply to the Family Court branch”. The regulation sets them for proceedings governed by the Family Law Rules, except appeals under rule 38. (ontario.ca, Family court fees; O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1.2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: The fees are: “On the filing of an application, $214.” “On the filing of an answer, other than an answer referred to in paragraph 3, $171.” “On the filing of an answer that includes a request for a divorce by a respondent, $214.” “On the placing of an application on the list for hearing, $445.” (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1.2 (1), paras. 1-4)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: Also: “On the issue of a summons to a witness, $33.” “On the issue of a certificate, $25.” The family page describes the $25 item as a certificate “with not more than five pages of copies of the Court document annexed”. (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1.2 (1), paras. 5-6; ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: In addition, “anyone filing an application or an answer with a divorce claim must include the federal government’s $10 fee.” (ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: The regulation says “no fees are payable for the filing of an application, the filing of an answer or the placing of an application on the list for hearing” in proceedings under the Children’s Law Reform Act, the Family Law Act (except Parts I and II), the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, the Marriage Act or the Interjurisdictional Support Orders Act, 2002, or proceedings to enforce parenting, contact or support orders made under them. (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1.2 (2))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: The family page states this exemption for “proceedings in the Family Court branch” and also lists the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. The page relies in part on O. Reg. 417/95, which the site does not yet have as a source. (ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Superior Court and Family Court branch"

current_text: Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost

current_text: “There are no filing or listing fees in family proceedings in the Ontario Court of Justice. There are only fees for copies of documents and copies of recordings.” The page lists $1.00 per page for copies not requiring certification and $3.50 per page for copies requiring certification. (ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service"

current_text: “For the purposes of court fees, family appeals are treated like civil court proceedings.” Appeals under rule 38 of the Family Law Rules fall under section 1 of the regulation, which sets “In a family law appeal, a notice of motion served on another party, a notice of motion without notice, a notice of motion for a consent order or a notice of return of motion, $134.” (ontario.ca, Family court fees; O. Reg. 293/92, ss. 1 (1), para. 3 vi, 1.2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service"

current_text: Also under section 1: “A notice of motion for leave to appeal in a family law case, $134.” The notice of appeal and perfecting fees are the civil appeal fees listed above. (O. Reg. 293/92, s. 1 (1), para. 3 vii, x, xii, 5)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service"

current_text: The Online Child Support Service “is an alternative to going to court.” “There is a non-refundable $80 fee each time you use the service, whether you’re setting up or updating child support.” “A fee waiver may be available if you cannot afford to pay the $80 fee.” (ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service"

current_text: For witnesses, “In family proceedings, the attendance money payable is set out in Rule 23 of the Family Law Rules”. (ontario.ca, Family court fees)
appears_in: Guides, What court steps cost, "Family: Ontario Court of Justice, appeals and child support service"

current_text: Having court fees waived
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: This guide explains what the Ontario government says about fee waivers in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court: who can ask, who may qualify, how to apply, what is not covered and when a waiver applies.
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: What a fee waiver is
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: “You might need to pay fees if you go to court in Ontario. If you cannot afford to pay the fees, you can ask the court to waive them.” The court “will consider your financial situation and decide whether you meet the requirements to qualify.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"

current_text: If the person meets the requirements “and the court agrees to waive the fees”, they get “a certificate called a fee waiver.” The page says to “Show this certificate to court staff if they ask you to pay a fee.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"

current_text: “There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.” “You need to apply for a separate fee waiver for each case or proceeding you are involved in. A fee waiver will not apply to any fees you have already paid.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"

current_text: “Each request is reviewed based on the form and documents you submit. The decision of staff or a judge is final. If your financial situation changes, you can request a fee waiver again.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"

current_text: Who can ask, and who may qualify
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: A person can ask for a fee waiver if they “are or will be involved in a family, civil or small claims court matter”, “are not acting on behalf of a business or organization”, and their fees “are not being paid by a lawyer under a contingency fee agreement”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"

current_text: The court may approve the request if the main source of household income is from Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program, the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the War Veterans Allowance, or Canada Pension Plan benefits. It may also approve it if “your lawyer is being paid by a Legal Aid Certificate”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"

current_text: The financial requirements refer to “gross annual household income”, meaning what everyone in the household earns in a year before taxes or deductions. The page says it must be below $33,100 for one person, $49,600 for two people, $57,300 for three people, $68,700 for four people, and $80,200 for five or more people. It also lists household liquid assets of less than $2,800 and household net worth of less than $11,100. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"

current_text: Listed with the income limits, as part of the same financial eligibility requirements, are “your household liquid assets are less than $2,800” and “your household net worth is less than $11,100”. Net worth is “the value of all assets owned by the members of your household, minus their debts and other financial liabilities”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"

current_text: A person who does not meet the requirements but does not believe they can afford the fees “can make a request directly to the court to have your financial situation evaluated by a judge.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"

current_text: What a fee waiver does not cover
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: Fees that cannot be waived include “fees you pay to someone who is not part of the court (this includes lawyers, authorized court transcriptionists, official examiners, witnesses and mediators)”, “fees relating to criminal matters”, “the federal Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings fee”, and “fees for serving documents on another party”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver does not cover"

current_text: Also excluded are disbursements paid to the sheriff or small claims court bailiff to enforce an order (with one exception for orders under subsection 31(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006), and fees prescribed for bankruptcy proceedings. “A fee waiver does not apply to any costs a court has ordered you to pay to another party.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver does not cover"

current_text: How to apply: the forms and documents
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: A person who thinks they meet the financial requirements uses the Fee Waiver Request to Registrar, Clerk or Sheriff (form FW-A-3). A person who does not think they meet them uses the Fee Waiver Request to Court (form FW-A 4). Forms FW-A 6 and FW-A 7 are the versions for a litigation guardian or special party representative. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: The applicant must “provide proof of your gross annual household income. This includes proof of income for your spouse, if you have one.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: For form FW-A-3 or FW-A 6, any one of three documents may be given for the applicant and for their spouse: the tax return or notice of assessment for the most recent tax year; the most recent employer statement of earnings or three most recent pay stubs; or the most recent statement of income from employment insurance, social assistance, a pension, workers compensation or disability payments. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: “If you cannot provide any of these documents, explain why and continue to fill out the rest of the form”. No proof of income is needed “if your lawyer is being paid by a Legal Aid Certificate.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: With form FW-A 4 or FW-A 7, the applicant fills out Exhibit B listing household members’ income, expenses and assets, with a recent financial document for each item. With Exhibit C, they provide the first document filed in the case showing their position, or “a copy of the order you wish to enforce or continue enforcing”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: The page describes a Guided Pathway for requesting a court fee waiver as “a free online tool developed by Community Legal Education Ontario ( CLEO ) and the Ministry of the Attorney General.” It “asks you questions and inserts your answers into the required court form.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "How to apply: the forms and documents"

current_text: Swearing, submitting and timing
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: The applicant “must swear or affirm that the information you provided is accurate and true to the best of your knowledge.” This can be done “for free at the court or enforcement office”, or by a lawyer, paralegal, notary public or commissioner for taking affidavits, who may charge a fee. “It is a criminal offence to knowingly swear or affirm a false affidavit.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Swearing, submitting and timing"

current_text: The request can be submitted online, by mail or in person. “You can submit the form on its own or along with any court document that you wish to file.” A lawyer or representative can also submit it. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Swearing, submitting and timing"

current_text: By mail, the form goes to the court or enforcement office where the fee would be paid, and “You will get a response in the mail.” In person, “You will find out immediately if you qualify for the fee waiver.” More generally, the page says: “Court staff will review your request first. If they determine that you do not meet the requirements, your request will be presented to a judge for review.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Swearing, submitting and timing"

current_text: Online, “If you have a fee waiver or want to apply for a fee waiver, you must use the online portals listed above when submitting your documents.” Toronto-region filings use the Ontario Courts Public Portal; other regions use the Justice Services Online portal. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Swearing, submitting and timing"

current_text: After a fee waiver is granted
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: A fee waiver “can be revoked (cancelled or invalidated) by a judge if they think that your actions in your case or proceeding are frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of the court’s process.” A judge can also require the person to get permission before asking for another fee waiver. “You will have a chance to submit a statement or argument to a judge before they revoke your fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "After a fee waiver is granted"

current_text: With a fee waiver, a person “can request the help of a court interpreter for free for any language other than English or French”, for themselves or a witness, using form FW-A 5. The form is to be submitted “as soon as you find out the date and time of the court appearance when the interpreter will be required.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "After a fee waiver is granted"

current_text: Small Claims Court
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” In the part of the page on filing in the Toronto region through the Ontario Courts Public Portal, it says “you must indicate if you have a fee waiver or want to apply for a fee waiver”, and to select “Request fee waiver” when applying for a certificate at the same time. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Small Claims Court"

current_text: In the part of the page on filing outside the Toronto region through the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal, it describes two choices for a document that would normally have a fee: “Fee waiver request” when applying for a certificate at the same time, or “Document is being submitted by a person with a fee waiver certificate” when a certificate is already held. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Small Claims Court"

current_text: In its section on a summonsed witness who needs an interpreter, the Ministry’s trial guide says the court provides English-French and visual language interpretation, that the party summonsing the witness arranges interpretation for other languages, and that “The court will provide an interpreter for other languages to parties who have qualified for a fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Small Claims Court"

current_text: Superior Court of Justice (civil)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Superior Court of Justice (civil)"

current_text: For filing outside the Toronto region, the page says: “If you have a fee waiver or want to apply for one, you must use the Civil Submissions Online portal below to submit your documents.” It adds that “The Civil Claims Online portal will not apply the relevant fee exemptions. You will not receive a fee refund if you file a document using Civil Claims Online.” (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Superior Court of Justice (civil)"

current_text: In the Civil Submissions Online portal (outside the Toronto region), to apply together with a document, the filer selects “Fee waiver request” for any document that usually requires a fee. A filer who already has a certificate chooses “Document is being submitted by a person with a fee waiver certificate”. (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Superior Court of Justice (civil)"

current_text: Family court
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived

current_text: The general fee waiver rules above apply to a person who is “involved in a family, civil or small claims court matter”. The Guided Pathway for requesting a court fee waiver is listed under Guided Pathways to Family Court Forms. The page notes that the federal Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings fee cannot be waived. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Family court"

current_text: The site does not yet have a source on how fee waivers are handled when filing family court documents online. The general page says that anyone who has or wants a fee waiver “must use the online portals listed above when submitting your documents”, choosing the fee waiver option for any document requiring a fee, and links to a separate page on filing family court documents online. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Having court fees waived, "Family court"

current_text: Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: This guide sets out who may represent a party in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court, where the sources on this site say legal help and information can be found, and what they say about language rights and interpreters.
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: The Courts of Justice Act says “A party may be represented in a proceeding in the Small Claims Court by a person authorized under the Law Society Act to represent the party”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"

current_text: The same section lets the court exclude a representative from a hearing. The court may exclude “anyone, other than a person licensed under the Law Society Act, appearing on behalf of the party if it finds that such person is not competent properly to represent the party, or does not understand and comply at the hearing with the duties and responsibilities of an advocate.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"

current_text: Steps to Justice says “You do not have to hire a lawyer or paralegal when you go to Small Claims Court.” It also says “both lawyers and paralegals can represent you in Small Claims Court. However, only a lawyer can represent you in Superior Court, or the Court of Appeal.” (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"

current_text: That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017; the family court section below sets out what the Family Law Rules now say about family legal services providers. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"

current_text: Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, “A party to a proceeding who is under disability or acts in a representative capacity shall be represented by a lawyer.” A party that is a corporation “shall be represented by a lawyer, except with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: Every other party has a choice: “Any other party to a proceeding may act in person or be represented by a lawyer.” This includes a lawyer “acting under a limited scope retainer”, but such a retainer “does not, in itself, make a lawyer the lawyer of record for the party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: When a party acts in person, “anything these rules require or permit a lawyer to do shall be done by the party.” A party acting in person may appoint a lawyer of record by serving and filing a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01.1 (1), 15.03 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: Subject to the rules that require some parties to have a lawyer, a party with a lawyer of record may elect to act in person by serving and filing a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (1), (2), 15.03 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: Who can represent a party in family court
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, a party may “act in person”, “be represented by a lawyer”, be represented by a family legal services provider in certain listed cases (such as some uncontested divorces, some child support motions and some support enforcement) unless the court decides that is inappropriate, or, “if the court gives permission in advance, be represented by any other person, on terms set out by the court.” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1), (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: A party may also be represented by a “family legal services provider” in a limited list of cases and matters “as authorized under the Law Society Act”. The list includes an uncontested divorce or one started by a joint application where the only claim is for divorce, filing a domestic contract, a change of name application, some motions under rule 15 to change child support, and some enforcement of support. Each item has its own conditions, set out in the rule. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: This does not apply “if the court determines that representation by a family legal services provider is inappropriate in the circumstances” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: A lawyer or family legal services provider may act under a limited scope retainer, which the rules define, for a lawyer, as legal services for “part, but not all, of a party’s case, by agreement” and, for a family legal services provider, as “some, but not all, of the services that a family legal services provider is authorized to provide in a party’s case or matter”. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (0.1), (1.2), (1.4), (1.5))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: A party acting in person may choose a licensed representative “by serving on every other party and filing a notice of change in representation (Form 4) containing the consent of the licensed representative to act.” This is not needed for a limited scope representative who is not the representative of record (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (9), (9.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: A represented party may use Form 4 to change representatives or act in person, but in a child protection case scheduled for trial or on a trial list, acting in person needs the court’s permission in advance. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (10), (10.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"

current_text: Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Steps to Justice explains that “Lawyers can give legal advice. This means they can explain what the law says and how it applies to your situation.” A paralegal “is another kind of legal professional that can give legal advice about Small Claims Court.” It says “a paralegal is not allowed to work in all the legal areas that a lawyer can.” That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: “The Law Society of Ontario regulates lawyers and paralegals in Ontario.” It has rules about who can become a lawyer or paralegal and how they must behave, and it deals with complaints. That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: The Law Society Referral Service “can provide you with the name of a lawyer or paralegal in your area, who will provide a free initial consultation of up to 30 minutes to help determine your rights and options.” A request can be made through the online form at www.lawsocietyreferralservice.ca. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: For people unable to use the online service, “A crisis line is available Monday to Friday, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm.” The number given is 416-947-5255 (toll free 1-855-947-5255). The Law Society also has a Lawyer and Paralegal Directory at www.lawyerandparalegal.directory. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: Some lawyers offer “unbundled services” or “limited scope retainer” services: “This means you pay them to help you with part of your case.” Examples given are summary advice, preparing documents, appearances, and coaching on the court process. Steps to Justice says “Some lawyers and paralegals do not charge for the first meeting.” (Steps to Justice, How do I prepare for my meeting with a lawyer or paralegal?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: A complaint can be made to the Law Society only if a lawyer or paralegal “did not do their job properly, or behaved unprofessionally.” The Law Society does not deal with legal fees. A complaint must be made “within 3 years of when the problem happened or when you became aware of it.” The page adds that there is no time limit for a complaint about sexual abuse. (Steps to Justice, How do I complain to the Law Society of Ontario about a lawyer or paralegal?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"

current_text: Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Steps to Justice lists these next steps for legal help with a Small Claims issue: “Find a lawyer or paralegal”, “Get help from Pro Bono Ontario”, “Contact JusticeNet” and “Call a community legal clinic”. That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters"

current_text: “If you earn a low income, you might be able to get legal help from Pro Bono Ontario . Pro Bono Ontario helps with cases in Small Claims Court and Superior Court.” (Steps to Justice, How can I sue in Small Claims Court?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters"

current_text: “PBO has a hotline where you can get up to 30 minutes of free legal advice.” Steps to Justice also says “PBO offer services in some court locations in Toronto and Ottawa”; that page was last reviewed on July 14, 2022. (Steps to Justice, What happens at my Small Claims Court trial?; Steps to Justice, I filed a claim with the Small Claims online service. What happens next?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters"

current_text: “If you earn a low income, a community legal clinic might be able to help you with your case.” (Steps to Justice, I filed a claim with the Small Claims online service. What happens next?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters"

current_text: “The Small Claims Court Guided Pathways is a free online tool that asks you questions and puts your answers into the required court forms.” The page also points to Community Legal Education Ontario (CLEO) and Steps to Justice for more information about Small Claims Court. (ontario.ca, File Small Claims Court documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Free and low-cost help for Small Claims matters"

current_text: Finding help for a Superior Court civil matter
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: The Ontario government page on filing civil claims says a person without a lawyer can find one through the “Law Society of Ontario's referral service or directory of lawyers” or through “Pro Bono Ontario , if you can't afford a lawyer and need help with a civil matter”. (ontario.ca, File civil claim documents online)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Finding help for a Superior Court civil matter"

current_text: Steps to Justice says that suing for more than $50,000 must be done in Superior Court, and that a person owed more than $50,000 who is “willing to waive the amount over $50,000” can still file in Small Claims Court. (Steps to Justice, How can I sue in Small Claims Court?)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Finding help for a Superior Court civil matter"

current_text: English, French and interpreters
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: “The official languages of the courts of Ontario are English and French.” Unless French-language rules apply, hearings are in English and “evidence adduced in a language other than English shall be interpreted into the English language”. Documents filed must be in English or come with a translation “certified by affidavit of the translator.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 125)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "English, French and interpreters"

current_text: Pleadings and other documents filed by a party may be written in French. “A party to a proceeding who speaks French has the right to require that it be conducted as a bilingual proceeding”. The hearings the party specifies are then “presided over by a judge or officer who speaks English and French.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 126 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "English, French and interpreters"

current_text: The Ontario government says “You have the right to use a court interpreter if you or a witness are deaf or do not understand the language of the proceeding.” A person with a fee waiver “can request the help of a court interpreter for free for any language other than English or French”, using form FW-A 5. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "English, French and interpreters"

current_text: Without a fee waiver, “you are responsible for booking and paying for interpreter services for yourself or for your witness.” A fee waiver is not needed for an English-French or French-English interpreter in a civil, family or small claims court matter. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "English, French and interpreters"

current_text: Interpreters for witnesses, by court
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: Small Claims Court: “If a party serves a summons on a witness who requires an interpreter, the party shall arrange for a qualified interpreter to attend at the trial unless the interpretation is from English to French or French to English and an interpreter is provided by the Ministry of the Attorney General.” If not, every other party may request an adjournment of the trial, with costs. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 18.03 (5.1), (5.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Interpreters for witnesses, by court"

current_text: The Ministry’s guide adds that for a summonsed witness “the court will provide an interpreter from English to French or French to English or visual language interpretation.” It also says “The court will provide an interpreter for other languages to parties who have qualified for a fee waiver.” (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Getting ready for court)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Interpreters for witnesses, by court"

current_text: Superior Court: where a witness at the trial of an action does not understand the language of the examination or is deaf or mute, “the party calling the witness shall provide the interpreter, unless the interpretation is to be from English to French or from French to English and an interpreter is provided by the Ministry of the Attorney General.” A similar rule applies at oral examinations. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (1), (5), (6), 34.09)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Interpreters for witnesses, by court"

current_text: Family court, divorce proceedings: under the Divorce Act, a proceeding “may be conducted in English or French, or in both official languages of Canada.” The court “shall, at the request of any person, provide simultaneous interpretation from one official language into the other”. The site does not yet have a source on the Family Law Rules for interpreters in other languages. (Divorce Act, s. 23.2)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Interpreters for witnesses, by court"

current_text: What the site does not have a source for yet
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters

current_text: The sources on this site do not yet directly cover duty counsel, the services of Legal Aid Ontario, Family Law Information Centres, or how to ask a courthouse for a disability-related accommodation. One related item is a note that court forms in alternative formats can be requested by email at attorneygeneral@ontario.ca. (Ontario Court Forms, Rules of the Small Claims Court Forms)
appears_in: Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "What the site does not have a source for yet"

current_text: Getting a divorce
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, what the Divorce Act and rule 36 of Ontario's Family Law Rules say about getting a divorce: which court hears it, the ground for divorce, and how a divorce takes effect. It explains what the law and rules say; it does not say whether any particular person can get a divorce.
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: Which court and who can apply
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: The Divorce Act defines a “divorce proceeding” as “a proceeding in a court in which either or both spouses seek a divorce alone or together with a child support order, a spousal support order or a parenting order”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"

current_text: For Ontario, the Act names the court as “the Superior Court of Justice”. The definition also includes any other court in the province whose judges are appointed by the Governor General and that the province designates as a court for the purposes of the Act. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"

current_text: “A court in a province has jurisdiction to hear and determine a divorce proceeding if either spouse has been habitually resident in the province for at least one year immediately preceding the commencement of the proceeding.” If divorce proceedings between the same spouses are pending in two courts with jurisdiction, started on different days, and the first one “is not discontinued”, the court where the proceeding was started first has exclusive jurisdiction, and the second proceeding “is deemed to be discontinued.” (Divorce Act, s. 3 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"

current_text: “A court of competent jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, grant a divorce to the spouse or spouses on the ground that there has been a breakdown of their marriage.” The power to grant a divorce “shall be exercised only by a judge of the court without a jury.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7, 8 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"

current_text: The ground: breakdown of the marriage
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: Under the Divorce Act, “Breakdown of a marriage is established only if” one of the situations in subsection 8 (2) applies. The first is that “the spouses have lived separate and apart for at least one year immediately preceding the determination of the divorce proceeding and were living separate and apart at the commencement of the proceeding”. (Divorce Act, s. 8 (2) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"

current_text: The other situations are that the spouse against whom the proceeding is brought has, since the marriage, “committed adultery”, or “treated the other spouse with physical or mental cruelty of such a kind as to render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses.” (Divorce Act, s. 8 (2) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"

current_text: For the one-year separation in paragraph 8 (2) (a), spouses are deemed to have lived separate and apart “for any period during which they lived apart and either of them had the intention to live separate and apart from the other”. A period of separation is not interrupted or ended “by reason only that the spouses have resumed cohabitation during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose.” (Divorce Act, s. 8 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"

current_text: A period of separation is also not interrupted by reason only that a spouse has become incapable of forming or having an intention to continue to live separate and apart, or of doing so of their own volition, “if it appears to the court that the separation would probably have continued if the spouse had not become so incapable”. (Divorce Act, s. 8 (3) (b) (i))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"

current_text: Reconciliation and the bars to divorce
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: In a divorce proceeding, the court has a duty, before considering the evidence, “to satisfy itself that there is no possibility of the reconciliation of the spouses, unless the circumstances of the case are of such a nature that it would clearly not be appropriate to do so.” (Divorce Act, s. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: If it appears to the court at any stage that reconciliation is possible, the court shall adjourn the proceeding “to afford the spouses an opportunity to achieve a reconciliation” and, “with the consent of the spouses or in the discretion of the court”, nominate a person with experience or training in marriage counselling or guidance (or, in special circumstances, some other suitable person) to assist. Once fourteen days have passed, the court shall resume the proceeding on the application of either or both spouses. (Divorce Act, s. 10 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: The court must also “satisfy itself that there has been no collusion in relation to the application for a divorce and to dismiss the application if it finds that there was collusion in presenting it”. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: Under section 11, collusion is an agreement or conspiracy, to which an applicant for a divorce is directly or indirectly a party, “for the purpose of subverting the administration of justice”, including to “fabricate or suppress evidence or to deceive the court”. It excludes an agreement to the extent it provides for separation, financial support, division of property or “the exercise of parenting time or decision-making responsibility.” (Divorce Act, s. 11 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: The court must “satisfy itself that reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage, having regard to the applicable guidelines”. If such arrangements have not been made, the court is “to stay the granting of the divorce until such arrangements are made”. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: Where divorce is sought for adultery or cruelty, the court must satisfy itself that there has been no condonation or connivance by the spouse bringing the proceeding. It dismisses the application if there was, “unless, in the opinion of the court, the public interest would be better served by granting the divorce.” Continuing or resuming cohabitation “during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose” is not condonation. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (c), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"

current_text: Duties of the parties and legal advisers
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: The Divorce Act sets out duties for parties. “A party to a proceeding under this Act shall, to the best of their ability, protect any child of the marriage from conflict arising from the proceeding.” “To the extent that it is appropriate to do so, the parties to a proceeding shall try to resolve the matters that may be the subject of an order under this Act through a family dispute resolution process.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.2, 7.3)
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: A “family dispute resolution process” means “a process outside of court that is used by parties to a family law dispute to attempt to resolve any matters in dispute, including negotiation, mediation and collaborative law”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: A party or a person subject to an order “shall provide complete, accurate and up-to-date information if required to do so under this Act.” A person subject to an order “shall comply with the order until it is no longer in effect.” A person with parenting time or decision-making responsibility for a child of the marriage, or contact under a contact order, exercises it “in a manner that is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.1, 7.4, 7.5)
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: Every document that formally starts or responds to a proceeding under the Act and is filed by a party “shall contain a statement by the party certifying that they are aware of their duties under sections 7.1 to 7.5.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.6)
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: A legal adviser acting for a spouse in a divorce proceeding has duties, unless it “would clearly not be appropriate”: to draw the spouse's attention to the Act's provisions aimed at reconciliation, to discuss the possibility of reconciliation, and to inform the spouse of known marriage counselling or guidance facilities that might help the spouses reconcile. (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: In any proceeding under the Act, a legal adviser must also encourage the person to use a family dispute resolution process unless that would clearly not be appropriate, inform the person of known family justice services, and inform them “of the parties’ duties under this Act.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: A document filed by a legal adviser that starts or responds to a proceeding “shall contain a statement by the legal adviser certifying that they have complied with this section.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"

current_text: Starting a divorce case in Ontario
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, “Either spouse may start a divorce case by,” “filing an application naming the other spouse as a respondent” or “filing a joint application with no respondent.” In a joint application, “the divorce and any other order sought shall be made only with the consent of both spouses.” (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: To start a case, a person files an application in one of the forms listed in rule 8 (1). The rules' table of forms lists Form 8A as “APPLICATION (DIVORCE)”. (Family Law Rules, r. 8 (1); Table of Forms)
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: Special service of an application must be carried out “by a person other than the party required to serve the document”, unless an exception in subrule 6 (4.2) applies, such as where “the court orders otherwise.” (Family Law Rules, r. 6 (4.1), (4.2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: If an application claims that the other spouse committed adultery with another person, “that person does not need to be named, but if named, shall be served with the application and has all the rights of a respondent in the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: “The court shall not grant a divorce until the following have been filed”: a marriage certificate or marriage registration certificate, “unless the application states that it is impractical to obtain a certificate and explains why”, and a report on earlier divorce cases started by either spouse, issued under the Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings Regulations (Canada). (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: The mandatory information program in rule 8.1 applies to certain family cases. Its attendance requirements do not apply to “parties in cases in which the only claims made are for a divorce, costs or the incorporation of the terms of an agreement or prior court order”. (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (1), (2) (d))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"

current_text: A divorce decided on affidavit evidence
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: An affidavit in Form 36 is filed by the applicant “if the respondent files no answer or files an answer and later withdraws it”, or by the applicants in a joint application. It confirms the information in the application, gives proof of the marriage if no certificate was filed, and includes the information about arrangements for support of any children required by paragraph 11 (1) (b) of the Divorce Act, among other things. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (5), (5.1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "A divorce decided on affidavit evidence"

current_text: With the affidavit, the applicant files “three copies of a draft divorce order (Form 25A)”, “a stamped envelope addressed to each party”, and, if the divorce order is to contain a support order, an extra copy of the draft order and two copies of a draft support deduction order. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "A divorce decided on affidavit evidence"

current_text: Once these requirements are met, the clerk prepares a certificate (Form 36A) and presents the documents to a judge. The judge may grant the divorce as set out in the draft order, have the documents returned for corrections, or change or refuse the order “after giving the applicant a chance to file an additional affidavit or come to court to explain why the order should be made without change.” (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "A divorce decided on affidavit evidence"

current_text: When a divorce takes effect
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: “Subject to this section, a divorce takes effect on the thirty-first day after the day on which the judgment granting the divorce is rendered.” (Divorce Act, s. 12 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "When a divorce takes effect"

current_text: The court may order that a divorce take effect earlier if it is of the opinion that “by reason of special circumstances the divorce should take effect earlier”, and “the spouses agree and undertake that no appeal from the judgment will be taken, or any appeal from the judgment that was taken has been abandoned”. (Divorce Act, s. 12 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "When a divorce takes effect"

current_text: If an appeal is pending at the end of the period referred to in subsection 12 (1), the divorce, unless voided on appeal, takes effect when the time for appealing the appeal decision expires without a further appeal. If an appeal goes to the Supreme Court of Canada, the divorce, unless voided, “takes effect on the day on which the judgment on the appeal is rendered.” (Divorce Act, s. 12 (3), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "When a divorce takes effect"

current_text: “On taking effect, a divorce granted under this Act dissolves the marriage of the spouses.” It “has legal effect throughout Canada.” (Divorce Act, ss. 13, 14)
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "When a divorce takes effect"

current_text: The divorce certificate
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce

current_text: When a divorce takes effect, a judge or officer of the court “shall, on request, issue to any person a certificate that a divorce granted under this Act dissolved the marriage of the specified persons effective as of a specified date.” The certificate “is conclusive proof of the facts so certified”. (Divorce Act, s. 12 (7), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The divorce certificate"

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, when a divorce takes effect, the clerk, “on either party’s request”, checks the record to verify that no appeal has been taken or any appeal has been disposed of, and that no order extended the time for an appeal or any extended time has expired without an appeal. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (8) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The divorce certificate"

current_text: If satisfied, the clerk issues “a divorce certificate (Form 36B)” and, unless the court orders otherwise, mails it to the parties if stamped envelopes have been filed, or emails it to them. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (8) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Getting a divorce, "The divorce certificate"

current_text: Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: This guide explains, in general terms, what Ontario’s Children’s Law Reform Act and the federal Divorce Act say about decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact and the best interests of the child. It describes what the law says; it does not say how a court would decide any particular family’s situation.
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: Words the law uses
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: In Ontario’s Children’s Law Reform Act, “decision-making responsibility” means “responsibility for making significant decisions about a child’s well-being, including with respect to,” health, education, culture, language, religion and spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Words the law uses"

current_text: “Parenting time” means “the time a child spends in the care of a parent of the child, whether or not the child is physically with the parent during that time”. “Contact” means “the time a child spends in the care of a person other than the child’s parent, whether or not the child is physically with the person during that time”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Words the law uses"

current_text: The Act says that, unless the context requires otherwise, “a reference in an Act or regulation to custody of a child, including lawful custody or legal custody of a child, includes reference to decision-making responsibility with respect to the child under this Act”. A reference to access to a child includes parenting time or contact. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Words the law uses"

current_text: The federal Divorce Act uses the same ideas. It defines decision-making responsibility as “the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child’s well-being”, including health, education, culture, language, religion and spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is “the time that a child of the marriage spends in the care of a person referred to in subsection 16.1(1), whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Words the law uses"

current_text: Which Act, and who can apply
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: The Divorce Act deals with a “child of the marriage”. That means “a child of two spouses or former spouses who, at the material time,” is under the age of majority and has not withdrawn from their charge, or is the age of majority or over and under their charge but unable, by reason of illness, disability or other cause, to withdraw from their charge or to obtain the necessaries of life. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: For Ontario, “court” in the Divorce Act means “the Superior Court of Justice”. The definition also includes any other court in the province whose judges are appointed by the Governor General and that the province designates as a court for the purposes of the Act. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: Under the Divorce Act, a court may make a parenting order on application by “either or both spouses” or by “a person, other than a spouse, who is a parent of the child, stands in the place of a parent or intends to stand in the place of a parent.” A person in that second group may apply “only with leave of the court.” (Divorce Act, s. 16.1 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: Under the Children’s Law Reform Act, “A parent of a child may apply to a court for a parenting order respecting,” decision-making responsibility and parenting time. Any person other than a parent, “including a grandparent,” may apply for a parenting order about decision-making responsibility, or for a contact order. In this Part of the Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court or the Superior Court of Justice”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 18 (1), 21 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: If a divorce action is started under the Divorce Act, an application under this Part of the Children’s Law Reform Act about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact that has not been determined “is stayed except by leave of the court.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 27)
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: A person applying under the Children’s Law Reform Act for a parenting order or contact order files an affidavit with “the person’s proposed plan for the child’s care and upbringing”, information about their involvement in any family proceedings or criminal proceedings, and other information relevant to the best-interests factors in section 24. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 21 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: Neither Act, in the text this site holds, contains one general statement that sorts parents into one Act or the other by whether they were married. This site does not yet have a source for such a rule. (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 21, 27; Divorce Act, ss. 2 (1), 16.1)
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Which Act, and who can apply"

current_text: The best interests of the child
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: In making a parenting order or contact order, the court “shall only take into account the best interests of the child in accordance with this section.” The court considers all factors related to the child’s circumstances and gives “primary consideration to the child’s physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "The best interests of the child"

current_text: The listed factors include the child’s needs, given age and stage of development, “such as the child’s need for stability”; the nature and strength of the child’s relationship with each parent, siblings, grandparents and other important people; “each parent’s willingness to support the development and maintenance of the child’s relationship with the other parent”; the history of care of the child; and “the child’s views and preferences, giving due weight to the child’s age and maturity, unless they cannot be ascertained”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "The best interests of the child"

current_text: Other listed factors are the child’s cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage, “including Indigenous upbringing and heritage”; any plans for the child’s care; the ability and willingness of each person the order would apply to, to care for and meet the child’s needs and to communicate and co-operate; any family violence and its impact; and “any civil or criminal proceeding, order, condition or measure that is relevant to the safety, security and well-being of the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "The best interests of the child"

current_text: The court “shall not take into consideration the past conduct of any person, unless the conduct is relevant to the exercise of the person’s decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with respect to the child.” In allocating parenting time, the court applies the principle that “a child should have as much time with each parent as is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "The best interests of the child"

current_text: The Divorce Act has the same structure. “The court shall take into consideration only the best interests of the child of the marriage in making a parenting order or a contact order.” It lists factors in nearly the same words, speaking of each “spouse” where the Ontario Act speaks of each “parent”, and it applies the principle that “a child should have as much time with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Divorce Act, s. 16 (1), (3), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "The best interests of the child"

current_text: Family violence
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: The Children’s Law Reform Act defines family violence as “any conduct by a family member towards another family member that is violent or threatening, that constitutes a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour, or that causes the other family member to fear for their own safety or for that of another person, and, in the case of a child, includes direct or indirect exposure to such conduct”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Family violence"

current_text: The conduct “need not constitute a criminal offence”. It includes physical abuse (including forced confinement, but not reasonable force to protect oneself or another person), sexual abuse, threats to kill or cause bodily harm, harassment including stalking, failure to provide the necessaries of life, psychological abuse, financial abuse, threats to kill or harm an animal or damage property, and killing or harming an animal or damaging property. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Family violence"

current_text: When considering the impact of family violence, the court takes into account, among other things, “the nature, seriousness and frequency of the family violence and when it occurred”; “whether there is a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour in relation to a family member”; whether the child is exposed to it; “the physical, emotional and psychological harm or risk of harm to the child”; safety and fear; steps taken to prevent further violence; and “any other relevant factor.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Family violence"

current_text: The court also takes into account any compromise to the safety of the child or other family member; whether the violence causes the child or other family member to fear for their own safety or that of another person; any steps taken by the person engaging in the violence “to prevent further family violence from occurring and improve the person’s ability to care for and meet the needs of the child”; and “any other relevant factor.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Family violence"

current_text: The Divorce Act defines family violence in similar words, covering conduct “whether or not the conduct constitutes a criminal offence”, and lists the same kinds of conduct. It sets out the same factors for the court to consider about the impact of family violence. (Divorce Act, ss. 2 (1), 16 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Family violence"

current_text: What a parenting or contact order can say
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact
