current_text: On an application under section 21, the court may grant decision-making responsibility to one or more persons, parenting time to one or more parents of the child, or contact to one or more persons other than a parent, according to the kind of application made under that section. It may “determine any aspect of the incidents of the right to decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (a), (b))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: The court may also make “any additional order the court considers necessary and proper in the circumstances”. The listed examples include orders limiting the duration, frequency, manner or location of contact or communication between any of the parties, or between a party and the child, and prohibiting a party or other person from engaging in specified conduct in the child’s presence or at any time when the person is responsible for the child’s care. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: Other listed examples are orders prohibiting a party from changing the child’s residence, school or day care facility, or removing the child from Ontario, without another party’s consent or a court order; requiring delivery of the child’s passport, health card or another specified document; requiring a party to give, or consent to the release of, information about the child’s well-being; and requiring a party to facilitate the child’s communication with another party or person. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: The court may allocate decision-making responsibility, “or any aspect of it, to one or more persons”, and may allocate parenting time “by way of a schedule.” Unless the court orders otherwise, a person with parenting time “has exclusive authority during that time to make day-to-day decisions affecting the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (4)-(6))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: The court includes in a parenting order or contact order any written parenting plan the parties submit with the elements they agree on, “subject to any changes the court may specify if it considers it to be in the best interests of the child to do so.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: Unless a court orders otherwise, a person granted decision-making responsibility or parenting time under a parenting order may ask for and, “subject to any applicable laws”, receive information about the child’s well-being, including health and education. The information may come from any other person granted decision-making responsibility or parenting time under a parenting order, or from any other person likely to have it. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: The Divorce Act gives similar powers. An order may allocate parenting time and decision-making responsibility, may “require that parenting time or the transfer of the child from one person to another be supervised”, and may “authorize or prohibit the relocation of the child.” A contact order can be made on application by “a person other than a spouse”, with leave of the court unless leave was already obtained under section 16.1. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.1 (4), (7), (8), 16.5 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: In deciding on a contact order under the Divorce Act, the court considers all relevant factors, “including whether contact between the applicant and the child could otherwise occur, for example during the parenting time of another person.” (Divorce Act, s. 16.5 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: The Divorce Act also sets out duties. A person with parenting time, decision-making responsibility or contact “shall exercise that time, responsibility or contact in a manner that is consistent with the best interests of the child.” A party “shall, to the best of their ability, protect any child of the marriage from conflict arising from the proceeding.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.1, 7.2)
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "What a parenting or contact order can say"

current_text: Changing an existing order
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: Under the Children’s Law Reform Act, a court shall not vary a parenting order or contact order “unless there has been a material change in circumstances that affects or is likely to affect the best interests of the child who is the subject of the order.” A relocation in accordance with section 39.4 is a material change in circumstances. If a court had prohibited the relocation, it “does not, in itself, constitute a material change in circumstances.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 29 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Changing an existing order"

current_text: Under the Divorce Act, before varying a parenting order or contact order, the court shall “satisfy itself that there has been a change in the circumstances of the child since the making of the order or the last variation order made in respect of the order”. The relocation of a child is deemed to be a change in circumstances, but a relocation a court has prohibited is not, in itself, such a change. (Divorce Act, s. 17 (5), (5.2), (5.3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Changing an existing order"

current_text: Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: The Act defines “relocation” as a change in residence of the child, or of a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time (or an applicant for a parenting order), that “is likely to have a significant impact on the child’s relationship with” another such person or a person who has contact under a contact order. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: For a change in residence that is not a relocation, a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time must notify any other person who has decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact under a contact order. The notice must be in writing and set out the expected date of the change and the new address and contact information. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.1 (1), (2), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: For a relocation, a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time must give the notice “at least 60 days before the expected date of the proposed relocation”. It is in the form prescribed by the regulations or, if no form is prescribed, in writing. It sets out the expected date, the new address and contact information, “a proposal as to how decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, as the case may be, could be exercised”, and any other information the regulations prescribe. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.3 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: On application, the court may provide that the notice rules do not apply, or apply with changes it specifies, if it is of the opinion that it is appropriate to do so, “including if there is a risk of family violence.” That application “may be made without notice to any other party.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 39.1 (3), (4), 39.2 (4), (5), 39.3 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: A person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time who receives a relocation notice may, “no later than 30 days after receiving the notice,” object by notifying the person who gave it, in writing with reasons and their views on the proposal, or by making an application under section 21. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.3 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: A person who has given notice of a proposed relocation in accordance with section 39.3 may relocate the child as of the date in the notice if the relocation is authorized by a court, or if no objection is made in accordance with subsection 39.3 (5) “and there is no order prohibiting the relocation.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: In deciding whether to authorize a relocation, the court considers the best interests of the child under section 24, and also factors that include the reasons for the relocation, its impact on the child, and the time spent with the child, and involvement in the child’s life, of each person with parenting time or a pending parenting application. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: The court also considers whether the person who intends to relocate the child complied with the notice requirements and any applicable Act, regulation, order, award or agreement; any order, award or agreement specifying where the child is to reside; the reasonableness of the proposal, including travel expenses; and each person’s compliance with their obligations and likelihood of future compliance. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (3) (d)-(g))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: The court “shall not consider whether, if the child’s relocation were to be prohibited, the person who intends to relocate the child would relocate without the child or not relocate.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: If the parties substantially comply with an order, family arbitration award or agreement providing that the child spend “substantially equal time in the care of each party”, the party who intends to relocate the child must prove the relocation would be in the child’s best interests. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: If they substantially comply with one providing that the child spend “the vast majority of time” in the care of the party who intends to relocate, the opposing party must prove the relocation would not be in the child’s best interests. In any other case, both parties have the burden of proving whether it is. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (6), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: If the order behind either of the first two burden rules is an interim order, “the court may determine that the subsection does not apply.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: A person who has contact under a contact order and intends to change residence must also give written notice to each person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time. If the change is likely to have a significant impact on the child’s relationship with that person, the notice is given “at least 60 days before the date on which the change is expected to occur.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.2 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act"

current_text: Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact

current_text: The Divorce Act has parallel rules. For a change of residence that is not a relocation, written notice sets out the expected date and the new address and contact information. For a relocation, notice is given “at least 60 days before the expected date of the proposed relocation and in the form prescribed by the regulations”. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.7, 16.8 (1), (2), 16.9 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act"

current_text: The court may, on application, provide that the notice requirements do not apply or modify them, “including where there is a risk of family violence.” The application may be made without notice to any other party. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.8 (3), (4), 16.9 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act"

current_text: A person with parenting time or decision-making responsibility who has received a relocation notice may object “within 30 days after the day on which the notice is received”, in a prescribed form or in an application under subsection 16.1(1) or paragraph 17(1)(b). The person who gave notice under section 16.9 may relocate the child as of the date in the notice if a court authorizes it, or if there is no such objection and no order prohibiting the relocation. (Divorce Act, s. 16.91 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act"

current_text: In deciding whether to authorize a relocation, the court considers, “in addition to the factors referred to in section 16,” a list of factors in close to the same words as the Ontario Act. The burden-of-proof rules are also parallel, and a court “may decide not to apply” the first two of them if the order involved is an interim order. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.92, 16.93, 16.94)
appears_in: Guides, Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact, "Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Child support
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: This guide explains, in general terms, what Ontario’s Family Law Act, the federal Divorce Act and the child support guidelines say about child support and how the amount is worked out. It does not calculate any amount and does not say what any particular person would pay or receive.
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: Ontario’s Family Law Act says “Every parent has an obligation to provide support, to the extent that the parent is capable of doing so, for his or her unmarried child who,” is a minor, is enrolled in a full-time program of education, or is unable by reason of illness, disability or other cause to withdraw from parental care. The obligation “does not extend to a child who is sixteen years of age or older and has withdrawn from parental control.” (Family Law Act, s. 31 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The obligation does not extend to a child “who is sixteen years of age or older and has withdrawn from parental control.” (Family Law Act, s. 31 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: “A court may, on application, order a person to provide support for his or her dependants and determine the amount of support.” A dependant is “a person to whom another has an obligation to provide support under this Part”. The application may be made by “the dependant or the dependant’s parent”, and in some cases by an agency that provides social assistance or disability support for the dependant. (Family Law Act, ss. 29, 33 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: An order for the support of a child should “recognize that each parent has an obligation to provide support for the child” and apportion the obligation according to the child support guidelines. A court making the order “shall do so in accordance with the child support guidelines.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (7), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The Act allows a different amount in two situations. The first is where special provisions in an order or written agreement benefit the child and the guidelines amount would be “inequitable given those special provisions”; the court records its reasons. The second is on the consent of both parents, where “reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of the child” and, if support for the child is payable out of public money, the arrangements do not provide for less than the guidelines amount. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (12)-(14))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: When a divorce proceeding is started under the Divorce Act, a support application under this Part of the Family Law Act that has not been adjudicated “is stayed, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 36 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The duty to support a child under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Child support under the Divorce Act
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: Under the federal Divorce Act, “A court of competent jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, make an order requiring a spouse to pay for the support of any or all children of the marriage.” The court may also make an interim order while the application is pending. (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Child support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: The court makes the order “in accordance with the applicable guidelines.” It may award a different amount where special provisions benefit the child and the guidelines amount would be inequitable, or on the consent of both spouses if “reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of the child”. (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (3), (5), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Child support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Arrangements are not unreasonable “solely because the amount of support agreed to is not the same as the amount that would otherwise have been determined in accordance with the applicable guidelines.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.1 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Child support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Where a court is considering applications for both child support and spousal support, “the court shall give priority to child support in determining the applications.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.3 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Child support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Which guidelines and which table
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: The Divorce Act defines “applicable guidelines”. If both spouses habitually reside in the same province at the time the application is made and that province has been designated by an order under subsection 2 (5), they are “the laws of the province specified in the order”. Otherwise (“in any other case”), they are the Federal Child Support Guidelines. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: This site does not yet have a source on disk that says whether Ontario has been designated under that subsection. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: Ontario’s regulation covers both kinds of case. In it, “child” means a dependant under the Family Law Act or, “in cases where the Divorce Act (Canada) applies, a child of the marriage under that Act”. In a Divorce Act case, “spouse” means “either of two persons who are married to each other and includes a former spouse”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: Under the Ontario regulation, the “table” is a table in the Federal Child Support Guidelines. If the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought ordinarily resides in Ontario at the time of the application, it is “the table set out in the Federal Child Support Guidelines for Ontario”; if elsewhere in Canada, the table for that province or territory. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1), (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: The Ontario regulation has further rules for a change of residence since the application, a move expected in the near future, and a parent or spouse who resides outside Canada or whose residence is unknown. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: The Federal Child Support Guidelines also choose the applicable table by where the spouse against whom the order is sought habitually resides, with rules for a change of province, a move expected in the near future, and a spouse who resides outside Canada or whose residence is unknown. (Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 3 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Which guidelines and which table"

current_text: The basic amount: the table amount
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: Unless the guidelines provide otherwise, the amount for children under the age of majority is “the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent or spouse against whom the order is sought”, plus any amount under section 7. The federal wording is the same except that it refers only to the spouse. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 3 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The basic amount: the table amount"

current_text: For a child who is the age of majority or over, the amount is found by applying the guidelines as if the child were under that age, or, if the court considers that inappropriate, the amount it considers appropriate “having regard to the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child and the financial ability of each parent or spouse to contribute to the support of the child.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 3 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The basic amount: the table amount"

current_text: Where the income of the person against whom the order is sought is over $150,000, the amount is the section 3 amount or, if the court considers that inappropriate, the table amount on the first $150,000 plus an amount the court considers appropriate on the balance, plus any section 7 amount. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 4; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 4)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The basic amount: the table amount"

current_text: Where medical or dental insurance for the child is available to either parent or spouse “through his or her employer or otherwise at a reasonable rate, the court may order that coverage be acquired or continued.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 6; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 6)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The basic amount: the table amount"

current_text: This guide does not calculate any amount. The guidelines say that an order must include, among other things, the income of any parent or spouse whose income is used and the amount determined under the table. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 13; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 13)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "The basic amount: the table amount"

current_text: Special or extraordinary expenses
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: On request, the court may provide for an amount to cover all or part of certain expenses, “taking into account the necessity of the expense in relation to the child’s best interests and the reasonableness of the expense in relation to the means of the parents or spouses and those of the child”, and to the spending pattern during cohabitation. The federal wording refers to “the family’s spending pattern prior to the separation”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Special or extraordinary expenses"

current_text: The listed expenses are: child care expenses related to the employment, illness, disability or education or training for employment of the parent or spouse with the majority of parenting time; the child’s portion of medical and dental insurance premiums; health-related expenses “that exceed insurance reimbursement by at least $100 annually”; extraordinary expenses for primary or secondary school or other educational programs meeting the child’s particular needs; post-secondary education expenses; and extraordinary expenses for extracurricular activities. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Special or extraordinary expenses"

current_text: For school and extracurricular expenses, “extraordinary expenses” means expenses that exceed what the requesting parent or spouse can reasonably cover, taking into account their income and the table amount they would receive (or the amount the court has otherwise determined is appropriate). (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1.1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Special or extraordinary expenses"

current_text: Where that does not apply, the court considers the amount of the expense relative to the requesting person’s income, the nature and number of programs and activities, any special needs and talents of the child, the overall cost, and other similar factors. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (1.1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 7 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Special or extraordinary expenses"

current_text: “The guiding principle” is that the expense “is shared by the parents or spouses in proportion to their respective incomes after deducting from the expense, the contribution, if any, from the child.” The court takes into account subsidies, benefits and income tax deductions or credits relating to the expense, and any eligibility to claim them, but not any universal child care benefit or eligibility to claim it. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 7 (2)-(4))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Special or extraordinary expenses"

current_text: Split and shared parenting time
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: In the guidelines, “majority of parenting time” means “a period of time that is more than 60 per cent of parenting time over the course of a year”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Split and shared parenting time"

current_text: Split parenting time: if there are two or more children and each parent or spouse has the majority of parenting time with one or more of them, the amount is “the difference between the amount that each parent or spouse would otherwise pay if such an order were sought against each of the parents or spouses.” The federal guidelines say the same thing in slightly different words. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 8; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 8)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Split and shared parenting time"

current_text: Shared parenting time: where each parent or spouse exercises parenting time “for not less than 40 per cent of the time over the course of a year”, the amount is determined by taking into account the table amounts for each of them, “the increased costs of shared parenting time arrangements”, and the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each of them and of the child. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 9; Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 9)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Split and shared parenting time"

current_text: Undue hardship
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: On the application of either spouse (or, under the Ontario regulation, an applicant under section 33 of the Family Law Act), a court may award a different amount from the amount under sections 3 to 5, 8 or 9 “if the court finds that the parent or spouse making the request, or a child in respect of whom the request is made, would otherwise suffer undue hardship.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Undue hardship"

current_text: Listed circumstances that may cause undue hardship include an “unusually high level of debts reasonably incurred” to support the family during cohabitation or to earn a living; “unusually high expenses in relation to exercising parenting time with respect to a child”; a legal duty under a judgment, order or written separation agreement to support any person; and a legal duty to support other children, or a person unable to obtain the necessaries of life due to illness or disability. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Undue hardship"

current_text: Even if undue hardship is found, the application “must be denied” if the court is of the opinion that the household of the person claiming undue hardship would, after child support is determined under sections 3 to 5, 8 or 9, have a higher standard of living than the other household. The court may use the test in Schedule II to compare. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (3), (4); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Undue hardship"

current_text: Where the court orders a different amount because of undue hardship, it “must record its reasons for doing so.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 10 (6); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 10 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Undue hardship"

current_text: How income is determined
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: Income is determined using the sources of income under the heading “Total income” in the T1 General form issued by the Canada Revenue Agency, adjusted under Schedule III, subject to sections 17 to 20. If both agree in writing on a person’s income, the court may use that amount if it is reasonable given the income information provided. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, ss. 15, 16; Federal Child Support Guidelines, ss. 15, 16)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "How income is determined"

current_text: If the section 16 figure “would not be the fairest determination of that income”, the court may look at income over the last three years. Special rules apply to a shareholder, director or officer of a corporation. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, ss. 17 (1), 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "How income is determined"

current_text: “The court may impute such amount of income to a parent or spouse as it considers appropriate in the circumstances”. Listed circumstances include being intentionally under-employed or unemployed (with exceptions for a child’s needs or the person’s reasonable educational or health needs), income diverted, and having “failed to provide income information when under a legal obligation to do so”. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 19 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "How income is determined"

current_text: An applicant whose income information is necessary to determine the amount includes with the application income tax returns and notices of assessment and reassessment “for each of the three most recent taxation years”, and other listed documents. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 21 (1); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 21 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "How income is determined"

current_text: A person served with the application whose income information is necessary must provide those documents to the court and the other party “within 30 days after the application is served” if they reside in Canada or the United States, or within 60 days if they reside elsewhere, or another time the court specifies. (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 21 (2); Federal Child Support Guidelines, s. 21 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "How income is determined"

current_text: Changing a child support order
appears_in: Guides, Child support

current_text: Where the amount includes a table determination, a change of circumstances for a variation includes “any change in circumstances that would result in a different order for the support of a child or any provision thereof.” Where it does not, it includes “any change in the condition, means, needs or other circumstances of either parent or spouse or of any child who is entitled to support.” (Child Support Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97, s. 14)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Changing a child support order"

current_text: The Federal Child Support Guidelines set out the same circumstances for varying a child support order under the Divorce Act, and the guidelines also apply to interim orders and to orders varying a child support order. (Federal Child Support Guidelines, ss. 2 (4), 14)
appears_in: Guides, Child support, "Changing a child support order"

current_text: Spousal support
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Family Law Act and the federal Divorce Act say about support between spouses and former spouses. It describes the law generally; it does not work out whether support is payable in any particular situation or how much.
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: Who is a “spouse” for support
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: In the Family Law Act, a “spouse” is either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Who is a “spouse” for support"

current_text: For support, Part III of the Act goes further. There, “spouse” “in addition includes either of two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited,” either “continuously for a period of not less than three years” or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 29)
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Who is a “spouse” for support"

current_text: The Act defines “cohabit” as “to live together in a conjugal relationship, whether within or outside marriage”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Who is a “spouse” for support"

current_text: In the Divorce Act, “spouse” “includes, in subsection 6(1) and sections 15.1 to 16.96, 21.1, 25.01 and 25.1, a former spouse”. Section 15.2 is the spousal support section. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Who is a “spouse” for support"

current_text: The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: The Act says: “Every spouse has an obligation to provide support for himself or herself and for the other spouse, in accordance with need, to the extent that he or she is capable of doing so.” (Family Law Act, s. 30)
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: “A court may, on application, order a person to provide support for his or her dependants and determine the amount of support.” A “dependant” is “a person to whom another has an obligation to provide support under this Part”. (Family Law Act, ss. 29, 33 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: An application for support of a dependant “may be made by the dependant or the dependant’s parent.” Certain government agencies may also apply for the support of a respondent’s spouse or child “if the agency is providing or has provided a benefit” of the kinds the Act lists in respect of the dependant’s support, “or if an application for such a benefit or assistance has been made to the agency by or on behalf of the dependant.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Under this Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. The Act also says “The Limitations Act, 2002 applies to an application made by the dependant’s parent or by an agency referred to in subsection (3) as if it were made by the dependant himself or herself.” (Family Law Act, ss. 1 (1), 33 (2.1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "The obligation and who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: What a spousal support order should do
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: Under the Family Law Act, “An order for the support of a spouse should,” (a) “recognize the spouse’s contribution to the relationship and the economic consequences of the relationship for the spouse”; (b) “share the economic burden of child support equitably”; (c) “make fair provision to assist the spouse to become able to contribute to his or her own support”; and (d) “relieve financial hardship, if this has not been done by orders under Parts I (Family Property) and II (Matrimonial Home).” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What a spousal support order should do"

current_text: What the court considers under the Family Law Act
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: “In determining the amount and duration, if any, of support for a spouse or parent in relation to need, the court shall consider all the circumstances of the parties”. The listed circumstances include each party’s “current assets and means” and those they are “likely to have in the future”, the dependant’s “capacity to contribute to his or her own support”, the respondent’s “capacity to provide support”, and their “age and physical and mental health”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (a)-(e))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The list also includes the dependant’s needs, having regard to “the accustomed standard of living while the parties resided together”; the measures available for the dependant to become self-supporting and their time and cost; other legal support obligations; “the desirability of the dependant or respondent remaining at home to care for a child”; and “a contribution by the dependant to the realization of the respondent’s career potential”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (f)-(j))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Where the dependant is a spouse, the court also considers “the length of time the dependant and respondent cohabited”, “the effect on the spouse’s earning capacity of the responsibilities assumed during cohabitation”, care or education of a child eighteen or over who cannot withdraw from the parents’ charge, “any housekeeping, child care or other domestic service performed by the spouse for the family”, and “the effect on the spouse’s earnings and career development of the responsibility of caring for a child”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (l))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: It also considers “any housekeeping, child care or other domestic service performed by the spouse for the family, as if the spouse were devoting the time spent in performing that service in remunerative employment and were contributing the earnings to the family’s support”. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (l) (v))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The last listed item is “any other legal right of the dependant to support, other than out of public money.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (9) (m))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: On conduct, the Act says “The obligation to provide support for a spouse exists without regard to the conduct of either spouse”. However, in setting the amount the court may consider “a course of conduct that is so unconscionable as to constitute an obvious and gross repudiation of the relationship.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (10))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "What the court considers under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Kinds of support orders under the Family Law Act
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: On a support application the court “may make an interim or final order”. Among other things, it may require “that an amount be paid periodically, whether annually or otherwise and whether for an indefinite or limited period, or until the happening of a specified event”, “that a lump sum be paid or held in trust”, or “that support be paid in respect of any period before the date of the order”. (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (a), (b), (f))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Kinds of support orders under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The court may also order property transferred to the dependant, require a spouse with life insurance or a pension or benefit plan to name the other spouse or a child as beneficiary, and require “the securing of payment under the order, by a charge on property or otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (c), (i), (j), (k))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Kinds of support orders under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The Ontario Court of Justice “shall not make an order under clause (1) (b), (c), (i), (j) or (k) except for the provision of necessities or to prevent the dependant from becoming or continuing to be a public charge, and shall not make an order under clause (d).” Clause (d) is an order respecting matrimonial home matters under clause 24 (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e). (Family Law Act, s. 34 (1) (d), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Kinds of support orders under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Spousal support under the Divorce Act
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: Under the Divorce Act, a court “may, on application by either or both spouses, make an order requiring a spouse to secure or pay, or to secure and pay, such lump sum or periodic sums, or such lump sum and periodic sums, as the court thinks reasonable for the support of the other spouse.” The court may also make an interim order while the application is pending. (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: An order may be “for a definite or indefinite period or until a specified event occurs”, and the court “may impose terms, conditions or restrictions in connection with the order as it thinks fit and just.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: The court “shall take into consideration the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, including” (a) “the length of time the spouses cohabited”; (b) “the functions performed by each spouse during cohabitation”; and (c) “any order, agreement or arrangement relating to support of either spouse.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: The court “shall not take into consideration any misconduct of a spouse in relation to the marriage.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: An order “should” (a) “recognize any economic advantages or disadvantages to the spouses arising from the marriage or its breakdown”; (b) “apportion between the spouses any financial consequences arising from the care of any child of the marriage”, over and above child support; (c) “relieve any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the breakdown of the marriage”; and (d) “in so far as practicable, promote the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period of time.” (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Where a court has applications for both child support and spousal support, it “shall give priority to child support in determining the applications.” If that reduces or prevents spousal support, a later reduction or end of child support “constitutes a change of circumstances” for applying for spousal support or a variation. (Divorce Act, s. 15.3 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Spousal support under the Divorce Act"

current_text: Agreements about support
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements and separation agreements are kinds of “domestic contract”, and each may deal with “support obligations”. A domestic contract is “unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed.” (Family Law Act, ss. 51, 52 (1) (b), 53 (1) (b), 54 (b), 55 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Agreements about support"

current_text: “A domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails unless this Act provides otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (10))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Agreements about support"

current_text: The court “may set aside a provision for support or a waiver of the right to support in a domestic contract” and order support, even if the contract says the support section does not apply, in three situations: if the provision or waiver “results in unconscionable circumstances”; if it involves a dependant “who qualifies for an allowance for support out of public money”; or “if there is default in the payment of support under the contract at the time the application is made.” (Family Law Act, s. 33 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Agreements about support"

current_text: Under the Divorce Act, “any order, agreement or arrangement relating to support of either spouse” is one of the listed factors the court considers. (Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support, "Agreements about support"

current_text: What the site does not have a source for yet
appears_in: Guides, Spousal support

current_text: This site does not yet have a source for the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines, so this guide does not describe them, what they contain, or how they are used. What this guide covers is limited to the purposes, objectives and factors set out in the Family Law Act and Divorce Act sections above. (Family Law Act, s. 33 (8)-(9); Divorce Act, s. 15.2 (4), (6))

current_text: Dividing property when a marriage ends
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: This guide explains what Part I of Ontario's Family Law Act says about sharing the value of property when spouses separate, divorce or a spouse dies, and what the Family Law Rules require parties to disclose. It describes the law generally; it does not calculate anyone's entitlement.
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: Who Part I applies to
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: Part I (Family Property) uses the Act’s general definition of “spouse”: either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"

current_text: Part I’s own definitions do not add unmarried partners. By contrast, the wider definition in Part III (Support Obligations), stated to apply “In this Part”, adds two persons “who are not married to each other and have cohabited,” either “continuously for a period of not less than three years” or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, ss. 4 (1), 29)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"

current_text: For Part I, “court” means a court as defined in subsection 1 (1), “but does not include the Ontario Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"

current_text: Net family property and the valuation date
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: “Net family property” means “the value of all the property, except property described in subsection (2), that a spouse owns on the valuation date”, after deducting the spouse’s debts and other liabilities, and the value of property, “other than a matrimonial home”, that the spouse owned on the date of the marriage. That date-of-marriage value is net of the spouse’s debts and liabilities at that date, “other than debts or liabilities related directly to the acquisition or significant improvement of a matrimonial home”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"

current_text: The liabilities deducted in calculating net family property “include any applicable contingent tax liabilities in respect of the property.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"

current_text: The “valuation date” is “the earliest of” these dates: “The date the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; “The date a divorce is granted”; “The date the marriage is declared a nullity”; the date an application for improvident depletion is started that is later granted; and “The date before the date on which one of the spouses dies leaving the other spouse surviving.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"

current_text: “Property” is defined broadly as “any interest, present or future, vested or contingent, in real or personal property”. For a pension plan, it includes the “imputed value, for family law purposes, of the spouse’s interest in the plan”, for the period from the date of marriage to the valuation date. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"

current_text: When section 4 requires a value to be calculated as of a given date, it “shall be calculated as of close of business on that date.” If a spouse’s net family property as calculated under subsections (1), (2) and (4) is less than zero, “it shall be deemed to be equal to zero.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"

current_text: Excluded property
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: Some property a spouse owns on the valuation date “does not form part of the spouse’s net family property”. The list includes property, “other than a matrimonial home, that was acquired by gift or inheritance from a third person after the date of the marriage”, and income from that property if the donor or testator “has expressly stated that it is to be excluded”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 1, 2)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"

current_text: The list also includes damages, or a right to damages, for personal injuries, nervous shock, mental distress or loss of guidance, care and companionship, or the part of a settlement that represents those damages. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), para. 3)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"

current_text: The list also includes certain life insurance proceeds payable on death; property, other than a matrimonial home, into which property described in paragraphs 1 to 4 “can be traced”; “Property that the spouses have agreed by a domestic contract is not to be included in the spouse’s net family property”; and “Unadjusted pensionable earnings under the Canada Pension Plan.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 4-7)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"

current_text: The Act places the onus of proving a deduction from net family property, or an exclusion under subsection 4 (2), on the person claiming it: the onus “is on the person claiming it.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"

current_text: Equalization and unequal shares
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: When a divorce is granted, a marriage is declared a nullity, or the spouses are separated with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, “the spouse whose net family property is the lesser of the two net family properties is entitled to one-half the difference between them.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: When a spouse dies, the surviving spouse is entitled to one-half the difference only “if the net family property of the deceased spouse exceeds the net family property of the surviving spouse”. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: While spouses are cohabiting, “if there is a serious danger that one spouse may improvidently deplete his or her net family property”, the other spouse may apply under section 7 to have the difference divided as if they had separated. After such an order, “neither spouse may make a further application under section 7 in respect of their marriage.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: The Act states the purpose of section 5: to recognize that “child care, household management and financial provision are the joint responsibilities of the spouses” and that “inherent in the marital relationship there is equal contribution, whether financial or otherwise, by the spouses to the assumption of these responsibilities, entitling each spouse to the equalization of the net family properties, subject only to the equitable considerations set out in subsection (6).” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: The court “may award a spouse an amount that is more or less than half the difference between the net family properties if the court is of the opinion that equalizing the net family properties would be unconscionable”. The circumstances it has regard to include failure to disclose debts existing at marriage, debts “incurred recklessly or in bad faith”, gifts from the other spouse, and “a spouse’s intentional or reckless depletion of his or her net family property”. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (a)-(d))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: The other listed circumstances are an amount “disproportionately large in relation to a period of cohabitation that is less than five years”; one spouse incurring “a disproportionately larger amount of debts or other liabilities than the other spouse for the support of the family”; “a written agreement between the spouses that is not a domestic contract”; and “any other circumstance relating to the acquisition, disposition, preservation, maintenance or improvement of property.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (e)-(h))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"

current_text: Applying to the court and the time limits
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: “The court may, on the application of a spouse, former spouse or deceased spouse’s personal representative, determine any matter respecting the spouses’ entitlement under section 5.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"

current_text: An application based on subsection 5 (1) or (2) “shall not be brought after the earliest of,” (a) “two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity”; (b) “six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; (c) “six months after the first spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"

current_text: Separately, the Act says the court “may, on motion, extend a time prescribed by this Act” if it is satisfied that “there are apparent grounds for relief”, that “relief is unavailable because of delay that has been incurred in good faith”, and that “no person will suffer substantial prejudice by reason of the delay.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"

current_text: What the court can order
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: In an application under section 7, the court may order one spouse to pay the other the amount the court finds that spouse is entitled to, and that security be given. If “necessary to avoid hardship”, payment may be made in instalments or delayed for “a period not exceeding ten years”. If appropriate to satisfy an obligation imposed by the order, property may be transferred to a spouse, or “partitioned or sold”. (Family Law Act, s. 9 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"

current_text: An order made under section 9 or 10 “shall not be made so as to require or result in the sale of an operating business or farm or so as to seriously impair its operation, unless there is no reasonable alternative method of satisfying the award.” (Family Law Act, s. 11 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"

current_text: In an application under section 7 or 10, if the court “considers it necessary for the protection of the other spouse’s interests under this Part”, it may make an interim or final order “restraining the depletion of a spouse’s property” and for its “possession, delivering up, safekeeping and preservation”. (Family Law Act, s. 12)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"

current_text: Separately, a person may apply for a determination of a question with a spouse or former spouse “as to the ownership or right to possession of particular property, other than a question arising out of an equalization of net family properties under section 5”. (Family Law Act, s. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"

current_text: Financial disclosure
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: In an application under section 7, each party must serve and file a sworn or declared statement “disclosing particulars of” the party’s property, debts and other liabilities as of the date of marriage, the valuation date and the date of the statement; the deductions and exclusions claimed; and property disposed of “during the two years immediately preceding the making of the statement, or during the marriage, whichever period is shorter.” (Family Law Act, s. 8)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, when an application, answer or motion contains “a property claim”, the party making the claim “shall serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1)” with it, and the other party must do so within the time for responding. If there is a property claim, the financial statement “shall be in Form 13.1, whether a claim for support is also included or not.” (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (1), (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"

current_text: For a Part I claim, unless the court orders otherwise, a party must, “no later than 30 days after the day by which the financial statement is required to be served”, serve further documents. These include statements closest to the valuation date for accounts, savings and investments; any pension valuation request made; property assessments; life insurance statements; and business, partnership, corporation and trust records. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (3.3), paras. 1-9)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"

current_text: They also include documentation of the valuation-date value of any other property; “Documentation that supports a claim, if any, for an exclusion under subsection 4 (2) of the Family Law Act”; statements for debts owed on the valuation date; and “Any available documentation showing the value, on the date of marriage,” of property and debts. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (3.3), paras. 10-13)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"

current_text: A party serving these documents confirms service with “a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A)”. If a party thinks the other’s disclosure is not enough, “the party shall make a request in writing to the other party for the necessary additional information”, and if it is not given “within seven days of the request”, the court may order it. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (5.0.2), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"

current_text: Agreements about property
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

current_text: Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements and separation agreements may each deal with “ownership in or division of property”. A domestic contract is “unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed.” (Family Law Act, ss. 52 (1) (a), 53 (1) (a), 54 (a), 55 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Agreements about property"

current_text: “A domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails unless this Act provides otherwise.” Property the spouses have agreed by domestic contract is not to be included is excluded property. (Family Law Act, ss. 2 (10), 4 (2), para. 6)
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Agreements about property"

current_text: A court may, on application, set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it “if a party failed to disclose to the other significant assets, or significant debts or other liabilities, existing when the domestic contract was made”, “if a party did not understand the nature or consequences of the domestic contract”, or “otherwise in accordance with the law of contract.” (Family Law Act, s. 56 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Agreements about property"

current_text: The matrimonial home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, what Part II of Ontario's Family Law Act says about the matrimonial home: what it is, who may live in it, and the orders a court may make about it. It explains what the law says; it does not say how the law applies to any particular home or family.
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: What counts as a matrimonial home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: Part II of the Family Law Act deals with the matrimonial home. It says: “Every property in which a person has an interest and that is or, if the spouses have separated, was at the time of separation ordinarily occupied by the person and his or her spouse as their family residence is their matrimonial home.” In Part II, “property” means “real or personal property.” (Family Law Act, ss. 17, 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"

current_text: Part II does not give its own definition of “spouse”. The Act's general definition says “spouse” means either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"

current_text: Owning shares in a corporation that entitle the owner “to occupy a housing unit owned by the corporation” is treated as an interest in the unit. If property that includes a matrimonial home “is normally used for a purpose other than residential”, the matrimonial home is only the part “that may reasonably be regarded as necessary to the use and enjoyment of the residence.” (Family Law Act, s. 18 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"

current_text: Part II “applies to matrimonial homes that are situated in Ontario.” It applies whether the spouses were married before or after March 1, 1986, and whether the home was acquired before or after that day. (Family Law Act, s. 28)
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"

current_text: The Act defines “court” as “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. For Part II, “court” means a court as defined in subsection 1 (1) “but does not include the Ontario Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, ss. 1 (1), 17)
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"

current_text: The right to live in the home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: The Act says: “Both spouses have an equal right to possession of a matrimonial home.” (Family Law Act, s. 19 (1))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"

current_text: When only one spouse has an interest in the home, the other spouse's right of possession “is personal as against the first spouse” and “ends when they cease to be spouses, unless a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 19 (2))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"

current_text: A spouse who has no interest in a matrimonial home but is occupying it when the other spouse dies, “whether under an order for exclusive possession or otherwise, is entitled to retain possession against the spouse’s estate, rent free, for sixty days after the spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 26 (2))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"

current_text: If a spouse dies owning an interest in a matrimonial home as a joint tenant with a third person, and not with the other spouse, “the joint tenancy shall be deemed to have been severed immediately before the time of death.” (Family Law Act, s. 26 (1))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"

current_text: Designating a matrimonial home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: “One or both spouses may designate property owned by one or both of them as a matrimonial home, in the form prescribed by the regulations.” The designation may include property described in it that is contiguous to the matrimonial home, and it “may be registered in the proper land registry office.” (Family Law Act, s. 20 (1)-(3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"

current_text: When a designation made by both spouses is registered, any other property that is a matrimonial home under section 18 but is not designated by both spouses “ceases to be a matrimonial home.” When a designation made by one spouse only is registered, any other matrimonial home under section 18 “remains a matrimonial home.” (Family Law Act, s. 20 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"

current_text: A designation is cancelled, and the property stops being a matrimonial home, on the registration or deposit of a cancellation in the prescribed form signed by the person or persons who made it, “a decree absolute of divorce or judgment of nullity”, an order under clause 23 (e) cancelling it, or “proof of death of one of the spouses.” When a designation by both spouses is cancelled, section 18 applies again to other property that is a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 20 (6), (7))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"

current_text: Disposing of or encumbering the home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: “No spouse shall dispose of or encumber an interest in a matrimonial home unless,” “the other spouse joins in the instrument or consents to the transaction”; the other spouse “has released all rights under this Part by a separation agreement”; “a court order has authorized the transaction or has released the property from the application of this Part”; or the property is not designated by both spouses and a designation of another property by both spouses is registered and not cancelled. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (1))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: A transaction made contrary to subsection 21 (1) “may be set aside on an application under section 23”. That does not apply if the person holding the interest or encumbrance at the time of the application “acquired it for value, in good faith and without notice”, when acquiring it or agreeing to acquire it, that the property was a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (2))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: A statement by the person making the disposition or encumbrance, verifying one of the matters listed in subsection 21 (3) (for example, that the person “is not, or was not, a spouse at the time of the disposition or encumbrance”), is deemed to be “sufficient proof that the property is not a matrimonial home”, unless the person receiving it “had notice to the contrary”. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: On the application of a spouse or a person having an interest in property, the court may, among other things, “determine whether or not the property is a matrimonial home and, if so, its extent”, set aside a transaction made contrary to subsection 21 (1), or cancel a designation if the property is not a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 23 (a), (d), (e))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: The court may also authorize a disposition or encumbrance of the home if it finds that the spouse whose consent is required “cannot be found or is not available”, “is not capable of giving or withholding consent”, or “is unreasonably withholding consent”, subject to any conditions the court considers appropriate, “including provision of other comparable accommodation or payment in place of it”. (Family Law Act, s. 23 (b))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: When someone enforces a lien, encumbrance or execution, or exercises a forfeiture, against a matrimonial home, the spouse who has a right of possession under section 19 “has the same right of redemption or relief against forfeiture as the other spouse and is entitled to the same notice respecting the claim and its enforcement or realization.” For a power of sale, sections 33 and 34 of the Mortgages Act apply. (Family Law Act, s. 22 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"

current_text: Orders about possession of the home
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: “Regardless of the ownership of a matrimonial home and its contents, and despite section 19 (spouse’s right of possession), the court may on application, by order,” among other things, “direct that one spouse be given exclusive possession of the matrimonial home or part of it for the period that the court directs”, and direct the spouse given exclusive possession “to make periodic payments to the other spouse”. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (1) (b), (c))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: Other orders listed in subsection 24 (1) include providing for “the delivering up, safekeeping and preservation of the matrimonial home and its contents”, directing that contents stay in the home or be removed “for the use of a spouse or child”, ordering a spouse to pay for “all or part of the repair and maintenance of the matrimonial home”, and authorizing a disposition or encumbrance of a spouse’s interest “subject to the other spouse’s right of exclusive possession as ordered”. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (1) (a), (d), (e), (f))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: “The court may, on motion, make a temporary or interim order under clause (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e).” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (2))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: In deciding whether to make an order for exclusive possession, “the court shall consider,” “the best interests of the children affected”; “any existing orders under Part I (Family Property) and any existing support orders or other enforceable support obligations”; “the financial position of both spouses”; “any written agreement between the parties”; “the availability of other suitable and affordable accommodation”; and “any violence committed by a spouse against the other spouse or the children.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: In determining the best interests of a child, the court shall consider “the possible disruptive effects on the child of a move to other accommodation” and “the child’s views and preferences, if they can reasonably be ascertained.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (4))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: In making any order under Part II, the court may also make an interim order prohibiting a party “from directly or indirectly contacting or communicating with another party”, if it determines that the order “is necessary to ensure that an application under this Part is dealt with justly.” (Family Law Act, s. 25.1)
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"

current_text: Contravening, changing and registering orders
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: “A person who contravenes an order for exclusive possession is guilty of an offence”. On conviction, for a first offence the Act sets a fine of not more than $5,000 or imprisonment of not more than three months, or both; for a second or subsequent offence, a fine of not more than $10,000 or imprisonment of not more than two years, or both. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (5))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Contravening, changing and registering orders"

current_text: “A police officer may arrest without warrant a person the police officer believes on reasonable and probable grounds to have contravened an order for exclusive possession.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (6))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Contravening, changing and registering orders"

current_text: A person named in an order under clause 24 (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e), or their personal representative, may apply, and “if the court is satisfied that there has been a material change in circumstances, the court may discharge, vary or suspend the order.” Conditions imposed under clause 23 (b) or (d) or 24 (1) (g) may be discharged, varied or suspended on motion if the court is satisfied they “are no longer appropriate”. (Family Law Act, s. 25 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Contravening, changing and registering orders"

current_text: Orders made under Part II “are registrable against land under the Registry Act and the Land Titles Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 27)
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "Contravening, changing and registering orders"

current_text: The mandatory information program
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home

current_text: Rule 8.1 of the Family Law Rules applies to cases started after August 31, 2011 that deal with, among other things, “A claim respecting a matrimonial home under Part II of the Family Law Act.” The program provides parties “with information about separation and the legal process”. (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The mandatory information program"

current_text: “Each party to a case shall attend the program no later than 45 days after the case is started.” Subrule 8.1 (2) lists exceptions, including “parties in cases that are proceeding on consent” and “parties who have already attended a mandatory information program.” (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The mandatory information program"

current_text: The court may also, on motion, order that the attendance requirement and related subrules do not apply to a party “because of urgency or hardship or for some other reason in the interest of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (8))
appears_in: Guides, The matrimonial home, "The mandatory information program"

current_text: Restraining orders in family cases
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, the restraining orders available under section 46 of Ontario's Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act: who may apply, against whom, and what an order may contain. It explains what the law says; it does not say whether an order is available in any particular situation.
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases
