current_text: Two laws that provide restraining orders
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: Two Ontario laws let a family court make a restraining order: section 46 of the Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Under both, the court may make “an interim or final restraining order”. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Two laws that provide restraining orders"

current_text: In the Family Law Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. In Part III of the Children's Law Reform Act, where section 35 appears, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court or the Superior Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Two laws that provide restraining orders"

current_text: Who can apply under the Family Law Act
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: The wording of section 46 now in force says: “On application, the court may make an interim or final restraining order against a person described in subsection (2) if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or for the safety of any child in his or her lawful custody.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Under the wording now in force, the order may be made against “a spouse or former spouse of the applicant”, or against a person other than a spouse or former spouse of the applicant, “if the person is cohabiting with the applicant or has cohabited with the applicant for any period of time.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: The Act defines “cohabit” as “to live together in a conjugal relationship, whether within or outside marriage”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Section 46 is in Part III of the Act, where “spouse” means a spouse as defined in subsection 1 (1) and also includes either of two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited “continuously for a period of not less than three years”, or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 29)
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Family Law Act"

current_text: Who can apply under the Children's Law Reform Act
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: The wording of section 35 now in force says: “On application, the court may make an interim or final restraining order against any person if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or for the safety of any child in his or her lawful custody.” (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Children's Law Reform Act"

current_text: Unlike section 46 of the Family Law Act, section 35 does not limit who the order may be made against: it says “against any person”. (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1); Family Law Act, s. 46 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Who can apply under the Children's Law Reform Act"

current_text: What an order can include
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: Under both laws, a restraining order “shall be in the form prescribed by the rules of court and may contain one or more of the following provisions, as the court considers appropriate”. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (3); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "What an order can include"

current_text: The provisions listed in the wording now in force are: “Restraining the respondent, in whole or in part, from directly or indirectly contacting or communicating with the applicant or any child in the applicant’s lawful custody.”; “Restraining the respondent from coming within a specified distance of one or more locations.”; “Specifying one or more exceptions to the provisions described in paragraphs 1 and 2.”; and “Any other provision that the court considers appropriate.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (3); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "What an order can include"

current_text: Forms and court procedure
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: Under the Family Law Rules, a restraining order under section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act or section 46 of the Family Law Act “shall be in Form 25F or 25G.” The rules' table of forms lists Form 25F as “RESTRAINING ORDER” and Form 25G as “RESTRAINING ORDER ON MOTION WITHOUT NOTICE”. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (11) (b), (11.1); Table of Forms)
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: An order terminating one of these restraining orders “shall be in Form 25H.” The clerk prepares a restraining order, or an order terminating one, for signature “as soon as it is made”. (Family Law Rules, r. 25 (11) (b), (11.2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: The mandatory information program in rule 8.1 applies to cases started after August 31, 2011 that deal with, among other things, “A restraining order under the Family Law Act or the Children’s Law Reform Act.” Each party attends “no later than 45 days after the case is started”, subject to the exceptions in subrule 8.1 (2). (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (1), (2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: On motion, the court may order that any or all of the program's attendance requirements in subrules 8.1 (4) to (7) do not apply to a party “because of urgency or hardship or for some other reason in the interest of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 8.1 (8))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: “In a proceeding for corollary relief” under the Divorce Act, the court has a duty to consider whether “a civil protection order or a proceeding in relation to such an order” is pending or in effect, unless it “would clearly not be appropriate to do so”. (Divorce Act, s. 7.8 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: For that section, a “civil protection order” is “a civil order that is made to protect a person’s safety”, including an order prohibiting contacting or communicating with a specified person, directly or indirectly, or being within a certain distance of a specified place. (Divorce Act, s. 7.8 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Forms and court procedure"

current_text: Amendments that are not yet in force
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: The published text of both sections also prints replacement wording passed in 2025. For section 46, the Act notes that “On a day to be named by order of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, subsection 46 (1) of the Act is repealed and the following substituted”. Its amendment table lists “2025, c. 6, Sched. 6, s. 1 (1, 2) - not in force”. This guide describes only the wording now in force. (Family Law Act, s. 46)
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Amendments that are not yet in force"

current_text: Section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act carries the same kind of note, and its amendment table lists “2025, c. 6, Sched. 2, s. 1 (1-3) - not in force”. (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35)
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Amendments that are not yet in force"

current_text: Each section also says that the section “as it read on October 14, 2009, continues to apply to” proceedings begun under it before October 15, 2009 and to orders made under it that were in force on October 14, 2009. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (4); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Amendments that are not yet in force"

current_text: If an order is not followed
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases

current_text: The Family Law Act gives the Ontario Court of Justice a power, “In addition to its powers in respect of contempt”, to punish by fine or imprisonment, or by both, “any wilful contempt of or resistance to its process, rules or orders under this Act, other than orders under section 46”. The fine may not exceed $5,000 and the imprisonment may not exceed ninety days. (Family Law Act, s. 49 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "If an order is not followed"

current_text: The Children's Law Reform Act has a similar provision, with the same limits, that excludes “orders under section 35”. (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 38 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "If an order is not followed"

current_text: Neither section 46 of the Family Law Act nor section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act sets out what happens if a restraining order is breached. This site does not yet have a source on the consequences of breaching a restraining order. (Family Law Act, ss. 46, 49 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, ss. 35, 38 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "If an order is not followed"

current_text: Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 says about who it covers, the role of the Landlord and Tenant Board, repairs, rent deposits, ending a tenancy and applications to the Board. It describes the Act generally and does not say how it applies to any particular tenancy.
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: What the Act covers
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: Except for Part V.1, the Act says it “applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” A “rental unit” means “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises”. It includes “a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 3 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"

current_text: A “tenancy agreement” means “a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit”. Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, “a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 4 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"

current_text: If the Act conflicts with another Act, the Act applies, with one exception: “other than the Human Rights Code”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 3 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"

current_text: Housing the Act does not cover
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: Section 5 lists kinds of living accommodation the Act “does not apply with respect to”. Examples include accommodation for “the travelling or vacationing public” in places such as hotels, motels and campgrounds, and “short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (a), (f))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Housing the Act does not cover"

current_text: Another listed exemption is accommodation where the occupant is “required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner's spouse, child or parent or the spouse's child or parent”, and that person “lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”. The full list in section 5 has more categories, such as certain student housing and farm-employment housing. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (b), (g), (i))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Housing the Act does not cover"

current_text: A separate statute, the Commercial Tenancies Act, says: “This Act does not apply to tenancies and tenancy agreements to which the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.” (Commercial Tenancies Act, s. 2)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Housing the Act does not cover"

current_text: The Landlord and Tenant Board
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: The Act continues the former tribunal “under the name Landlord and Tenant Board”. It says: “The Board has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all applications under this Act and with respect to all matters in which jurisdiction is conferred on it by this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 168 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "The Landlord and Tenant Board"

current_text: The Board “has authority to hear and determine all questions of law and fact with respect to all matters within its jurisdiction under this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 174)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "The Landlord and Tenant Board"

current_text: Tribunals Ontario describes the Board as the place to “Resolve a dispute with a landlord or tenant, and/or end a tenancy or co-op member’s occupancy”. Its page says the Tribunals Ontario Portal can be used to “submit applications, check file status, upload evidence and use the dispute resolution tool to try and reach an agreement.” (Tribunals Ontario, Landlord and Tenant Board)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "The Landlord and Tenant Board"

current_text: Money limits and going to court
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: Where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, the Board may order payment “of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Money limits and going to court"

current_text: A person entitled to apply under the Act “but whose claim exceeds the Board's monetary jurisdiction may commence a proceeding in any court of competent jurisdiction”. The court may then exercise any powers the Board could have exercised. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Money limits and going to court"

current_text: If a party claims an amount at or below the Board's limit, “all rights of the party in excess of the Board's monetary jurisdiction are extinguished once the Board issues its order.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Money limits and going to court"

current_text: Repairs and maintenance
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: Under the Act, “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.” This applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair, or of “a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 20 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Repairs and maintenance"

current_text: If the Board determines on a tenant's application that a landlord breached this obligation, the orders it may make include to “Terminate the tenancy”, “Order an abatement of rent”, and “Order the landlord to do specified repairs or replacements or other work within a specified time.” The full list is in section 30. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 30 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Repairs and maintenance"

current_text: Rent deposits
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: The Act says: “The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.” A landlord may require a rent deposit “if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 105 (1), 106 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Rent deposits"

current_text: The deposit “shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.” The landlord “shall pay interest to the tenant annually” on the deposit at the rent increase guideline rate. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (2), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Rent deposits"

current_text: A landlord “shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (10))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Rent deposits"

current_text: Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: The Act says: “A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act.” A notice of termination must be in a form approved by the Board (or a prescribed form), and must identify the rental unit, state the termination date, and be signed by the person giving it or that person's agent. A landlord's notice must also “set out the reasons and details respecting the termination”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 37 (1), 43)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: A landlord's notice must tell the tenant that if the tenant does not move out, “the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant”, and that “the tenant is entitled to dispute the application.” A tenant may end a tenancy at the end of a period or term by giving notice under section 44. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 43 (2), 47)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: Grounds on which the Act lets a landlord give notice include: non-payment of rent; persistent late payment; an illegal act; undue damage; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; an act that seriously impairs safety; and more people living in the unit than health, safety or housing standards allow. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 58 to 67)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: Other grounds include the landlord or a purchaser requiring the unit in good faith for residential occupation by listed people (such as the landlord or purchaser, their spouse, or a child or parent). Each ground has its own conditions in the section that sets it out. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 48, 49)
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: A landlord may also give notice if the landlord requires possession of the rental unit to “demolish it”, to “convert it to use for a purpose other than residential premises”, or to do repairs or renovations “that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 50 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: For these notices, the termination date “shall be at least 120 days after the notice is given and shall be the day a period of the tenancy ends or, where the tenancy is for a fixed term, the end of the term.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 50 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"

current_text: Applications to the Board and their time limits
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

current_text: A tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for the orders listed in section 29, about: the landlord's repair obligation; withholding or deliberately interfering with the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference by the landlord, superintendent or agent; altering the locking system without giving replacement keys; and illegal entry. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"

current_text: For these tenant applications, “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"

current_text: A landlord who has given notice may apply for “an order terminating a tenancy and evicting the tenant”. That application “may not be made later than 30 days after the termination date specified in the notice”, but this does not apply to an application based on failure to pay rent. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 69 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"

current_text: A landlord may also apply for an order that a tenant or former tenant pay arrears of rent, or pay reasonable repair or replacement costs where the tenant, another occupant or a person the tenant permitted there wilfully or negligently caused undue damage. Each may be made “while the tenant is in possession of the rental unit” or “no later than one year after the tenant or former tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 87 (1), (1.1), 89 (1), (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"

current_text: Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Human Rights Code says about equal treatment and harassment, how an application to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario works, what the Tribunal can order, and when a court can deal with a human rights claim. It describes the law generally and does not say how it applies to anyone's situation.
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: Part I of the Code is headed Freedom from Discrimination. It gives every person a right to equal treatment “with respect to services, goods and facilities” and “with respect to the occupancy of accommodation”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 2 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"

current_text: Part I also covers contracts, employment and vocational associations. Every person having legal capacity “has a right to contract on equal terms”. Every person has a right to equal treatment “with respect to employment”, and with respect to “membership in any trade union, trade or occupational association or self-governing profession”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 3, 5 (1), 6)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"

current_text: The Code also says: “No person shall infringe or do, directly or indirectly, anything that infringes a right under this Part.” Part II then sets out cases in which a right under Part I “is not infringed”, for example by “the implementation of a special program” of the kind section 14 describes. (Human Rights Code, ss. 9, 14 (1), 17 (1), 18)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"

current_text: The protected grounds
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: For services, the listed grounds are “race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability.” The same list applies to contracts and to vocational associations. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 3, 6)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"

current_text: For housing, the list adds “the receipt of public assistance”. For employment, the list adds “record of offences”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (1), 5 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"

current_text: The Code defines some grounds. For example, “age” means “an age that is 18 years or more”. Section 10 has the other definitions, including “disability” and “marital status”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"

current_text: Community Legal Education Ontario describes the same protections in plain words: the Code “says that everyone has the right to be treated equally and not be discriminated against” at work, in housing, in a union or professional group, and by a service provider. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I make a claim to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"

current_text: Harassment and reprisal
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: The Code defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"

current_text: A person who occupies accommodation has a right to freedom from harassment “by the landlord or agent of the landlord or by an occupant of the same building” because of listed grounds. An employee has a right to freedom from harassment “in the workplace by the employer or agent of the employer or by another employee” because of listed grounds. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (2), 5 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"

current_text: Section 7 deals with harassment “because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression” in housing and at work. It also gives a right to be free from a sexual solicitation or advance by “a person in a position to confer, grant or deny a benefit or advancement” where that person “knows or ought reasonably to know that it is unwelcome”, and from a reprisal or threat of reprisal by such a person for rejecting one. (Human Rights Code, s. 7)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"

current_text: Every person has a right “to claim and enforce his or her rights under this Act, to institute and participate in proceedings under this Act and to refuse to infringe a right of another person under this Act, without reprisal or threat of reprisal for so doing.” (Human Rights Code, s. 8)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"

current_text: Disability and the duty to accommodate
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: A right under the Code is not infringed “for the reason only that the person is incapable of performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements attending the exercise of the right because of disability.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"

current_text: But no tribunal or court “shall find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.” In deciding whether there would be undue hardship, a tribunal or court “shall consider any standards prescribed by the regulations.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"

current_text: CLEO explains that for a tenant with a disability, a landlord “must make adjustments so that you can use and access your apartment and your building”, unless this would cause undue hardship. It adds that where a landlord and tenant cannot agree, “the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario might have to decide. In some situations, the Landlord and Tenant Board may also decide.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: I have mobility issues. Does my landlord have to make adjustments to the rental unit for me?, last reviewed March 4, 2021)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"

current_text: Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: Tribunals Ontario says the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) “resolves claims of discrimination and harassment under the Human Rights Code”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"

current_text: A person who believes their Part I rights were infringed may apply to the Tribunal “within one year after the incident to which the application relates” or, “if there was a series of incidents, within one year after the last incident in the series.” The application “shall be in a form approved by the Tribunal.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"

current_text: A person may apply after the one-year limit “if the Tribunal is satisfied that the delay was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"

current_text: A person or organization, other than the Commission, may apply on behalf of another person if that person would have been entitled to apply and “consents to the application.” Two or more people entitled to apply may file jointly, subject to any Tribunal rule that lets the Tribunal direct that an application be considered in a separate proceeding. (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"

current_text: Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: CLEO explains that “Mediation is when you, the Respondent, and an HRTO member try to resolve your case before it goes to a hearing.” The HRTO member “will not make any decisions” at mediation. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"

current_text: CLEO says that for applications filed after June 1, 2025, “you will have to do mediation first to try and resolve your issue.” For applications filed before June 1, 2025, it says the HRTO will ask the parties to try mediation, but it is not required. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"

current_text: If the parties agree, they sign a document “usually called a settlement agreement”, and the HRTO then closes the case. If they cannot agree, there is a hearing on another date with a different HRTO member. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"

current_text: At a hearing, both sides present their case to an HRTO member. The member listens to both sides and any witnesses, looks at the evidence, and then decides. CLEO notes: “The HRTO member usually does not give a decision at the hearing. They will send you one later.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at a Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario hearing?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"

current_text: The CLEO pages on mediation and hearings were last reviewed on June 12, 2025. Tribunals Ontario's HRTO page says that effective August 17, 2026, the HRTO “is introducing updates to its Rules of Procedure and Practice Directions along with process improvements”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"

current_text: What the Tribunal can order
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: If the Tribunal determines that a party infringed another party's Part I right, it may order the party who infringed the right “to pay monetary compensation to the party whose right was infringed for loss arising out of the infringement, including compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect.” It may also order restitution other than money. (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), paras. 1, 2)
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "What the Tribunal can order"

current_text: The Tribunal may also order any party “to do anything that, in the opinion of the Tribunal, the party ought to do to promote compliance with this Act.” Such an order “may direct a person to do anything with respect to future practices” and “may be made even if no order under that paragraph was requested.” (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), para. 3, (2))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "What the Tribunal can order"

current_text: Human rights claims in a court case
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario

current_text: If, “in a civil proceeding in a court, the court finds that a party to the proceeding has infringed a right under Part I of another party”, the court may order monetary compensation, restitution, or both. But this “does not permit a person to commence an action based solely on an infringement of a right under Part I.” (Human Rights Code, s. 46.1 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Human rights claims in a court case"

current_text: A person may not apply to the Tribunal about a right if a civil proceeding seeking an order under section 46.1 about the same alleged infringement “has not been finally determined or withdrawn”, or if “a court has finally determined the issue of whether the right has been infringed or the matter has been settled.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (11))
appears_in: Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Human rights claims in a court case"

current_text: Employment standards
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, what Ontario's Employment Standards Act, 2000 says about who it covers, some of the standards it sets, and how a complaint or a court case about those standards is started. It explains what the Act says; it does not say whether any standard applies to a particular job.
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: Who the Act covers
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: Subject to the exceptions in subsections (2) to (5), the employment standards in the Act apply to an employee and employer if “the employee's work is to be performed in Ontario”, or if the work is performed in Ontario and outside Ontario but “the work performed outside Ontario is a continuation of work performed in Ontario”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"

current_text: The Act “does not apply with respect to an employee and his or her employer if their employment relationship is within the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada.” It also lists other people it does not apply to, such as “A secondary school student who performs work under a work experience program authorized by the school board”, “A holder of political, religious or judicial office” and “Any prescribed individuals.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (2), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"

current_text: The Act also says “An employer shall not treat, for the purposes of this Act, a person who is an employee of the employer as if the person were not an employee under this Act.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5.1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"

current_text: Standards cannot be signed away
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: Section 5 is headed “No contracting out”. It says “no employer or agent of an employer and no employee or agent of an employee shall contract out of or waive an employment standard and any such contracting out or waiver is void.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Standards cannot be signed away"

current_text: There is one exception. If one or more provisions in an employment contract or in another Act “that directly relate to the same subject matter as an employment standard provide a greater benefit to an employee than the employment standard”, then “the provision or provisions in the contract or Act apply and the employment standard does not apply.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Standards cannot be signed away"

current_text: Getting paid
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: “An employer shall establish a recurring pay period and a recurring pay day and shall pay all wages earned during each pay period, other than accruing vacation pay, no later than the pay day for that period.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"

current_text: When employment ends, the employer must pay any wages owing no later than the later of “seven days after the employment ends” and “the day that would have been the employee's next pay day.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"

current_text: The Act says “An employer shall pay employees at least the minimum wage.” Minimum wages are adjusted each October 1 by a formula using the Consumer Price Index, with no adjustment if it would result in a decrease. “The Minister shall, not later than April 1 of every year after 2021, publish on a website of the Government of Ontario the minimum wages that are to apply starting on October 1 of that year.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 23 (1), 23.1 (4), (6), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"

current_text: This guide does not state current minimum wage amounts. The Act sets separate minimum wage classes, such as students under 18 and homeworkers, and allows a class and its minimum wage to be prescribed by regulation. The current rates are published by the Minister; the site does not yet hold a source for those rates or any such regulation. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 23.1 (1), (2), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"

current_text: Hours of work, overtime and public holidays
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: No employer shall require or permit an employee to work more than “eight hours in a day” (or the employee's regular work day, if the employer set one longer than eight hours) and “48 hours in a work week”. The limits may be exceeded where the employee “has made an agreement with the employer”, and the Act sets conditions for such an agreement to be valid. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 17 (1)-(5))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"

current_text: An employer “shall pay an employee overtime pay of at least one and one-half times his or her regular rate for each hour of work in excess of 44 hours in each work week or, if another threshold is prescribed, that prescribed threshold.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 22 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"

current_text: The Act lists the public holidays: New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, December 26, and “Any day prescribed as a public holiday”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 1 (1), “public holiday”)
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"

current_text: If a public holiday falls on a day that would ordinarily be a working day and the employee is not on vacation, “the employer shall give the employee the day off work and pay him or her public holiday pay for that day.” The Act sets out exceptions and rules for agreeing to work on the holiday. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 26, 27)
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"

current_text: Vacation and vacation pay
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: An employer shall give an employee a vacation of “at least two weeks after each vacation entitlement year that the employee completes, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “at least three weeks” if the period of employment is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 33 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Vacation and vacation pay"

current_text: Vacation pay must equal at least “4 per cent of the wages, excluding vacation pay, that the employee earned during the period for which the vacation is given, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “6 per cent” if it is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 35.2)
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Vacation and vacation pay"

current_text: Notice of termination or termination pay
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: “No employer shall terminate the employment of an employee who has been continuously employed for three months or more” unless the employer has given written notice under section 57 or 58 and the notice has expired, or has complied with section 61. The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay under this Part.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 54, 55)
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"

current_text: Under the Act, an employer terminates employment if it “dismisses the employee or otherwise refuses or is unable to continue employing him or her”, if it “constructively dismisses the employee and the employee resigns from his or her employment in response to that within a reasonable period”, or if it lays the employee off for longer than a temporary lay-off. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 56 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"

current_text: The notice period depends on the period of employment: “at least one week before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is less than one year”, rising by steps to “at least eight weeks before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is eight years or more.” Different rules apply when an employer terminates 50 or more employees at the employer's establishment in the same four-week period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 57, 58 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"

current_text: Instead of notice, an employer may pay “termination pay in a lump sum equal to the amount the employee would have been entitled to receive under section 60 had notice been given”, and must continue benefit plan contributions for the notice period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 60 (1), 61 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"

current_text: Severance pay
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: An employer who severs an employment relationship must pay severance pay “if the employee was employed by the employer for five years or more” and one of two conditions is met. The first is that the severance came from a permanent discontinuance of all or part of the business at an establishment and the employee “is one of 50 or more employees who have their employment relationship severed within a six-month period as a result”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"

current_text: The second is that “the employer has a payroll of $2.5 million or more”, measured as set out in subsection 64 (2). The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to severance pay under this section.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1), (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"

current_text: Severance pay is calculated by multiplying “the employee's regular wages for a regular work week” by the completed years of employment plus completed extra months divided by 12. It “shall not exceed an amount equal to the employee's regular wages for a regular work week for 26 weeks.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 65 (1), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"

current_text: Severance pay under section 65 is “in addition to any other amount to which an employee is entitled under this Act or his or her employment contract”, subject to the set-offs and deductions listed in subsection 65 (8). (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 65 (7), (8))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"

current_text: Filing a complaint and its time limit
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: “A person alleging that this Act has been or is being contravened may file a complaint with the Ministry in a written or electronic form approved by the Director.” A complaint not filed in an approved form “shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"

current_text: Where an employer is or has been bound by a collective agreement, subsection 99 (1) makes the Act “enforceable against the employer as if it were part of the collective agreement” for contraventions in the periods it lists. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 99 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"

current_text: An employee represented by a trade union that is or was a party to a collective agreement “may not file a complaint alleging a contravention of this Act that is enforceable under subsection (1) or have such a complaint investigated.” However, the Director “may permit an employee to file a complaint” despite this “if the Director considers it appropriate in the circumstances.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 99 (1), (2), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"

current_text: The Act sets a time limit: “A complaint regarding a contravention that occurred more than two years before the day on which the complaint was filed shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"

current_text: An employment standards officer investigating a complaint “may not issue an order for wages that became due to the employee” if “the wages became due more than two years before the complaint was filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 111 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"

current_text: A complaint or a court case
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards

current_text: The Act says “Subject to section 97, no civil remedy of an employee against his or her employer is affected by this Act.” An employee who starts a civil proceeding against the employer under the Act must serve notice on the Director, on a form approved by the Director, “on or before the date the civil proceeding is set down for trial.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 8 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"

current_text: An employee who files a complaint about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not commence a civil proceeding with respect to the same matter.” An employee who files a complaint claiming termination or severance pay “may not commence a civil proceeding for wrongful dismissal if the complaint and the proceeding would relate to the same termination or severance of employment.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"

current_text: There is a withdrawal window: an employee who has filed a complaint may start a civil proceeding on those matters “if he or she withdraws the complaint within two weeks after it is filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"

current_text: It works the other way too. An employee who starts a civil proceeding about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not file a complaint with respect to the same matter”, and one who starts a proceeding for wrongful dismissal may not file a complaint for termination or severance pay about the same termination or severance. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 98 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"

current_text: CLEO's Steps to Justice has plain-language questions on these subjects, grouped under headings including “Getting paid”, “Getting fired or laid off” and “Claiming your rights as a worker”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Employment and work)
appears_in: Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"

current_text: Debt collection and being sued for a debt
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: This guide describes, in general terms, the Ontario rules for collection agencies, the time limit for starting a court case, what happens when a creditor sues in Small Claims Court, and some basics about bankruptcy, consumer proposals and credit reports. It explains what the sources say; it does not say whether any particular debt is owed.
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: What a collection agency is
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: Under the Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, a “collection agency” includes “a person, other than a collector, who obtains or arranges for payment of money owing to another person” and “a person who purchases debts that are in arrears and collects them”. (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"

current_text: “No person shall carry on the business of a collection agency unless the person is registered by the Registrar under this Act.” A creditor may deal with a debtor for payment only “under the name in which the debt is lawfully owing or through a registered collection agency.” (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, ss. 4 (1), 5)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"

current_text: The Act does not apply to some people, including a lawyer in the regular practice of their profession (subject to the regulations), a bank, a credit union or its employees acting in the regular course of their employment, and “an isolated collection made by a person whose usual business is not collecting debts for other persons”. The Act also says “Any waiver or release of any right, benefit or protection provided by this Act or the regulations is void.” (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, ss. 2 (1), 22.1)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"

current_text: What collectors may not do
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: No collection agency or collector shall “collect or attempt to collect, on its own behalf or for a person for whom it acts, any money in addition to the amount owing by the debtor”, or “deal with a debtor in a name other than that authorized by the registration”, or “engage in any prohibited practice or employ any prohibited method in the collection of debts”. (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 22)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"

current_text: The detailed rules are in a regulation that the site does not yet hold. Ontario's guide for collection agencies summarizes them. Before contacting a debtor to demand payment, an agency “must send a written notice to the debtor”, and must “wait six calendar days after sending a written notice” before contacting the debtor or demanding payment. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"

current_text: The guide says an agency cannot contact anyone about a debt “between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. (debtor's local time) from Monday to Saturday”, “on a Sunday, except between 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. (debtor's local time)”, or “on a public holiday”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"

current_text: It also says “you can contact a debtor up to three times within a seven-day period on behalf of the same creditor”, and not more often “unless additional contact was agreed to, requested or initiated by the debtor, or if contact is by mail.” It adds: “This rule does not apply until you have spoken to the debtor in person or by phone.” (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"

current_text: When dealing with a debtor, the guide says an agency cannot “use threatening, profane, intimidating or coercive language”, “use excessive or unreasonable pressure”, “give false or misleading information”, or “threaten legal action without the creditor's written authority to commence legal proceedings”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"

current_text: Contacting other people, and disputed debts
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: The guide lists limited situations in which an agency can contact a debtor's employer, such as where “the debtor has given you written permission”, or once “to confirm that the debtor works there”. It can contact family, friends or neighbours only in listed situations, such as where that person “has guaranteed to pay the debt”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"

current_text: The guide says an agency cannot contact someone if “you know or reasonably should know they are not responsible for the debt”. It also says “If the debtor sends you a notice suggesting that the matter be taken to court, you cannot contact or attempt to contact the debtor”, unless the debtor consents to or requests contact. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"

current_text: CLEO explains that when someone is contacted about a debt they do not think they owe, “Your creditor or the collection agency may have made a mistake.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called about a debt I do not owe)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"

current_text: If talking to the agency or creditor does not work, CLEO describes sending “a formal letter by registered mail to the collection agency” disputing the debt and asking that a court decide the problem, after which “the collection agency can only contact you if they plan to take you to court.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called about a debt I do not owe)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"

current_text: CLEO also says that ignoring a collection agency can have consequences: “your credit rating could drop and you might get sued in court”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called me. Do I have to talk to them?)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"

current_text: Complaints about a collection agency
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: Ontario's guide says “Consumers can submit complaints about collection agencies to the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement.” When the Registrar receives a complaint and asks in writing, the collection agency “shall furnish the Registrar with such information respecting the matter complained of as the Registrar requires.” (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies; Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 12 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Complaints about a collection agency"

current_text: Ontario's consumer protection page for credit, loans and debt collection points to information on credit reports and on what to do “when a collection agency contacts you”. (ontario.ca, Consumer protection information for credit, loans and debt collection)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Complaints about a collection agency"

current_text: Time limits for suing on a debt
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: The Limitations Act, 2002 sets the general rule: “Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.” Section 15 also sets an ultimate limit: no proceeding “after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place”, subject to the exceptions in that section. (Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 4, 15 (2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"

current_text: If a person “acknowledges liability in respect of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum”, the act or omission the claim is based on is treated as having taken place “on the day on which the acknowledgment was made.” The acknowledgment must be “in writing and signed”, and “part payment of the sum” by the person against whom the claim is made “has the same effect”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (1), (10), (11))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"

current_text: An acknowledgment counts only if it is made to the person with the claim, their agent, or a bankruptcy trustee or official receiver “before the expiry of the limitation period applicable to the claim.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (9))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"

current_text: Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: The Small Claims Court “has jurisdiction in any action for the payment of money where the amount claimed does not exceed the prescribed amount exclusive of interest and costs”. A regulation says “The maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court is $50,000.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1); O. Reg. 626/00, s. 1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: “An action that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not, despite subsection 11 (2), be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice as provided in the rules of court.” This does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim where the main action was commenced in the Superior Court of Justice. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1.1), (1.2))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: “A defendant who wishes to dispute a plaintiff's claim shall, within 20 days of being served with the claim,” serve a defence (Form 9A) on every other party, and file it with proof of service with the clerk. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 9.01)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: “A defendant who admits liability for all or part of the plaintiff's claim but wishes to arrange terms of payment may in the defence admit liability and propose terms of payment.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 9.03 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: If a defendant “fails to file a defence to all or part of the claim with the clerk within the prescribed time, the clerk may note the defendant in default” when a request to note the defendant in default and proof that the claim was served within the court's territorial division are filed. Other requirements apply if all defendants were served outside that division. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: The rules also say: “A person under disability may not be noted in default under subrule (1), except with leave of the court.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"

current_text: Bankruptcy and consumer proposals
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: CLEO describes options other than bankruptcy, including making “a repayment plan with your creditors” and filing “a consumer proposal with a Licensed Insolvency Trustee”. It says “Bankruptcy is a legal process that you can only start with a Licensed Insolvency Trustee”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Are there options other than bankruptcy if I'm in debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021; How do I file for bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 10, 2023)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"

current_text: CLEO explains “A consumer proposal is a legal agreement between you and your creditors.” It says “A consumer proposal only helps you settle your unsecured debts” and that, for it to be accepted, “the creditors that you owe more than half of your debts to must agree to it.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can a consumer proposal help me get out of debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"

current_text: CLEO lists debts that “survive your bankruptcy”, including “child and spousal support payments”, “fines and court penalties”, “debts that are the result of a crime”, and “government student loans, if you have been out of school for less than 7 years”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can I still owe money after I have been discharged from bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"

current_text: Credit reports
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

current_text: CLEO says the two main consumer reporting agencies in Canada are TransUnion and Equifax. A bankruptcy “will stay on your credit report for 6 or 7 years after you are discharged”, and a note about a consumer proposal stays “for 3 years after your consumer proposal is completed.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I file for bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 10, 2023; Can a consumer proposal help me get out of debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Credit reports"

current_text: On mistakes, CLEO describes a letter to the consumer reporting agency asking it to “correct, remove, or explain any wrong information”. It says “The agency must put that letter in your file” and “the consumer reporting agency must answer your letter and tell you what they are doing about it.” If the agency does not fix the information, a complaint can be filed “with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: There's a mistake in my credit report)
appears_in: Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Credit reports"

current_text: Car accidents and insurance
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Insurance Act says about accident benefits, disputes about those benefits, limits on suing for injuries from a car accident, property damage claims, uninsured vehicles, and the notice and time limits the Act sets. It covers only what the Act itself says; the regulations it refers to are not covered because the site does not yet have a source for them.
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Statutory accident benefits
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Accident benefits are set out in a separate schedule. The Act says every contract evidenced by a motor vehicle liability policy “shall be deemed to provide for the statutory accident benefits set out in the Schedule and any amendments to the Schedule”. Those benefits are “subject to the terms, conditions, provisions, exclusions and limits set out in that Schedule”. (Insurance Act, s. 268 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Statutory accident benefits"

current_text: There is an exception for public transit. The Act says “no statutory accident benefits are payable in respect of an occupant of a public transit vehicle” for an incident on or after that rule came into force “if the public transit vehicle did not collide with another automobile or any other object in the incident”. (Insurance Act, s. 268 (1.1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Statutory accident benefits"

current_text: The Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule itself sets out what the benefits are and who qualifies. The site does not yet have a source for the Schedule, so this guide does not describe the benefits in detail. (Insurance Act, s. 268 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Statutory accident benefits"

current_text: Disputes about accident benefits go to the Licence Appeal Tribunal
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Section 280 deals with disputes “in respect of an insured person's entitlement to statutory accident benefits or in respect of the amount of statutory accident benefits to which an insured person is entitled”. For those disputes, “The insured person or the insurer may apply to the Licence Appeal Tribunal to resolve a dispute described in subsection (1).” (Insurance Act, s. 280 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Disputes about accident benefits go to the Licence Appeal Tribunal"

current_text: These disputes do not start in a court. The Act says: “No person may bring a proceeding in any court with respect to a dispute described in subsection (1), other than an appeal from a decision of the Licence Appeal Tribunal or an application for judicial review.” It also says “The dispute shall be resolved in accordance with the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule.” (Insurance Act, s. 280 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Disputes about accident benefits go to the Licence Appeal Tribunal"

current_text: After the Tribunal decides, “the insurer shall not reduce benefits to the insured person on the basis of an alleged change of circumstances, alleged new evidence or an alleged error except as provided under this section.” The insurer may reduce benefits if “the insured person agrees”, after “a successful appeal of the Licence Appeal Tribunal's decision”, or if it is “authorized to do so by the Licence Appeal Tribunal”. (Insurance Act, s. 281)
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Disputes about accident benefits go to the Licence Appeal Tribunal"

current_text: The Act leaves the Tribunal's orders and powers to the regulations. The site does not yet have a source for the Tribunal's own rules or for any time limit to apply to it, so those are not covered here. (Insurance Act, s. 280 (5), (6))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Disputes about accident benefits go to the Licence Appeal Tribunal"

current_text: Telling your insurer about an accident
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: If an insured automobile is involved in an incident “that is required to be reported to the police under the Highway Traffic Act or in respect of which the insured intends to make a claim under the contract”, the insured “shall give the insurer written notice of the incident, with all available particulars.” (Insurance Act, s. 258.1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Telling your insurer about an accident"

current_text: The notice “shall be given to the insurer within seven days of the incident.” If the insured cannot do this “because of incapacity”, the insured “shall comply as soon as possible thereafter.” (Insurance Act, s. 258.1 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Telling your insurer about an accident"

current_text: Steps before suing for injuries
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Sections 258.3 to 258.6 apply “only in respect of a claim for loss or damage from bodily injury or death arising from the use or operation” of an automobile “in Canada, the United States of America or a jurisdiction designated in the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule”, after section 29 of the Automobile Insurance Rate Stability Act, 1996 came into force. Under section 258.3, such an action “shall not be commenced unless” certain steps have happened. (Insurance Act, ss. 258.2, 258.3 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Steps before suing for injuries"

current_text: First, “the plaintiff has applied for statutory accident benefits”. Second, the plaintiff “served written notice of the intention to commence the action on the defendant within 120 days after the incident”, or within a longer period a court may authorize “on motion made before or after the expiry of the 120-day period”. Third, the plaintiff provided the defendant with “the information prescribed by the regulations within the time period prescribed by the regulations”. (Insurance Act, s. 258.3 (1) (a)-(c))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Steps before suing for injuries"

current_text: If the defendant requests them “within 90 days after receiving the notice”, the plaintiff undergoes examinations, at the defendant's expense, “by one or more persons selected by the defendant who are members of Colleges as defined in the Regulated Health Professions Act, 1991”. If the defendant requests them, the plaintiff also provides “a statutory declaration describing the circumstances surrounding the incident and the nature of the claim being made” and “evidence of the plaintiff's identity”. (Insurance Act, s. 258.3 (1) (d)-(f))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Steps before suing for injuries"

current_text: These steps have consequences but are not an absolute bar. The Act says “a person may commence an action without complying with subsection (1)”, but the court shall consider the non-compliance in awarding costs. Also, “no prejudgment interest shall be awarded under section 128 of the Courts of Justice Act for any period of time before the plaintiff served the notice under clause (1) (b).” (Insurance Act, s. 258.3 (8), (9))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Steps before suing for injuries"

current_text: An insured who receives the notice “shall give a copy of the notice to the insurer within seven days of receiving the notice”, or, if unable “because of incapacity”, “as soon as possible thereafter.” An insurer that receives the notice “shall promptly inform the plaintiff whether there is a motor vehicle liability policy issued by the insurer to the defendant” and, if so, “the liability limits under the policy” and “whether the insurer will respond under the policy to the claim.” (Insurance Act, ss. 258.3 (2), (3), 258.4)
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Steps before suing for injuries"

current_text: Limits on suing for injuries
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Section 267.5 protects “the owner of an automobile, the occupants of an automobile and any person present at the incident” from some kinds of damages. They “are not liable in an action in Ontario” for “Damages for income loss suffered in the seven days after the incident.” (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (1), para. 1)
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: For income loss after the first seven days and before trial, they are not liable for damages “in excess of 70 per cent of the amount of gross income that is lost during that period, as determined in accordance with the regulations.” The same 70 per cent limit applies to “loss of earning capacity” before trial. (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (1), paras. 2, 3)
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: For health care expenses and for “non-pecuniary loss”, those persons are not liable “unless as a result of the use or operation of the automobile the injured person has died or has sustained”, (a) “permanent serious disfigurement”; or (b) “permanent serious impairment of an important physical, mental or psychological function”. (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (3), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: Where damages for non-pecuniary loss can be awarded against a “protected defendant”, the court first determines the amount “without regard to this Part”, then reduces it. For damages other than under clause 61 (2) (e) of the Family Law Act, the reduction is “the greater of, A. $15,000, and B. the amount prescribed by the regulations”. For damages under that clause, it is the greater of “$7,500” and the amount prescribed by the regulations. (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: These reductions do not apply if the damages would exceed an amount set under subsections (8.3) and (8.4), which is revised every January 1 by the published indexation percentage. They also do not apply to damages for non-pecuniary loss “awarded in respect of a person who dies as a direct or indirect result of an incident that occurs after August 31, 2010.” (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (8), (8.1), (8.1.1), (8.3), (8.4))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: These protections have exceptions. They do not protect a person defended “by an insurer that is not licensed to undertake automobile insurance in Ontario unless the insurer has filed an undertaking under section 226.1.” For an incident on or after that rule came into force, they also do not protect “the owner or driver of a public transit vehicle if it did not collide with another automobile or any other object in the incident.” (Insurance Act, s. 267.5 (6), (6.1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Limits on suing for injuries"

current_text: Damage to a car: direct compensation
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Section 263 applies when a car or its contents is damaged “arising directly or indirectly from the use or operation in Ontario of one or more other automobiles”, the damaged car is insured by an insurer licensed in Ontario (or one that has filed an undertaking), and “at least one other automobile involved in the accident” is insured the same way. (Insurance Act, s. 263 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: When it applies, “an insured is entitled to recover for the damages to the insured's automobile and its contents and for loss of use from the insured's insurer under the coverage described in subsection 239 (1) as though the insured were a third party.” Recovery “shall be based on the degree of fault of the insurer's insured as determined under the fault determination rules.” (Insurance Act, s. 263 (2), (3))
