appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: When section 263 applies, an insured cannot sue the other people involved for this damage. The Act says “an insured has no right of action against any person involved in the incident other than the insured's insurer for damages to the insured's automobile or its contents or for loss of use”. (Insurance Act, s. 263 (5) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: An insured may sue their own insurer “if the insured is not satisfied that the degree of fault established under the fault determination rules accurately reflects the actual degree of fault or the insured is not satisfied with a proposed settlement”. Then “the matters in issue shall be determined in accordance with the ordinary rules of law.” (Insurance Act, s. 263 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: Section 263 does not apply in some situations, including “if both automobiles are owned by the same person”, to contents “being carried for reward”, and to damage to an automobile owned by the insured, or its contents, “if the damage is caused by the insured while driving another automobile.” (Insurance Act, s. 263 (7), (9), (10))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: An insured may elect, under the regulations, “not to recover damages from the insured's insurer under subsection (2).” If the insured makes that election, then, in addition to the restrictions in subsection (5), the insured “has no right of action under subsection (2) against the insured's insurer” for this damage or loss of use, and the insurer “shall not issue or offer collision or upset coverage” to the insured. (Insurance Act, s. 263 (2.2), (2.3))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: A proceeding against an insurer about damage to a car or its contents has its own time limit: it “shall be commenced within one year after the happening of the loss or damage.” (Insurance Act, s. 259.1)
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Damage to a car: direct compensation"

current_text: Uninsured and unidentified automobiles
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance

current_text: Every motor vehicle liability policy “shall provide for payment of all sums that” a person insured under the contract “is legally entitled to recover from the owner or driver of an uninsured automobile or unidentified automobile as damages for bodily injuries resulting from an accident involving an automobile”, “subject to the terms, conditions, provisions, exclusions and limits as are prescribed by the regulations.” (Insurance Act, s. 265 (1) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Uninsured and unidentified automobiles"

current_text: It also covers sums a person insured under the contract can recover “from the identified owner or driver of an uninsured automobile as damages for accidental damage to the insured automobile or its contents”. All of this is “subject to the terms, conditions, provisions, exclusions and limits as are prescribed by the regulations.” The site does not yet have a source for those regulations. (Insurance Act, s. 265 (1) (c))
appears_in: Guides, Car accidents and insurance, "Uninsured and unidentified automobiles"

current_text: Condominium disputes
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Condominium Act, 1998 and the Condominium Authority of Ontario say about condo disputes: the Condominium Authority Tribunal, the duty to follow the Act and the condo's documents, compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice, and common expenses and liens. The regulation that lists which disputes the Tribunal hears is not covered, because the site does not yet have a source for it.
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: What the Condominium Authority Tribunal is
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: In this part of the Act, “Tribunal” means “the Condominium Authority Tribunal established under subsection 1.32 (1).” The Condominium Authority of Ontario describes it as “Canada’s first fully online tribunal”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.31; condoauthorityontario.ca, Condominium Authority Tribunal — Dispute Resolution)
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "What the Condominium Authority Tribunal is"

current_text: The Authority says: “Regulation 179/17 defines the scope of disputes that can be resolved by the Tribunal.” The site does not yet have a copy of that regulation, so this guide does not list the types of disputes it covers. (condoauthorityontario.ca, Condominium Authority Tribunal — Dispute Resolution)
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "What the Condominium Authority Tribunal is"

current_text: Subject to one exception, “the Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to exercise the powers conferred on it under this Act and to determine all questions of fact or law that arise in any proceeding before it.” The exception: it “shall not inquire into or make a decision concerning the constitutional validity of a provision of an Act or a regulation.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.42)
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "What the Condominium Authority Tribunal is"

current_text: Who can apply to the Tribunal, and about what
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: A condo corporation “may apply to the Tribunal for the resolution of a prescribed dispute with one or more of its owners or one or more occupiers or mortgagees of a unit.” An owner or a mortgagee of a unit “may apply to the Tribunal for the resolution of a prescribed dispute with the corporation, another owner or an occupier or a mortgagee of a unit.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Who can apply to the Tribunal, and about what"

current_text: If the regulations so provide, a purchaser may apply about a dispute with the corporation regarding compliance with subsection 55 (3), “but not any other dispute.” An application “shall be in the form approved by the Tribunal.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (3), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Who can apply to the Tribunal, and about what"

current_text: Some disputes cannot go to the Tribunal. These include a dispute about “Part III, section 20, 26, 82.1, 82.2, 85 or 86, subsection 117 (1) or Part VII or VIII”, and “a dispute involving the determination of title to any real property.” Sections 85 and 86 deal with the condo lien described below. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Who can apply to the Tribunal, and about what"

current_text: Time limits for Tribunal applications
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: “Subject to any other provision of this Act, an application must be made within two years after the dispute to which the application relates arose.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Time limits for Tribunal applications"

current_text: If that deadline is missed, “the Tribunal may extend the deadline for a time of no more than one additional year if the Tribunal is satisfied that the delay in not applying was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (7))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Time limits for Tribunal applications"

current_text: Parties can settle. A signed written settlement “is binding on the parties.” A party who believes another party has broken the settlement may apply to the Tribunal “within six months after the contravention to which the application relates”, or later if the Tribunal is satisfied the delay “was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.47 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Time limits for Tribunal applications"

current_text: How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: A Tribunal proceeding “may be held orally or in writing, in person, by telephone, video conference or electronic mail, or through use of other electronic means in accordance with the rules of the Tribunal.” The Tribunal may direct the parties to take part in an “alternative dispute resolution mechanism”, which “includes mediation, conciliation, negotiation or any other means of facilitating the resolution of issues in dispute.” (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 1.39 (2), 1.40)
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: The Tribunal may refuse to allow a person to make an application, or may dismiss an application without holding a hearing, if it “is of the opinion that the subject matter of the application is frivolous or vexatious or that the application has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action.” It may also dismiss without a hearing if the applicant filed documents “that the applicant knew or ought to have known to have contained false or misleading information.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.41)
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: Orders the Tribunal may make include an order “prohibiting a party to the proceeding from taking a particular action or requiring a party to the proceeding to take a particular action”, and an order to pay “compensation for damages incurred by another party to the proceeding as a result of an act of non-compliance up to the greater of $25,000 or the amount, if any, that is prescribed.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.44 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: The Tribunal may also order a party to pay the costs of another party or the costs of the Tribunal. Those costs are determined “in accordance with the rules of the Tribunal.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.44 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: The Tribunal “shall not make an order requiring a person to vacate a property permanently.” The party against whom an order for compensation, costs or a penalty is made pays the amount “within 30 days, unless the order specifies another time limit.” (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 1.44 (4), 1.45 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: A Tribunal order “is final and binding”, except that a party “may appeal the order to the Divisional Court on a question of law in accordance with the rules of court.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.46 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order"

current_text: The duty to follow the Act, declaration, by-laws and rules
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: A condo corporation's objects “are to manage the property and the assets, if any, of the corporation on behalf of the owners.” It “has a duty to take all reasonable steps to ensure that the owners, the occupiers of units, the lessees of the common elements and the agents and employees of the corporation comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 17 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "The duty to follow the Act, declaration, by-laws and rules"

current_text: The corporation, its directors, officers and employees, the declarant, an owner, an occupier of a unit and others listed “shall comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules.” An owner “shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that an occupier of the owner's unit and all invitees, agents and employees of the owner or occupier comply”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 119 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "The duty to follow the Act, declaration, by-laws and rules"

current_text: A corporation, an owner and every person with a registered mortgage against a unit “have the right to require that a person who is required to comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules shall do so.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 119 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "The duty to follow the Act, declaration, by-laws and rules"

current_text: Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: An owner, a corporation, a mortgagee of a unit and others listed “may make an application to the Superior Court of Justice for an order enforcing compliance with any provision of this Act, the declaration, the by-laws, the rules” or certain agreements between corporations. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: This court route does not apply “to any matter in dispute for which a person may apply for resolution under section 1.36 to the Condominium Authority Tribunal established under Part I.2, if the Tribunal has been established under that Part.” Also, if the mediation and arbitration processes in section 132 are required, a person may not apply “until the person has failed to obtain compliance through using those processes.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (2), (2.4))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: On an application, the court may “grant the order applied for”, require payment of “the damages incurred by the applicant as a result of the acts of non-compliance” and “the costs incurred by the applicant in obtaining the order”, or “grant such other relief as is fair and equitable in the circumstances.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: One limit on those orders: the court may not grant an order terminating a lease of a unit for residential purposes unless it is satisfied that “the lessee is in contravention of an order that has been made under subsection (3)”, or that the lessee has received a notice described in subsection 87 (1) and “has not paid the amount required by that subsection.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: If a corporation obtains an award of damages or costs against an owner or occupier of a unit, those amounts, “together with any additional actual costs to the corporation in obtaining the order, shall be added to the common expenses for the unit”, and the corporation may specify a time for payment by the owner. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (5))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice"

current_text: Common expenses and condo liens
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes

current_text: “Subject to the other provisions of this Act, the owners shall contribute to the common expenses in the proportions specified in the declaration.” An owner is not exempt even if the owner “has waived or abandoned the right to use the common elements or part of them”, “the owner is making a claim against the corporation”, or the declaration, by-laws or rules restrict the owner's use. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 84 (1), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Common expenses and condo liens"

current_text: If an owner defaults, “the corporation has a lien against the owner's unit and its appurtenant common interest for the unpaid amount together with all interest owing and all reasonable legal costs and reasonable expenses incurred by the corporation in connection with the collection or attempted collection of the unpaid amount.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 85 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Common expenses and condo liens"

current_text: “The lien expires three months after the default that gave rise to the lien occurred unless the corporation within that time registers a certificate of lien in a form prescribed by the Minister.” “At least 10 days before the day a certificate of lien is registered, the corporation shall give written notice of the lien to the owner”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 85 (2), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Common expenses and condo liens"

current_text: “The lien may be enforced in the same manner as a mortgage.” Upon payment of the amounts the certificate covers, the corporation “shall prepare and register a discharge of the certificate of lien” and advise the owner in writing of the particulars of the registration. A dispute about section 85 or 86 cannot be brought to the Tribunal. (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 85 (6), (7), 1.36 (4))
appears_in: Guides, Condominium disputes, "Common expenses and condo liens"

current_text: Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: This guide explains what Ontario's Construction Act says about who can claim a construction lien, holdbacks, the time limits for preserving and perfecting a lien, where lien actions are heard, prompt payment and adjudication. Numbers are given exactly as the Act states them.
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: Who can claim a lien
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “A person who supplies services or materials to an improvement for an owner, contractor or subcontractor, has a lien upon the interest of the owner in the premises improved for the price of those services or materials.” (Construction Act, s. 14 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Who can claim a lien"

current_text: An “improvement” means, in respect of any land, “any alteration, addition or capital repair to the land”, “any construction, erection or installation on the land” (including some equipment the Act describes), or “the complete or partial demolition or removal of any building, structure or works on the land”. (Construction Act, s. 1 (1), “improvement”)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Who can claim a lien"

current_text: “A person's lien arises and takes effect when the person first supplies services or materials to the improvement.” No person is entitled to a lien “for any interest on the amount owed to the person”, but this does not affect any right the person may otherwise have to recover that interest. (Construction Act, ss. 15, 14 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Who can claim a lien"

current_text: A lien “does not attach to the interest in a premises of”, “the Crown” or “a municipality”. Where either has an interest in a premises but is not an owner, “the lien may attach to the interest of any other person in the premises.” Where the owner is the Crown or a municipality, or the premises is a railway right-of-way, the lien does not attach to the premises but “constitutes a charge under section 21”. (Construction Act, s. 16)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Who can claim a lien"

current_text: These rules do not apply to every project. The Act and regulations “as they read on June 29, 2018, continue to apply” to an improvement if, for example, “a contract for the improvement was entered into before July 1, 2018” or the owner commenced a procurement process for it before that date. The prompt payment and adjudication Parts (I.1 and II.1) also do not apply to certain older contracts and their subcontracts, as the Act lists. (Construction Act, s. 87.3 (1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Who can claim a lien"

current_text: Holdbacks
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “Each payer upon a contract or subcontract under which a lien may arise shall retain a holdback equal to 10 per cent of the price of the services or materials as they are actually supplied under the contract or subcontract until all liens that may be claimed against the holdback in respect of the supplied services or materials have expired or been satisfied, discharged or otherwise provided for under this Act.” (Construction Act, s. 22 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Holdbacks"

current_text: Where a contract has been certified or declared substantially performed but work remains, the payer keeps “a separate holdback equal to 10 per cent of the price of the remaining services or materials”. The duty to keep holdbacks applies “irrespective of whether the contract or subcontract provides for partial payments or payment on completion.” (Construction Act, s. 22 (2), (3))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Holdbacks"

current_text: Subject to limits, an owner “is personally liable for holdbacks that the owner is required to retain under this Part to those lien claimants who have valid liens against the owner's interest in the premises.” Where the defaulting payer is the contractor, that liability “does not exceed the holdbacks the owner is required to retain”. Where it is a subcontractor, a lower cap can apply. This liability “may only be determined by an action under this Act.” (Construction Act, s. 23)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Holdbacks"

current_text: Preserving a lien and the time limits
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “Unless preserved under section 34, the liens arising from the supply of services or materials to an improvement expire as provided in this section.” (Construction Act, s. 31 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: A contractor's lien for work up to substantial performance “expires at the conclusion of the 60-day period next following the occurrence of the earlier of” the date a copy of the certificate or declaration of substantial performance “is published as provided in section 32”, and “the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated”. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: For other lien claimants, such as subcontractors and suppliers, the lien for work up to substantial performance expires at the end of a 60-day period following “the earliest of” publication of the certificate or declaration, “the date on which the person last supplies services or materials to the improvement”, the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, and the date a subcontract is certified complete under section 33, where the services or materials were supplied under that subcontract. (Construction Act, s. 31 (3) (a))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: Where there is no certificate or declaration, or for work after substantial performance, a contractor's lien expires “at the conclusion of the 60-day period next following the occurrence of the earlier of” the date the contract is completed and the date it is abandoned or terminated. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: In the same situations, another person's lien expires at the end of a 60-day period following the earlier of the date the person last supplied services or materials, the date the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, and the date a subcontract is certified complete under section 33, where the services or materials were supplied under that subcontract. (Construction Act, s. 31 (3) (b))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: Separate rules apply to the lien of the trustee of a workers' trust fund. A person who supplied services or materials both before and after substantial performance has separate liens, and the earlier one can expire without affecting the later one. (Construction Act, s. 31 (2.1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: “No later than seven days after a contract is terminated, either the owner or the contractor or other person whose lien is subject to expiry shall publish a notice of the termination in the prescribed form and manner.” If a notice is published, the termination date for these expiry rules is the date it (or the first such notice) was published. This “does not prevent a person from contesting the validity of a termination.” (Construction Act, s. 31 (6)-(8))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: Subsections 31 (6) and (7) were amended with effect from January 1, 2026. The earlier versions “continue to apply with respect to a notice of termination that was published in accordance with subsection 31 (6) before that day.” (Construction Act, s. 87.4 (6))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: “A lien may be preserved during the supplying of services or materials or at any time before it expires”. Where the lien attaches to the premises, this is done “by the registration in the proper land registry office of a claim for lien on the title of the premises”. Where it does not attach, it is done “by giving to the owner a copy of the claim for lien.” (Construction Act, s. 34 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: Where the owner is the Crown, the copy goes “to the prescribed office”, or if none is prescribed, to the ministry or Crown agency for whom the improvement is made. Where the owner is a municipality, it goes “to the clerk of the municipality.” For a railway right-of-way, it goes to “the manager or any person apparently in charge of any office of the railway in Ontario.” (Construction Act, s. 34 (3), (3.1), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Preserving a lien and the time limits"

current_text: Perfecting a lien
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “A lien may not be perfected unless it is preserved.” “A lien that has been preserved expires unless it is perfected prior to the end of the 90-day period next following the last day, under section 31, on which the lien could have been preserved.” (Construction Act, s. 36 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Perfecting a lien"

current_text: Where the lien attaches to the premises, it is perfected “when the lien claimant commences an action to enforce the lien” and, unless an order vacating the registration is made, “registers a certificate of action in the prescribed form on the title of the premises”. Where it does not attach, it is perfected when the claimant “commences an action to enforce the lien.” A preserved lien can also be perfected by “sheltering” under another claimant's perfected lien, under the rules in the Act. (Construction Act, s. 36 (3), (4))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Perfecting a lien"

current_text: “A perfected lien expires immediately after the second anniversary of the commencement of the action that perfected the lien”, unless, on or before that anniversary, an order is made for the trial of an action in which the lien may be enforced, or such an action “is set down for trial.” (Construction Act, s. 37 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Perfecting a lien"

current_text: “The expiration of a lien under this Act shall not affect any other legal or equitable right or remedy otherwise available to the person whose lien has expired.” (Construction Act, s. 38)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Perfecting a lien"

current_text: Where lien actions are heard
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “A lien claim is enforceable in an action in the Superior Court of Justice.” Except where inconsistent with the Act and its prescribed procedures, “the Courts of Justice Act and the rules of court apply to actions under this Part.” (Construction Act, s. 50)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Where lien actions are heard"

current_text: After all statements of defence are delivered, or the time for delivering them has expired, a judge may, on motion, refer all or part of the action for trial to an associate judge, to a person agreed on by the parties, or, “if the action is for an amount that is within the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court”, to a deputy judge of that Court or to the Small Claims Court Administrative Judge. (Construction Act, s. 58 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Where lien actions are heard"

current_text: A reference to a person agreed on by the parties “shall not be made unless the persons entitled to notice under subsection (1.1) consent to the reference.” A person given notice who “does not oppose the motion or does not appear at the hearing of the motion shall be deemed to consent” to that reference. (Construction Act, s. 58 (1.1)-(1.3))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Where lien actions are heard"

current_text: Prompt payment
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: A “proper invoice” is “a written bill or other request for payment for services or materials in respect of an improvement under a contract” that contains information the Act lists, such as the contractor's name and address, the invoice date and a description of what was supplied, and, “subject to subsection 6.3 (2)”, meets any other requirements the contract specifies. (Construction Act, s. 6.1 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: “Proper invoices shall be given to an owner on a monthly basis, unless the contract provides otherwise.” A contract term that makes giving a proper invoice “conditional on the prior certification of a payment certifier or on the owner's prior approval is of no force or effect.” (Construction Act, s. 6.3 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: An invoice missing required information is treated as a proper invoice unless, “no later than seven days after receiving the invoice, the owner notifies the contractor in writing of the deficiency and of what is required to address it.” (Construction Act, s. 6.1 (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: Subject to a notice of non-payment, an owner “shall pay the amount payable under a proper invoice no later than 28 days after receiving the proper invoice from the contractor.” An owner who disputes an invoice may refuse to pay if, “no later than 14 days after receiving the proper invoice”, it gives a notice of non-payment, in the prescribed form and manner, “specifying the amount of the proper invoice that is not being paid and detailing all of the reasons for non-payment.” (Construction Act, s. 6.4 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: Any amount under the proper invoice that is not the subject of the owner's notice of non-payment is still to be paid within the 28 days. (Construction Act, s. 6.4 (3))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: A contractor who receives full payment of a proper invoice within those 28 days pays each subcontractor whose services or materials were in the invoice “no later than seven days after receiving payment”. If the owner pays only part, the contractor pays those subcontractors from the amount paid, within the same seven days. Both are subject to a notice of non-payment and, like every payment under this Part, “subject to any requirement to retain a holdback”. (Construction Act, ss. 6.2, 6.5 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: If the owner does not pay some or all of a proper invoice on time, the contractor pays those subcontractors “no later than 35 days after giving the proper invoice to the owner”, unless it gives a notice of non-payment. A notice given because the owner has not paid must include “an undertaking to refer the matter to adjudication under Part II.1 no later than 21 days after giving the notice to the subcontractor”. (Construction Act, s. 6.5 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: A contractor who disputes a subcontractor's entitlement may instead give a notice “specifying the amount that is not being paid and detailing all of the reasons for non-payment.” The contractor's notice is due no later than seven days after receiving the owner's notice of non-payment or, if the owner gave none, before the 35-day period expires. Similar rules apply between subcontractors. (Construction Act, ss. 6.5 (6), (7), 6.6)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Prompt payment"

current_text: Adjudication
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment

current_text: “Adjudication” means “construction dispute interim adjudication under this Part”. A party to a contract “may refer a dispute with the other party to the contract respecting any prescribed matter or any matter agreed to by the parties to adjudication.” The same applies to a subcontract. (Construction Act, ss. 13.1, 13.5 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: For a contract, adjudication “may not be commenced if the notice of adjudication is given more than 90 days after the date on which the contract is completed, abandoned or terminated, unless the parties to the adjudication agree otherwise.” For a subcontract, the 90 days run from the earliest of that date, “the date on which the subcontract is certified to be completed under section 33”, and “the date on which the subcontractor last supplies services or materials to the improvement.” (Construction Act, s. 13.5 (3), (3.1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: A dispute may be referred to adjudication “even if the dispute is the subject of a court action or of an arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1991, unless the action or arbitration has been finally determined.” An adjudication may only address a single dispute, unless the parties and the adjudicator agree otherwise. (Construction Act, s. 13.5 (4), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: Except as provided by the regulations, a written notice of adjudication includes the parties' names and addresses, “the nature and a brief description of the dispute, including details respecting how and when it arose”, “the nature of the redress sought”, “the name of a proposed adjudicator to conduct the adjudication”, and “the date, nature and substance of any previous adjudication in which the party was involved in respect of the contract or subcontract, including a copy of any determination made by the adjudicator.” (Construction Act, s. 13.7 (1))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: The adjudicator decides “no later than 30 days after receiving the documents required by section 13.11”. Before it expires, and after those documents are provided, that deadline may be extended on the adjudicator's request, with the parties' written consent, for “no more than 14 days”, or by the parties' written agreement, with the adjudicator's consent, “for the period specified in the agreement.” A determination made after the deadline “is of no force or effect.” (Construction Act, s. 13.13 (1), (2), (5))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: The determination “is binding on the parties to the adjudication until a determination of the matter by a court”, an arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1991, or a written agreement between the parties. A party required to pay “shall pay the amount no later than 15 days after the determination has been communicated to the parties to the adjudication”, subject to any requirement to retain a holdback. (Construction Act, ss. 13.15 (1), 13.19 (1), (2))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: Judicial review of a determination “may only be made with leave of the Divisional Court”, and the motion for leave is filed, with proof of service, “no later than 35 days after the determination is communicated to the parties.” The determination may only be set aside on the grounds the Act lists. An application for judicial review “does not operate as a stay of the operation of the determination unless the Divisional Court orders otherwise.” (Construction Act, s. 13.18 (1), (2), (5), (7))
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: Subject to section 13.17, the parties “shall bear their own costs of the adjudication.” Under section 13.17, if the adjudicator determines a party acted in a manner that is “frivolous, vexatious, an abuse of process or other than in good faith”, the adjudicator may require that party to pay some or all of the other party's costs, part of the adjudicator's fee the other party would otherwise pay, or both. (Construction Act, ss. 13.16, 13.17)
appears_in: Guides, Construction liens, holdbacks and prompt payment, "Adjudication"

current_text: A court case that is not an application. The civil rules say it includes cases started by a statement of claim, notice of action, counterclaim, crossclaim, or third or later party claim. The Courts of Justice Act list also includes a claim and a divorce petition or counterpetition.

current_text: In the family rules, a person's address covers their street or municipal address, mailing address, telephone number, fax number and email address.

current_text:
Support if family violence is part of your situation

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.
appears_in: Family intake and overview

current_text:
Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB)

This sounds like it may involve a landlord-tenant relationship — rent, eviction, repairs, or a residential lease. CourtSimplified does not cover matters that go to the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB). The LTB is a separate tribunal from Family, Small Claims, and Civil court. The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies to rental units in residential complexes despite any other Act, and gives the LTB exclusive jurisdiction to determine all applications under that Act.
appears_in: Home, when a story points outside the three court paths

current_text:
Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO)

This sounds like it may involve discrimination or a human rights issue — for example, based on a protected ground like disability, race, sex, or family status, or a request for accommodation. CourtSimplified does not cover matters that go to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO). The HRTO is a separate tribunal from Family, Small Claims, and Civil court. Under the Human Rights Code, a person who believes their rights under Part I of the Code have been infringed may apply to the Tribunal — generally within one year of the incident, or of the last incident in a series, though the Tribunal may accept a later application in some circumstances.

current_text:
Workplace Safety and Insurance Appeals Tribunal (WSIAT)

This sounds like it may involve a workplace injury or a workers' compensation claim. CourtSimplified does not cover matters that go through the Workplace Safety and Insurance Board (WSIB) or the Workplace Safety and Insurance Appeals Tribunal (WSIAT). WSIB and WSIAT are separate from Family, Small Claims, and Civil court. Under the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997, WSIAT has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and decide appeals from final decisions of the Board on entitlement to benefits under the insurance plan.
appears_in: Home, when a story points outside the three court paths

current_text:
Condominium Authority Tribunal (CAT)

This sounds like it may involve a dispute with a condominium corporation or board — for example, about condo rules, records, or by-laws. CourtSimplified does not cover matters that go to the Condominium Authority Tribunal (CAT). The CAT is a separate tribunal from Family, Small Claims, and Civil court. Under the Condominium Act, 1998 a corporation, an owner, a mortgagee and (where the regulations provide) a purchaser may apply to the Tribunal to resolve a PRESCRIBED dispute — the categories are set by regulation rather than open-ended. The Act also carves matters OUT of the Tribunal's reach, including disputes about a corporation's lien for unpaid common expenses and disputes involving the determination of title to real property, so not every condominium disagreement goes there.

Under the Insurance Act, where there is a dispute about an insured person's entitlement to statutory accident benefits, or the amount of those benefits, the insured person or the insurer may apply to the Licence Appeal Tribunal to resolve it.

This sounds like it may involve asking a court to review a decision made by a government body, tribunal, or official — a judicial review. CourtSimplified does not cover judicial review applications. The Act does allow an application to be made instead to a judge of the Superior Court of Justice, with that judge's leave, where the delay of proceeding in the Divisional Court is likely to involve a failure of justice.

current_text:
Money judgments

Small Claims Court can order one party to pay money to another, up to $50,000 (not counting interest and costs). See the education topic on the $50,000 limit for how that cap works.
appears_in: Readiness gate, remedy confirmation

current_text:
Return of personal property

Alongside money, Small Claims Court can order the return of specific personal property -- for example, an item someone is holding onto that belongs to someone else. This is generally only available for personal property (belongings, not land or buildings), and is part of the same $50,000 jurisdiction that applies to money claims.
appears_in: Readiness gate, remedy confirmation

current_text:
What Small Claims Court generally doesn't handle

Small Claims Court's jurisdiction is generally limited to two kinds of remedies: money, and the return of personal property, each up to $50,000. Under s. 23(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, the court has jurisdiction in actions for the payment of money and for the recovery of possession of personal property, up to the prescribed amount; under s. 96(3), only the Court of Appeal and the Superior Court of Justice, exclusive of the Small Claims Court, may grant equitable relief, unless otherwise provided. If what someone is looking for doesn't fit either of those -- for example, asking a court to order someone to do or stop doing something, rather than pay money or return an item -- that generally falls outside what Small Claims Court can order, and would typically need to go to a different court instead.
appears_in: Readiness gate, remedy confirmation

current_text:
Interest and costs

Interest and costs (such as court filing fees) are generally handled separately from, and in addition to, the amount claimed -- they don't count against the $50,000 limit. Whether interest or costs are awarded, and how much, depends on the specific case; this is general information that these can be part of an order, not a specific amount for any claim. Under s. 29 of the Courts of Justice Act, an award of costs in Small Claims Court, other than disbursements, shall not exceed 15 per cent of the amount claimed or the value of the property sought to be recovered, unless the court considers it necessary in the interests of justice to penalize a party or a party's representative for unreasonable behaviour in the proceeding. Costs can go either way: Ontario's page on suing in Small Claims Court says the judge might order the defendant to pay some of the costs if the plaintiff wins, and a plaintiff who loses might have to pay their own costs and some of the defendant's costs.
appears_in: Readiness gate, remedy confirmation

current_text:
Monetary Jurisdiction

Small Claims Court can only hear claims up to a set dollar limit. Claims for more than that must go to the Superior Court of Justice, unless the excess is waived.

Key facts:
- The claim limit is $50,000, excluding interest and costs.
- This limit increased from $35,000 effective October 1, 2025.
- The appeal threshold also rose, from $3,500 to $5,000: an appeal to the Divisional Court lies from a final order for the payment of money in excess of that amount, excluding costs (Courts of Justice Act, s. 31).
- Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim generally cannot be started more than two years after the day it was discovered (s. 4).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Confirm the claim amount fits Small Claims Court before starting a case.
- Use Evidence to support the dollar amount claimed.

Common risks:
- Filing in the wrong court for the amount claimed.
- Missing the two-year limitation period.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Filing a Claim

Starting a Small Claims Court case requires the correct form, served on the defendant within a fixed window.

Key facts:
- A claim is started with the Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A).
- An action is commenced by filing the Plaintiff's Claim with the clerk, together with a copy for each defendant — not required if it is filed electronically.
- Counter-claims use the Defendant's Claim (Form 10A). Form 1A is a continuation sheet, appended to a form when its first page has no room to list all the parties.
- The claim must be served on the defendant within six months after it is issued, but the court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has passed (r. 8.01(2)).
- Service of the claim is proved by an Affidavit of Service (Form 8A), or by a lawyer or paralegal's Certificate of Service (Form 8B) where that licensee served it, or caused it to be served, and is satisfied service was effected.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to locate and complete Form 7A.
- Use Evidence to organize proof of the amount and basis of the claim before filing.

Common risks:
- Letting the six-month service window lapse without asking the court to extend it.
- Serving the claim but never filing proof of how and when it was served.
- Using the wrong form for the type of claim.

current_text:
Responding to a Claim

A defendant has a short, fixed window to file a defence, with a specific form required.

Key facts:
- A defendant must serve and file a Defence (Form 9A) within 20 calendar days of being served with the claim.
- The defence is served on every other party and filed with proof of service — an Affidavit of Service (Form 8A), or a lawyer or paralegal's Certificate of Service (Form 8B).
- The Defence can be filed in person, or online: through the Ontario Courts Public Portal for Toronto-region cases (since October 14, 2025), and through the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal elsewhere.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to complete Form 9A before the deadline.
- Use Dashboard to track the 20-day response deadline.

Common risks:
- Missing the 20-day deadline.
- Filing the Defence without proof of service (Form 8A or 8B).
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
If a Defence Is Not Filed

Missing the defence deadline has a specific, serious procedural consequence.

Key facts:
- If no defence is filed in time, the plaintiff may ask the clerk to note the defendant in default.
- The plaintiff asks by filing a request to note the defendant in default, which may be made in Form 9B.
- The clerk also requires proof that the claim was served within the court's territorial division, except in the situation described next (r. 11.01(1)(b), (3)).
- If every defendant was served outside that territorial division, no defendant can be noted in default until an Affidavit for Jurisdiction (Form 11A) is filed with the clerk, or the point is proved before a judge.
- A defendant noted in default cannot file a defence or take further steps without the plaintiff's consent or the court's permission.
- For a debt or a fixed sum of money, the clerk may sign default judgment (Form 11B).
- The plaintiff may be entitled to a judgment without the defendant's participation.
- A defendant can bring a motion to set aside a default notation or judgment.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to flag cases at risk of default.
- Use Legal Strategy to organize the facts and documents a motion to set aside a default would involve (r. 11.06 lists what the court considers); a licensed paralegal or lawyer can assess it.

Common risks:
- Assuming a late defence will still be accepted without consequence.
- Asking to note a defendant in default without having filed proof that the claim was served.
- Not knowing that a motion is required to reverse a default.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Serving Documents

Different documents in a Small Claims case require different service methods and notice periods.

Key facts:
- Documents can be served personally, by mail, by courier, or by email where the Rules permit.
- A claim must be served within six months after it is issued, unless the court extends the time (r. 8.01(2)).
- Motions require at least 7 days' notice before the hearing.
- Examinations require at least 30 days' notice; witness summonses require at least 10 days' notice.
- Proof of service is filed using an Affidavit of Service (Form 8A), or a Certificate of Service (Form 8B) for licensees.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to track service deadlines for each document type.
- Use Evidence to preserve proof of how and when service occurred.

Common risks:
- Using a service method the Rules do not permit for a given document.
- Missing the notice period for a motion or examination.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Evidence and Witnesses for Trial

The court expects specific document deadlines and preparation before a settlement conference or trial.

Key facts:
- Types of evidence include oral testimony, documents such as business records and written estimates, expert reports, and photographs that the person who took them can properly identify.
- Documents not already attached to the claim or defence must be served and filed at least 14 days before a settlement conference.
- A document, written statement or audio or visual record served on all parties who were served with the notice of trial, at least 30 days before the trial date, will be received in evidence unless the trial judge orders otherwise (r. 18.02(1)).
- A List of Proposed Witnesses (Form 13A) must be served on every other party and filed with the court at least 14 days before the settlement conference (r. 13.03(2)).
- Service of a summons to witness, and the payment or tender of attendance money, may be proved by an Affidavit of Service (Form 8A) or a lawyer or paralegal's Certificate of Service (Form 8B).
- Parties should bring original documents plus at least three copies to trial.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Evidence to label and organize exhibits ahead of these deadlines.
- Use Trial Package to prepare document copies and the witness list.

Common risks:
- Serving documents or the witness list too close to the settlement conference or trial.
- Bringing only one copy of a document to trial.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Case Timeline

A Small Claims case moves through a defined sequence of stages, each with its own deadlines.

Key facts:
- The stages run: Claim, Default Proceedings (if applicable), Settlement Conference, Motions (if needed), Trial, and Enforcement.
- At or after the settlement conference, the clerk gives the parties a notice that one of them must request a trial date if the action is not disposed of within 30 days after the settlement conference, and pay the fee (r. 13.07). The clerk fixes a trial date when a party files a Request to Clerk (Form 9B) to fix a date for trial and pays the fee (r. 16.01(1)).
- Unless the court orders otherwise, the clerk dismisses an action for delay if, by the second anniversary of its start, it has not been disposed of by order and the plaintiff has neither taken a step under r. 11.03 to obtain judgment nor requested a trial date, subject to the exceptions in r. 11.1.01(2).
- A notice of motion and supporting affidavit (Form 15A) must be served at least 7 days before the hearing and filed, with proof of service, at least 3 days before it.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to see which stage a case is currently in.
- Use Court Package to prepare stage-appropriate materials.

Common risks:
- Skipping the settlement conference step by mistake.
- Letting two years pass from the start of the action without requesting a trial date (r. 11.1.01).
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Filing Fees

Filing a claim or taking further steps has fixed government fees, which vary by how often a party files.

Key facts:
- An infrequent claimant pays $108 to file a claim.
- A frequent claimant (one who has already filed 10 or more claims in the same Small Claims Court office in that calendar year) pays $228 to file a claim.
- Additional fees apply for judgments, trials, and motions.
- If you cannot afford the fees, you can ask the court to waive them. Applying costs nothing, and a fee waiver covers one case.
- You may qualify if, for example, your household's main income is Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program, or Old Age Security with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, or if your household's income and assets are under the limits Ontario sets (the income limit for one person is $33,100 a year before taxes).
- If you think you qualify, use the Fee Waiver Request to Registrar, Clerk or Sheriff (form FW-A-3). If you do not, but still cannot afford the fees, use the Fee Waiver Request to Court (form FW-A 4) and a judge will look at your finances.
- A fee waiver is not available to someone acting for a business, and it does not cover fees for serving documents, bailiff enforcement fees (except to enforce an order made under s. 31(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006), or costs a court orders you to pay the other side.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to budget for filing and later-stage fees.
- Apply for a fee waiver before you file: it does not refund fees already paid.

Common risks:
- Assuming filing is free.
- Not budgeting for motion or trial fees later in the case.
- Paying fees that could have been waived.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Starting a Claim

A civil claim above the Small Claims limit is started in the Superior Court of Justice with its own form, service window, and limitation period.

Key facts:
- A claim is started with a Statement of Claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for mortgage actions), or, where there is not enough time to prepare one, a Notice of Action (Form 14C), followed by a Statement of Claim (Form 14D) filed within 30 days after the notice of action is issued (r. 14.03).
- The claim must generally be served on each defendant within six months of being issued (r. 14.08).
- Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim generally cannot be started more than two years after the day it was discovered (s. 4).
- Service is proved by an Affidavit of Service (Form 16B) or, where a lawyer served the document or caused it to be served, a Lawyer's Certificate of Service (Form 16B.1) (r. 16.09).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to locate the Statement of Claim form.
- Use Dashboard to track the limitation period and service deadline.

Common risks:
- Missing the two-year limitation period.
- Letting the six-month service window lapse.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Defending a Claim

A defendant in a civil claim has a form-specific deadline that can be extended once, briefly.

Key facts:
- A Statement of Defence (Form 18A) must be delivered within 20 days after service of the statement of claim if the defendant was served in Ontario, 40 days if served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, or 60 days if served anywhere else (r. 18.01).
- A Notice of Intent to Defend (Form 18B), delivered within the time for the defence, gives an additional 10 days to deliver the Statement of Defence (r. 18.02).
- To deliver a document means to serve it and file it with proof of service (r. 1.03). Service may be proved by an Affidavit of Service (Form 16B); r. 16.09 also provides other forms of proof, such as a Lawyer's Certificate of Service (Form 16B.1) where a lawyer served the document.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to complete Form 18A or the Form 18B extension.
- Use Dashboard to track the Rule 18 deadline once it is confirmed for the specific case.

Common risks:
- Assuming the deadline is the same as Small Claims Court's 20 days — Rule 18.01 deadlines are 20, 40 or 60 days depending on where the defendant was served.
- Not filing a Notice of Intent to Defend when more time is needed.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Discovery

After pleadings close, both sides must exchange documents and may examine each other under oath, on a schedule.

Key facts:
- Where a party intends to obtain evidence under Rules 30 to 33 or 35, the parties must agree to a discovery plan before the earlier of 60 days after the close of pleadings (or a longer period they agree to) and attempting to obtain that evidence (r. 29.1.03).
- Each side exchanges an Affidavit of Documents (Form 30A or 30B).
- No party may exceed a total of seven hours of oral examination for discovery, regardless of the number of parties or other persons examined, except with the consent of the parties or leave of the court (r. 31.05.1(1)).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Evidence to prepare the Affidavit of Documents.
- Use Evidence to organize the documents and facts that examinations for discovery may cover.

Common risks:
- Missing the 60-day Discovery Plan deadline.
- Incomplete document disclosure in the Affidavit of Documents.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Mandatory Mediation

In some regions, mediation is a required step before trial, on a fixed timeline.

Key facts:
- Mandatory mediation applies to actions started in the City of Toronto, the City of Ottawa or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010, and to actions transferred there on or after January 1, 2014 unless the court orders otherwise, with listed exceptions (r. 24.1.04). The court may also exempt an action on a party's motion (r. 24.1.05).
- A mediation session must take place within 180 days after the first defence is filed, unless the court orders otherwise; for a transferred action, the court may instead set the date (r. 24.1.09(1), (2.1)). The session may be postponed to a later date if the parties consent to the date in writing and the consent is filed with the mediation co-ordinator (r. 24.1.09(3)).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Settlement Conference preparation tools if the case is in a mandatory mediation region.

Common risks:
- Not scheduling mediation within the 180-day window in a mandatory region.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Setting Down for Trial

A civil case must be actively moved toward trial or it can be dismissed for delay.

Key facts:
- Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must schedule a pre-trial conference with the registrar within 180 days after the action is set down for trial; if they do not, the registrar schedules one (r. 50.02).
- Unless the court orders otherwise, the registrar dismisses an action for delay if it has not been set down for trial or terminated by any means by the fifth anniversary of its start, subject to the exceptions in the rule (r. 48.14).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to track the five-year dismissal risk on older cases.
- Use Trial Package once the case is set down for trial.

Common risks:
- Letting a case sit without being set down for trial or settled.
- Missing the 180-day pre-trial conference window.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Forms

Superior Court civil cases use a distinct set of forms from Small Claims Court, organized under the Rules of Civil Procedure.

Key facts:
- Forms are catalogued under R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194 (Rules of Civil Procedure) and include pleadings, motion forms, and enforcement writs.
- Documents can be filed in hardcopy at the court counter, and in some cases by mail, email, or through online filing portals.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to locate the correct Rules of Civil Procedure form for each stage.

Common risks:
- Using a Small Claims Court form in a Superior Court civil case, or vice versa.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Serving Documents

Superior Court civil documents have their own service methods and their own ways of proving service.

Key facts:
- Service of a document may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).
- A lawyer may instead prove service by a Lawyer's Certificate of Service (Form 16B.1), where the lawyer served the document or caused it to be served and is satisfied service was effected.
- This is narrower than Small Claims Court: under the Rules of Civil Procedure a paralegal cannot certify service, and an affidavit of service is used instead.
- Where a lawyer admits or accepts service on a party's behalf, that written admission is itself sufficient proof and needs no other proof of service.
- Personal service by a sheriff may be proved by a Sheriff's Certificate of Service (Form 16C).
- The affidavit or certificate may be printed on the backsheet of the document served, or on a stamp or sticker affixed to it.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Evidence to preserve proof of how and when each document was served.
- Use Dashboard to track which documents still need proof of service filed.

Common risks:
- Assuming a paralegal's certificate of service is available in Superior Court as it is in Small Claims Court.
- Serving a document and never filing proof that it was served.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Starting a Case

Most family law cases begin with a required education session before the case proceeds.

Key facts:
- Attendance at a Mandatory Information Program (MIP) is required in most family cases, including claims about parenting, support, property and the matrimonial home, with exceptions such as cases proceeding on consent (r. 8.1(1)-(2)).
- Where the program applies, each party must attend it within 45 days after the case is started (r. 8.1(4)).
- Until a party's certificate of attendance is filed, that party may take no other step, except that a respondent may still serve and file an Answer and a party may make an appointment for a case conference (r. 8.1(7)).
- The party starting the case is the applicant; the party who receives it is the respondent.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Dashboard to confirm MIP attendance has been arranged before other steps proceed.

Common risks:
- Taking other steps before the MIP certificate of attendance is filed, apart from the exceptions in r. 8.1(7).
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Responding to an Application

A respondent has a fixed window to answer, and the applicant then has a further, shorter window to reply.

Key facts:
- An Answer (Form 10) must be served and filed within 30 days of being served with the application (60 days if the application is served outside Canada or the United States) (r. 10(1)-(2)).
- An Answer may include the respondent's own claim against the applicant, or against another person, who then also becomes a respondent (r. 10(3)).
- A party may serve and file a Reply (Form 10A) within 10 days after being served with an Answer, in response to a claim made in it (r. 10(6)).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to complete Form 10 or Form 10A.
- Use Dashboard to track the 30-day or 10-day response window.

Common risks:
- Missing the 30-day deadline to answer.
- Missing the 10-day window for a Reply to a claim made in an Answer.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Serving Documents

Family documents must be served, and in family court filing a document already means filing proof that it was served.

Key facts:
- In the Family Law Rules, to file a document means to file it with proof of service where service is required — so anywhere these steps say "serve and file", proof of service is part of filing.
- Service may be proved by an affidavit of service (Form 6B).
- A lawyer or paralegal may instead prove service by a Lawyer or Paralegal's Certificate of Service (Form 6C), where that licensee served the document or caused it to be served and is satisfied service was effected.
- Service may also be proved by the other person's written acceptance of service, by the return postcard for service by mail, by a document exchange date stamp, or by an electronic document exchange's record of service.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Evidence to preserve proof of how and when each document was served.
- Use Dashboard to track which documents still need proof of service filed.

Common risks:
- Reading "serve and file" as two steps and filing without the proof of service that filing requires.
- Assuming the Small Claims Court forms (8A, 8B) apply in a family case.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Conferences

A family case moves through a sequence of court conferences before any trial.

Key facts:
- In each case where an Answer is filed, a judge conducts at least one conference, subject to exceptions (r. 17(1)). The Family Law Rules name three kinds: the case conference, the settlement conference and the trial management conference (r. 17).
- On or before the first court date, the clerk confirms that all necessary documents have been served and filed (r. 39(5) for fast-track cases in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice; r. 40(4) in the Ontario Court of Justice).
- The Case Conference and Settlement Conference are opportunities to narrow or resolve disputed issues before trial.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Settlement Conference preparation tools ahead of each conference stage.
- Use Dashboard to see which conference stage the case has reached.

Common risks:
- Arriving at a conference without documents properly served or filed.
- Treating a Case Conference as optional.
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Motions

Bringing a family court motion has its own notice rules, including an emergency exception.

Key facts:
- Generally, no motion may be served or heard before a conference dealing with the substantive issues has been completed, unless the court finds urgency, hardship or another reason in the interest of justice, and some motions are excepted (r. 14(4), (4.2), (6)).
- A party making a motion with notice must serve the documents on all other parties at least six days before the motion date, file them at least four days before it, confer or try to confer with the other parties, give every other party a copy of the confirmation of motion (Form 14C), and then give it to the clerk by 2 p.m. three days before (r. 14(11)).
- A motion may be made without notice only in the situations listed in r. 14(12), such as an immediate danger to the health or safety of a child or of the party making the motion where the delay of serving notice would probably have serious consequences.
- An order made on a motion without notice must require the matter to come back to court within 14 days or on a date chosen by the court (r. 14(14)).

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Legal Strategy to organize the facts and documents for a motion; whether a motion fits a situation is a question for a licensed paralegal or lawyer.

Common risks:
- Bringing a motion without notice when none of the situations in r. 14(12) applies.
- Missing the return date set in an order made without notice.
- Not giving the clerk the confirmation of motion (Form 14C) on time: unless the court orders otherwise, the motion will not be heard (r. 14(11.1)).
appears_in: /legal-principles — a public page, live today

current_text:
Forms

Family Court uses its own set of forms under the Family Law Rules, distinct from civil or Small Claims forms.

Key facts:
- Forms are catalogued under the Family Law Rules, O. Reg. 114/99, including Application (Form 8), Answer (Form 10), and Financial Statement (Form 13 or 13.1).
- Since October 14, 2025, family documents filed online go through the Ontario Courts Public Portal for Toronto-region matters and Justice Services Online for matters outside Toronto; filing in person at the court counter remains available.

How CourtSimplified uses it:
- Use Forms to locate the correct Family Law Rules form for each stage.

Common risks:
- Using a civil or Small Claims form instead of the matching Family Law Rules form.

current_text: Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money or personal property of up to $50,000, not counting interest and costs. The two-year time limit counts from the day the claim was discovered, which is the earlier of two days. current_text: You can sue for money owed under an agreement, like an unpaid loan, or goods or services that were not paid for. You can also sue for harm done, like damage to property, an injury or a broken contract. Only the Landlord and Tenant Board can decide applications under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. For more than $50,000, you can go to the Superior Court of Justice, or waive the amount over $50,000 and file in Small Claims Court. A claim within that limit needs the Superior Court's leave to be started there.
