current_text: To have the debtor questioned, you file a Notice of Examination (Form 20H) and an Affidavit for Enforcement Request (Form 20P). Serve the notice personally, or by an alternative to personal service, at least 30 days before the hearing. Add a blank Financial Information Form (Form 20I) if the debtor is an individual. File proof of service at least three days before the hearing. To take pay or bank money owed to the debtor, you file a Notice of Garnishment (Form 20E) and Form 20P. Serve it on the garnishee with a blank Garnishee's Statement (Form 20F), then on the debtor with Form 20P within five days. The fees are $68 for a notice of examination or a writ of seizure and sale, and $144 for a notice of garnishment.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a default judgment — how do I actually get paid?"

current_text: The defendant can ask the court to set aside the judgment and any step taken to collect it, on terms that are just. The court must find a meritorious defence. It must also find a reasonable explanation for the default. And the motion must be made as soon as is reasonably possible.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a default judgment — how do I actually get paid?"

current_text: A defence has been filed, so a conference must be held to try to settle the case. This does not apply if the defence admits all of your claim and proposes terms of payment. The conference aims to settle or narrow the issues and to share the facts and evidence.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They filed a defence — what happens next?"

current_text: If the defence admits all or part of your claim and proposes terms of payment, you can dispute the terms. Within 20 days after the defence was served, you file a Request to Clerk (Form 9B) for a terms of payment hearing, and serve it on the defendant. At least 14 days before the conference, serve each other party with any document you will rely on at trial, such as an expert report, if not attached to your claim. File them in court. By the same date, serve and file a List of Proposed Witnesses (Form 13A), which also names others who know about the matters in dispute.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They filed a defence — what happens next?"

current_text:
The court holds the settlement conference within 90 days after the day the first defence was filed. This is the court's timetable, not a step you take. The clerk fixes the time, date and place and serves a notice of settlement conference on the parties. No conference is held if the defence admits all of the claim and proposes terms of payment.

Request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. You have 2 years, counted from the commencement of the action. This does not apply if the action was already decided by an order. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They filed a defence — what happens next?"

current_text: If you do not dispute a payment proposal in time, the defendant must pay as proposed, as if it were a court order. If the defendant then does not pay as proposed, you can serve a Notice of Default of Payment (Form 20L). Once 15 days have passed since you served it, you can file an Affidavit of Default of Payment (Form 20M), and the clerk signs judgment for the unpaid balance of the undisputed amount. If you do dispute the terms, the clerk fixes a time for a hearing and serves a notice of hearing on the parties. A party who got notice of the conference and does not attend may face costs or other sanctions, and another conference.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They filed a defence — what happens next?"

current_text: A defendant may make a claim against you, as the plaintiff, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A). With needed changes, the rules apply to it as if it were a plaintiff's claim. It is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They are suing me back — do I have to respond to that too?"

current_text: To dispute it, or to admit some or all of it and propose terms of payment, you can use a Defence (Form 9A). The fee for filing a defence is $77.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They are suing me back — do I have to respond to that too?"

current_text: If you want to dispute the defendant's claim, serve a defence (Form 9A) on every other party and file it, with proof of service, with the clerk. You have 20 days, counted from the day the defendant's claim was served.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They are suing me back — do I have to respond to that too?"

current_text: After the 20 days, the court office will still accept a defence if there has been no noting in default. A party noted in default cannot file a defence or take other steps without the court's leave or the other party's consent. The one exception is a motion to set aside the noting. If you are noted in default on it, judgment can be obtained against you only at trial or on motion. If the defendant's claim may unduly complicate or delay the trial, or cause undue prejudice, the court may order separate trials or a separate action.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They are suing me back — do I have to respond to that too?"

current_text: The clerk has set a time, date and place for the settlement conference. It aims to settle or narrow the issues, help you prepare for trial and share the facts and evidence. The judge at this conference will not be the trial judge. You must take part, unless the court orders otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: If you need someone's okay to settle, you must be able to reach them by phone during the conference. If you cannot attend on that date, you can ask the court to put it off to another date, and the court office can help. If it is not put off before that date, you or someone for you must still attend to ask, and the judge may fix costs against you. To ask to attend another way, serve on every other party and file a Request to Change Attendance Method (Form 1B), with your reasons and proof of service, at least 30 days before the conference. Other parties may object within seven days. The court may grant or reject the request, or choose another allowed method.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text:
Serve on every other party, and file with the court, your trial documents and a witness list (Form 13A). Do this at least 14 days before the date of the settlement conference. The documents are any you will rely on at the trial that are not attached to your claim or defence, including an expert report. The list names your proposed witnesses and other people who know about the matters in dispute.

Request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. You have 2 years, counted from the commencement of the action. This does not apply if the action was already decided by an order. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: If a party who got the notice does not come, the court may order costs or other sanctions. It may also order another conference if needed. It may also order costs against a person who comes but did not file the required papers. It can do the same if a person is so poorly prepared that the conference cannot do its job. At the end, the court writes down the issues still in dispute and the matters agreed on.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: At or after the settlement conference, the clerk gives the parties a notice. It says one of the parties must request a trial date and pay the fee if the action is not disposed of within 30 days. The judge who held the settlement conference will not preside at the trial.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The settlement conference did not settle it — how do I get a trial date?"

current_text: To get a trial date, you can file a Request to Clerk (Form 9B) asking the clerk to fix a date for trial. The fee to fix a date for trial is $308, or $403 for a frequent claimant. If the parties agree to settle, you can sign Terms of Settlement (Form 14D). File them, signed by all parties, to tell the court the action has settled.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The settlement conference did not settle it — how do I get a trial date?"

current_text: Request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. You have 2 years, counted from the commencement of the action. This does not apply if the action was already decided by an order. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The settlement conference did not settle it — how do I get a trial date?"

current_text: Once the request is filed and the fee paid, the clerk fixes a date for trial. The clerk serves a notice of trial by mail or email on each party who has filed a claim or defence. After the request, the court may, on its own, direct a trial management conference before a judge.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The settlement conference did not settle it — how do I get a trial date?"

current_text: The clerk has fixed a date for trial and served a notice of trial. At a trial, each party tells their own side of the case to a judge who makes a decision. A trial can be put off only by court order. If you have a very good reason for not attending, you can ask the court to put it off, and the court office can help.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a trial date — what do I need to do to get ready?"

current_text: You can serve documents and written statements on all parties who got the notice of trial, at least 30 days before trial. They are then received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise. Each must give the name, phone number and address for service of the witness or author, and for an expert, a summary of qualifications. The court can issue a Summons to Witness (Form 18A) for a fee, and you serve it personally at least 10 days before trial, with attendance money. If you summon the author of a served statement, serve a copy of the summons on every other party at the same time. If a witness you summon needs an interpreter, you must arrange for a qualified one to attend. This does not apply if the Ministry provides an English-French interpreter. If you miss either step, the other parties may ask to put off the trial, with costs.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a trial date — what do I need to do to get ready?"

current_text: If the trial is not put off before the date, you or someone for you must attend court that day to ask for this. If the defendant does not attend, the judge may go ahead without them, or strike out the defence and let you prove your claim. You would then prove only the amount of the claim, not liability. If you do not attend, the judge may go ahead, dismiss the action and let the defendant prove their own claim, if any, or make another just order. Usually the judge gives judgment right after both sides finish, but sometimes the decision comes later.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a trial date — what do I need to do to get ready?"

current_text: A judgment does not guarantee payment. It is up to you to enforce it. A writ or garnishment notice must be issued within 6 years of the order. After that, you need the court's leave. The law limits how much of a debtor's wages can be garnished.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I won but they are not paying — how do I collect?"

current_text: You can ask for a notice of examination [Form 20H] or garnishment [Form 20E], or a writ of seizure and sale [Form 20C or 20D]. Each is filed with an Affidavit for Enforcement Request [Form 20P]. Either notice needs a Certificate of Judgment [Form 20A] in another court's area where the debtor lives or does business. You file an issued writ at the enforcement office, which has its own fees and deposits. For an examination, you serve the notice at least 30 days before the hearing.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I won but they are not paying — how do I collect?"

current_text: A debtor who is a person also gets a blank Financial Information Form [Form 20I], and you use personal service or an alternative. You file proof at least 3 days before, and the court may order payments. For garnishment, you serve the garnishee the notice and a blank Garnishee's Statement [Form 20F]. Within 5 days, you serve the debtor the notice and your affidavit, and file proof of both. The garnishee pays the clerk what it owes the debtor, up to the notice amount, within 10 days of service, or of the debt coming due if later.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I won but they are not paying — how do I collect?"

current_text: The clerk has made an order dismissing the action for delay. Unless the court orders otherwise, the clerk does this if no order ends the action within two years of its start. It also applies only if you took no step under rule 11.03 to get judgment and asked for no trial date. It does not apply if an accepted offer to settle was filed, the defence admitted the claim and proposed payment, or you were under disability then.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The court dismissed my case for delay — can I do anything about it?"

current_text: You can make a motion before a judge to set aside the order. A motion is made with a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit [Form 15A]. The fee to file a notice of motion is $127. If all parties agree, you can instead file a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent [Form 11.2A] to put the case back on the list.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The court dismissed my case for delay — can I do anything about it?"

current_text: For a motion, you first get a hearing date from the clerk. At least 7 days before the hearing, you serve it on each party who filed a claim and each defendant not noted in default. You file it with proof of service at least 3 days before the hearing. On a consent request, the clerk makes the order if all parties signed and it says each got a copy and no affected party is under disability.
appears_in: Stage answer for "The court dismissed my case for delay — can I do anything about it?"

current_text: You have been served with a claim, and the 20 days to deliver a defence have not run out. A defence is your answer to the claim. If it relies on a document, a copy goes with each copy of the defence, or the defence says why it is not attached. The first day is not counted, and if the last day is a holiday, the time ends on the next day that is not one. If you ignore a claim, the plaintiff can get judgment with no further notice, as if there had been a trial.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"

current_text: To dispute the claim, you can serve a Defence [Form 9A] on every other party. You then file it, with an affidavit of service for each party served, at the court office named on the claim. The fee to file a defence is $77. If you agree you owe all or part of the claim, you can admit it in the defence and propose terms of payment. You can also file a Defendant's Claim [Form 10A] against the plaintiff, or against someone else about the same events or related to the claim.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"

current_text: Serve a defence on every other party and file it with the clerk, with proof of service. You have 20 days, counted from the day of being served with the claim. If the claim was left at your home with an adult and a copy mailed or couriered, service takes effect on the fifth day after the mailing or the courier's confirmed delivery. The same is true when a company cannot be found at its last address on record and is served by mail or courier to that address and to its directors. If the claim was sent by registered mail or courier and signed for, service takes effect on the date of the signature. The parties can lengthen the time by filing their consent, and the court can lengthen it.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"

current_text: If you dispute all or part of the claim, you attend a settlement conference. The plaintiff has 20 days after your defence is served to dispute a payment proposal by asking for a hearing. If you admit the whole claim and the plaintiff does not dispute your payment plan, no more steps are needed while you pay on time. If no defence is filed in time, the clerk may note you in default when the plaintiff files a request. A defendant's claim is due within 20 days after your defence is filed, or later with leave, before trial or default judgment.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"

current_text: More than 20 days have passed since you were served, and no defence has been filed. After 20 days, the plaintiff can have you noted in default. The court may lengthen any time set by the rules, on just terms, if you ask by a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit [Form 15A]. A time for serving or filing a document can also be lengthened by filing the consent of the parties.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed the 20 days — is it too late to defend myself?"

current_text: After the 20 days, you can still try to file a Defence [Form 9A]. It is accepted for filing as long as the plaintiff has not filed a request to note you in default. You serve the defence on every other party and file it with the clerk, with proof of service. The fee to file a defence is $77.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed the 20 days — is it too late to defend myself?"

current_text: If your defence disputes all or part of the claim, you attend a settlement conference. If the plaintiff files a request to note you in default, with the required proof of service, the clerk may note you in default. Once noted in default, you cannot take any step except a motion to set aside, without the court's permission or the plaintiff's consent. The plaintiff can then get default judgment without further notice to you.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed the 20 days — is it too late to defend myself?"

current_text: The clerk has noted you in default, and no judgment has been signed yet. While noted in default, the only step you can take is a motion to set it aside, unless the court permits or the plaintiff consents. The plaintiff can get default judgment without further notice to you. A default judgment, if one is signed, must still be served on you.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still fight this?"

current_text: You can make a motion to set aside the noting with a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit [Form 15A]. In your materials, you explain what your defence is and why you did not file it in time. Even if you were deemed served, the motion can show the claim never reached you, or reached you later. The fee to file a notice of motion is $127. If all parties agree, you can instead file a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent [Form 11.2A].
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still fight this?"

current_text: For a motion, you get a hearing date from the clerk, serve the motion at least 7 days before it, and file it with proof of service at least 3 days before. The court may set aside the noting on just terms if satisfied you have a meritorious defence and a reasonable explanation for the default. It must also find you moved as soon as is reasonably possible. If it is set aside, you will need to file a Defence [Form 9A].
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still fight this?"

current_text: A default judgment has been signed against you after no defence was filed. The clerk must serve it on you by mail or email. A plaintiff can start steps to enforce a judgment as soon as it is given. The court can set aside a default judgment and any steps taken to enforce it. The court may also stay enforcement of the judgment, for a time and on terms that are just.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and I never knew about the case — what can I do?"

current_text: You can ask by motion to set aside the judgment, using a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit [Form 15A]. In it, you explain what your defence is and why you did not file it in time. Even if you were deemed served, the motion can show the claim never reached you, or reached you later. The fee to file a notice of motion is $127. If all parties agree, you can file a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent [Form 11.2A] instead.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and I never knew about the case — what can I do?"

current_text: Bring a motion to set aside. The rule sets no fixed number of days: the motion must be made as soon as is reasonably possible in all the circumstances.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and I never knew about the case — what can I do?"

current_text: You get a hearing date from the clerk, serve all parties at least 7 days before it, and file the motion with proof of service at least 3 days before. The court may set the judgment aside on just terms if it finds a meritorious defence, a reasonable explanation for the default, and a motion made as soon as reasonably possible. A clerk's order can set aside only listed enforcement steps not yet done, and a copy is filed at each court where they were requested. If the judgment is set aside, you will need to file a Defence [Form 9A].
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and I never knew about the case — what can I do?"

current_text: A defence was filed, so a conference is held unless the defence admits the whole claim and proposes payment terms. It aims to narrow the issues, encourage settlement and help both sides get ready for trial. If you need someone's approval to settle, you must arrange phone access to them for the whole conference.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I filed my defence — what happens next?"

current_text: At least 14 days before the conference, you serve each other party and file any document for trial not attached to your defence. By then, you also serve and file a List of Proposed Witnesses [Form 13A], naming others who know about the dispute. The court may award costs against a person who attends without having filed this material. If you cannot attend on the date set, you can ask the court to adjourn it, and the court office can help. If it is not adjourned in time, you or someone for you must attend to ask, and the judge may consider costs against you.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I filed my defence — what happens next?"

current_text:
If you want to make a defendant's claim (Form 10A), it can be issued without the court's leave. You have 20 days, counted from the day the defence is filed. After that, it may be issued only with leave of the court, and only before trial or default judgment.

The court holds the settlement conference within 90 days after the day the first defence was filed. This is the court's timetable, not a step you take. The clerk fixes the time, date and place and serves a notice of settlement conference on the parties. No conference is held if the defence admits all of the claim and proposes terms of payment.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I filed my defence — what happens next?"

current_text: Each party takes part in the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. A party with notice who does not come may face costs or other penalties, and the court may order another conference. If you miss the first conference and a second one you had notice of, the court may strike out your defence or make another just order. At the end, the court writes a memo of the issues left and matters agreed for the trial judge, who will be a different judge. The clerk's notice says a party must ask for a trial date and pay the fee if the case is not resolved within 30 days after the conference.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I filed my defence — what happens next?"

current_text: You may make a claim against the plaintiff, called a defendant's claim, or against someone else if it arises from the same events or relates to the plaintiff's claim. A defendant's claim is tried at the same trial as the main case, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may order a separate trial or a separate action if your claim may unduly complicate or delay the trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party. If the case is about a debt, a defendant may also claim in the defence to set off a debt the plaintiff owes them. To dispute the plaintiff's claim, you must still serve and file a Defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served with it.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They owe me money too — can I sue them back in the same case?"

current_text: You can make your claim on a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) and give a copy to the court. Among other things, it must give the parties' full names, the nature and amount of the claim, and the court file number of the plaintiff's claim. It must also give the address where you believe each person you claim against may be served. If it is based on a document, a copy must be attached, or the claim must say why it is not. The fee for filing a defendant's claim is $108.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They owe me money too — can I sue them back in the same case?"

current_text: A defendant's claim (Form 10A) can be issued without the court's leave. You have 20 days, counted from the day the defence is filed. After that, it may be issued only with leave of the court, and only before trial or default judgment.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They owe me money too — can I sue them back in the same case?"

current_text: The clerk issues the defendant's claim and gives it the same court file number as the plaintiff's claim. You must serve it on each person you claim against, personally or by another way the rules allow, within six months after it is issued. The court may extend that time, even after the six months end. To dispute it, a person has 20 days after service to serve a Defence (Form 9A) on every other party and file it with the clerk, with proof of service.
appears_in: Stage answer for "They owe me money too — can I sue them back in the same case?"

current_text: The clerk has set the date and served a notice on the parties, with a List of Proposed Witnesses (Form 13A). The goal is to narrow the issues, help settle the case, and help the parties get ready for trial. It is also meant to give full disclosure between the parties of the relevant facts and evidence.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: You and your representative, if any, must take part, unless the court orders otherwise. If you need someone's approval to settle, you must set up a way to reach them by phone for the whole conference, even after business hours. Set this up before the day. On the day, the parties must talk openly and frankly about the issues.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: Serve on every other party, and file with the court, your trial documents and a witness list (Form 13A). Do this at least 14 days before the date of the settlement conference. The documents are any you will rely on at the trial that are not attached to your claim or defence, including an expert report. The list names your proposed witnesses and other people who know about the matters in dispute.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: If a party does not come, the court may order costs or other sanctions, and set another conference if needed. It may also order costs if a person comes but did not file what was required, or is too unprepared for the meeting to work. If you miss a first conference and then a second one you had notice of, the court may strike out your defence, dismiss your defendant's claim, if any, and let the plaintiff prove their claim. Or it may make some other order that is just.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I have a settlement conference date — what do I have to send in, and when?"

current_text: A settlement conference was held, a party asked for a trial date, and the clerk set the date. Before the trial, the court may also call a trial management conference with a judge. If so, you and your representative, if any, must take part, unless the court directs otherwise. If you get notice of it and do not attend, the court may order costs or other sanctions. A trial can be put off to a later date only by order of the court.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a trial date — how do I get ready to defend myself?"

current_text: At least 30 days before trial, you can serve documents, statements, and audio or visual records on all parties who got the notice of trial. They are then received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise, but a statement only counts for what its writer could say in court. With each one, give the writer's name, phone number and address for service, and a summary of an expert's qualifications. You can summon a witness in Ontario, such as the writer of a statement served on you, with a Summons to Witness (Form 18A). If you summon such a writer, you must serve a copy of the summons on every other party at the same time.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a trial date — how do I get ready to defend myself?"

current_text: The clerk issues a summons for a fee of $33. You must serve it personally, with attendance money, at least 10 days before trial. If the plaintiff attends and you do not, the judge may go ahead without you, or make another order that is just. The judge may instead strike out your defence, dismiss your defendant's claim, if any, and let the plaintiff prove their claim. In that case, the plaintiff must prove the amount but not that you are liable, and the judge must decide any place of trial issue in your defence.
appears_in: Stage answer for "There is a trial date — how do I get ready to defend myself?"

current_text: If you must pay money, you are the debtor, and the creditor can enforce right away. This can be by garnishment, or a writ of seizure and sale of your goods or land. Serving and filing a notice of appeal puts the money parts on hold until the appeal ends, unless an appeal judge lifts it. If you do not pay, the creditor can have a Notice of Examination (Form 20H) issued to you. If you are served and do not go, the court may order you to a contempt hearing.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I lost — what happens now, and what if I cannot pay?"

current_text: If you cannot pay in full, you can contact the creditor to set up payments. On a motion (Form 15A), the court may pause enforcement on just terms, or change when and how much you pay if things change. With more than one such judgment, you can ask the court where you live for a consolidation order. When it is all paid, you can both sign and file a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent (Form 11.2A). If the creditor will not sign, you can bring a motion.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I lost — what happens now, and what if I cannot pay?"

current_text:
If you want to ask for a new trial, bring a motion for a new trial. You have 30 days, counted from the day the final order was made. The court can grant one only for a purely arithmetical error in the amount of damages, or for relevant evidence that was not available at the trial and could not reasonably have been expected to be.

If you want to appeal to the Divisional Court, serve a notice of appeal (Form 61A.3) with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days, counted from the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after serving it, and file the certificate with it. An appeal lies only from an order for the payment of more than $5,000, not counting costs, or for the recovery of personal property worth more than $5,000.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I lost — what happens now, and what if I cannot pay?"

current_text: A new trial motion also needs proof, served and filed, that you asked for a transcript of the reasons and key parts. An individual served with Form 20H must serve a Financial Information Form (Form 20I) on the creditor. Do not file it, but give the judge a copy, bring papers to back it up, and be ready to answer questions. After the examination, or if you file your consent, the court may order how you pay. While that order stands, creditors named in it can only use a writ of seizure and sale of land.

current_text: A party who got a notice of settlement conference did not attend it. Each party must take part, with their representative if any, unless the court orders otherwise.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my settlement conference — what happens to me now?"

current_text: If the court orders another conference, the clerk sets the time and place and sends a notice. At least 14 days before it, each party must serve and file any paper for trial, such as an expert report, not attached to their claim or defence. By then, each party must also serve and file a List of Proposed Witnesses (Form 13A), which also names others who know about the matters in dispute. The court may order costs against a person who comes without filing these.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my settlement conference — what happens to me now?"

current_text: If a party misses a conference, the court may order costs or other sanctions, and another conference if needed. If a defendant misses the first one, gets notice of a second one, and misses that too, the court may strike out the defence, dismiss the defendant's claim, if any, and let the plaintiff prove their claim. Or it may make some other order that is just. The judge at the second conference may order judgment this way.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my settlement conference — what happens to me now?"

current_text: If all the parties are absent, the trial judge may strike the action off the trial list. If one party is absent, the judge may go ahead without them, or make another order that is just. The judge may strike out an absent defendant's defence and any claim of theirs, and must rule on any place of trial issue it raises. The judge may dismiss an absent plaintiff's action and let the defendant prove any claim of their own. In those two cases, the party with the claim must prove its amount, but not that the absent party is liable.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my trial date — is my case over?"

current_text: A party who missed the trial can ask the court, by motion, to set aside or change a judgment made against them. The motion uses a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit (Form 15A), and the clerk gives a hearing date. It must be served on all parties at least seven days before the hearing, and filed, with proof of service, at least three days before. The fee to file a notice of motion served on another party is $127.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my trial date — is my case over?"

current_text: Ask the court, by making a motion, to set aside or change a judgment made when you did not attend. You have 30 days, counted from the day you became aware of the judgment. A party may instead make a motion to extend the 30 days, and the court may extend them if satisfied that special circumstances justify it.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my trial date — is my case over?"

current_text: Another party can reply with an Affidavit (Form 15B), served on each party who filed a claim or defence. It must be filed, with an affidavit of service for each party served, at least 2 days before the hearing. At the hearing, the court may set aside or vary the judgment, on terms that are just.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I missed my trial date — is my case over?"

current_text: A case must be started where the problem arose or where a defendant lives or does business, or at the court nearest that home or business. The court hears only claims for money, not counting interest and costs, or to get back personal property, up to a set amount. The limit is $50,000, and a larger claim goes to the Superior Court of Justice, unless the claimant gives up the amount over $50,000. A claim may not be split into two or more actions to bring it within the court's limit. A claim within that limit cannot be started in the Superior Court of Justice without that court's leave.

current_text: A defendant who disputes the claim must still serve and file a Defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served. The defence can raise the place of trial. The court may also move a trial to another place, but only if the balance of convenience substantially favours it. A party can ask for this by motion, using a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit (Form 15A). The fee to file a notice of motion served on another party is $127.
appears_in: Stage answer for "I think the case is in the wrong court or the wrong city — does that matter?"

current_text: At a settlement conference, trial management conference or trial, a judge may find the case was started in the wrong place. If so, the court may order it tried in any other place where it could have been started. A judge at a settlement conference may also make an order changing the place of trial. Under the Courts of Justice Act, a case brought before the wrong court may be moved to the proper court and go on there.
